0.title: The Fear of the LORD Is the Beginning of Wisdom
0.overview:
Proverbs is the Bible's most practical book — and its most misread. It is habitually approached as a collection of timeless life-tips, a biblical self-help manual for the successful and the prudent. But Proverbs is not primarily about success; it is about wisdom. And wisdom in Proverbs is not a technique or a set of principles. It is a person. "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom" (9:10) — wisdom begins in a relationship, in the right posture before the living God, and every practical instruction in the book flows from that foundation. Timothy Keller puts it well: the wisdom Proverbs offers is not a ladder you climb to a better life, but a reorientation of the whole person — mind, heart, will, and desire — toward the God who made you and the world he made you for.

The book is not a random anthology. It has a deliberate architecture. Chapters 1–9 are not proverbs at all but extended wisdom poems — a father's passionate, sustained appeal to his son to choose the path of wisdom over the path of folly. Lady Wisdom calls from the highest point of the city; Lady Folly calls from her doorway. Both are inviting; both promise life. Only one delivers. These nine chapters are the theological and moral foundation for everything that follows. They establish what wisdom is (the fear of the LORD, 1:7), who wisdom is (a figure present at creation, 8:22–31), and what is at stake (life and death, 8:35–36).

Chapters 10–31 are the proverbs proper — individual observations, comparisons, and commands drawn from every domain of human life: work and laziness, wealth and poverty, speech and silence, marriage and family, friendship and conflict, pride and humility, justice and oppression. The collections are not random: 10:1–22:16 are the proverbs of Solomon; 22:17–24:34 are the words of the wise; 25–29 are Solomonic proverbs compiled by Hezekiah's scribes; chapter 30 contains the words of Agur; and chapter 31 closes with the words of King Lemuel and the famous portrait of the excellent wife — who is, in the book's final irony, the embodiment of Lady Wisdom herself.

The christological dimension of Proverbs is signalled in chapter 8, where Wisdom speaks of herself as present with God before creation, as the craftsman beside him, as his delight (8:22–31). The New Testament identifies this Wisdom with Jesus Christ: "Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God" (1 Cor 1:24); "in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Col 2:3); "who became to us wisdom from God" (1 Cor 1:30). When Proverbs calls you to pursue wisdom at all costs — "Get wisdom; whatever you get, get insight" (4:7) — it is, in the fullest biblical sense, calling you to pursue Christ. Every failure of human wisdom that Proverbs exposes is implicitly pointing to the one who is Wisdom incarnate, the one who lived the perfectly wise human life, and the one who gives wisdom generously to all who ask (Jas 1:5).

This commentary follows the approach of Timothy Keller, whose work on Proverbs insists that wisdom is not moralism. The fool in Proverbs is not simply the immoral person; the fool is the person who lives as if God does not exist — who makes decisions about money, relationships, speech, and ambition without reference to the Creator. And the wise person is not simply the prudent, disciplined achiever; the wise person is the one whose whole life is ordered around the fear of the LORD, whose practical decisions flow from a heart reoriented by grace. The path from folly to wisdom is not self-improvement; it is the path that leads, ultimately, to Christ.

1.title: Proverbs 1 — The Beginning of Wisdom and Wisdom's Street Sermon

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Book's Purpose: Wisdom from Father to Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prologue of Proverbs identifies its author (Solomon, son of David, king of Israel), its purpose (wisdom, instruction, understanding, righteous living, prudence for the simple, knowledge for the young), and its foundational motto: 'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.' Before a single proverb is given, the book declares its governing principle. Everything that follows is commentary on what it means to fear the LORD and live accordingly.
verseByVerse.theology: The fear of the LORD (yir'at YHWH) is not merely the first lesson of Proverbs but its organizing center. Waltke describes it as 'the religious response of awe, reverence, trust, and obedience to the living God who reveals himself through his word.' It is simultaneously intellectual (a right understanding of who God is), emotional (awe and reverence), volitional (obedience and trust), and relational (a living orientation toward a personal God). The 'beginning' (reshit) means both starting point and foundation: wisdom does not merely begin with fear of the LORD; it rests on it at every level.
verseByVerse.examples: The seven purposes of Proverbs (vv. 2–6) move from the most basic (wisdom, instruction) to the most sophisticated (understanding a proverb and its interpretation). The book is designed for multiple audiences: the simple who need prudence, the young who need knowledge, and even the wise who can always go deeper. Kidner: 'Proverbs does not invite the expert to look elsewhere; it invites the expert to go further in.'

verseByVerse.quote: The proverbs of Solomon, son of David, king of Israel: To know wisdom and instruction, to understand words of insight, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the book gives a single piece of advice it tells you who is speaking and what he is for. The proverbs of Solomon, son of David, king of Israel — and every word of that is load-bearing. This is not a philosopher offering observations about life. It is a king, in the covenant line, whose wisdom was not achieved but asked for and given: a young man who could have prayed for long life or riches and prayed instead for an understanding mind to govern a people too numerous to count (1 Kings 3:5-12). Proverbs comes to us from a man who knew he did not have what he needed.

Then the purpose clause begins, and it runs on for five verses without stopping. To know wisdom and instruction, to understand words of insight. Two of those words need unpacking. Wisdom in this book is not cleverness; the Hebrew hokmah is used elsewhere of a craftsman who knows how to work metal (Exodus 31:3) — skill, the ability to handle real material without ruining it. Instruction is musar, and it is a harder word than it looks: it means teaching, and it also means the correction that makes the teaching stick. There is no version of musar that leaves a man comfortable.

So the opening sentence has already ruled something out. A person can finish this book knowing all of it and having gained nothing, because the aim named here is not information but competence in living — and competence is only ever acquired the way a trade is, by being corrected while you are doing it badly.

verseByVerse.quote: to receive instruction in wise dealing, in righteousness, justice, and equity; to give prudence to the simple, knowledge and discretion to the youth— (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The purposes keep coming, and now they get specific. Wise dealing renders a word about skilful handling — the same root used of a servant who succeeds at what he is given to do. Then three nouns that between them cover the whole moral field: righteousness (being straight yourself), justice (giving others their due), and equity (judging without a thumb on the scale). Proverbs will not let personal piety and public fairness come apart. A man who is upright at home and crooked in the market has not got two out of three.

Then the audience, and both words have been misread. The simple is peti, and he is not stupid. He is open — the man whose door has no lock. He believes what he is told, he has not yet been lied to by anyone who mattered, and he is therefore available to whoever gets to him first. Proverbs is not sneering at him. It is trying to get to him first.

And the youth is na‘ar, a young man at the age when the shape of a life is being decided by choices that feel small. Which is the sober thing about this verse. Nobody is formed by a decision they recognised as formative. The friends you fall in with at nineteen, the habit you start because everyone does, the thing you laughed at rather than object to — those are the hinges, and Proverbs is written because the young man is standing at one right now and does not know it.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the wise hear and increase in learning, and the one who understands obtain guidance, to understand a proverb and a saying, the words of the wise and their riddles. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here the book turns and speaks over the young man’s head to somebody else in the room. Let the wise hear and increase in learning. The person who has arrived is told to keep going, and that single sentence saves Proverbs from being a manual for beginners. Wisdom is a direction, not an address.

The word rendered guidance is a picture. Hebrew tahbulot comes from the world of ships — the ropes and steering-gear a pilot works to keep a vessel on course in weather. What the wise man obtains is not a map of the sea. It is the ability to steer in it, which is a different thing entirely and cannot be got by reading.

Then a promise about the sayings themselves: they are given so the reader may understand a proverb and a saying, the words of the wise and their riddles. Proverbs expects to be worked at. Its lines are compressed on purpose, and the compression is a teaching method — a saying you had to chew stays with you in a way an explanation never does. Kidner puts it exactly: the book does not invite the expert to look elsewhere, it invites the expert to go further in.

There is a test in this for anyone who has been a Christian a long while. When did you last learn something that changed how you actually behave — not a fact about the Bible, but a correction you took? If the honest answer is that you cannot remember, v. 5 is describing somebody else, and the danger is not that you know too little. It is that you have stopped being a learner while continuing to be a reader.

verseByVerse.quote: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge; fools despise wisdom and instruction. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the sentence the whole book is built on, and it is placed here like a foundation stone: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge. Everything after it — every line about money, speech, marriage, work, laziness and friendship — is an application of this one verse.

So it matters enormously that fear is understood rightly, because two wrong readings between them have ruined the verse. It is not terror. A child who is frightened of his father hides from him, and this book is written by a father whose son is invited to come close. But it is not merely respect either, which is where most modern readers land, and that reading is too small. Respect is what you give a man you could, at a pinch, disagree with.

The fear of the LORD is what happens when a creature grasps that God is real, present, and not answerable to him. It is the state of a man who has stopped auditioning for the position of judge in his own life. Isaiah, who saw more of God than most, did not report feeling respectful; he said woe is me, for I am lost (Isaiah 6:5) — and it was that man, undone, who was then sent and used.

The word for beginning is reshit, and it is also the word for firstfruits: the first and best part of a harvest, given to God before anything else is touched. So the verse is not saying that fearing God is the introductory module and wisdom is the degree. It is saying that fearing God is the best part of knowing anything, and the part everything else is built on.

Which explains the second line, and the second line is where most readers get uncomfortable. Fools despise wisdom and instruction. The fool of Proverbs is not a man of low intelligence — the book never once says he is stupid. He is a man who has decided that the question of God is not going to be allowed to affect his decisions. He may be brilliant. He is not teachable, and those are separate faculties.

And here is where the New Testament picks the verse up and carries it somewhere Solomon could not. Paul says that Christ crucified is the power of God and the wisdom of God, and that he became to us wisdom from God (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30). The beginning of knowledge is the fear of the LORD; the sum of it is a person. In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3) — not a syllabus, not a system, but a man who can be known, who took the fool’s verdict on himself and was despised in the place of everyone who ever despised instruction.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–19 — The Father's First Lesson: Avoiding the Path of Violence
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The father's first extended lesson warns his son against the most immediate threat to a young man entering the world: the enticement of violent company. Gang life is depicted with remarkable accuracy—the promises of easy wealth, the camaraderie, the excitement. The father's counter is not merely moral prohibition but a piercing analysis of the self-defeating nature of the violent path: they lay an ambush for themselves.
verseByVerse.theology: The parental authority invoked throughout Proverbs 1–9 is not merely cultural custom but theological design. The father mediates covenant wisdom to the son, who is simultaneously the natural child, the student of wisdom, and (by extension) every reader. 'My son' creates a relationship of intimacy and urgency: the instruction is personal, not merely informational. The mother's teaching (v. 8) is given equal standing—wisdom is not gendered but is transmitted through both parents.
verseByVerse.examples: The warning against violent companions anticipates the book's deepest concern: the company we keep shapes the people we become. Proverbs returns to this theme repeatedly (13:20; 22:24–25; 24:1–2). The choice of companions is among the most consequential choices a young person makes—more than most realize at the time. Waltke: 'The young person who thinks they can maintain their character in corrupt company is naive about the power of social influence.'

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, my son, your father's instruction, and forsake not your mother's teaching, for they are a graceful garland for your head and pendants for your neck. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the voice changes. Up to this point the book has been describing itself; from here it speaks, and the first word it says is my son. That address will recur throughout these nine chapters, and it sets the temperature of everything that follows. This is not a lecture. It is a father with limited time and one child in front of him.

Two commands, and they are not the same command twice. Hear your father’s instruction — take it in. Forsake not your mother’s teaching — keep hold of it. Most of us fail at the second, not the first. The thing we were taught was received at the time and then quietly put down somewhere in our twenties.

Notice also that the mother’s teaching stands beside the father’s with equal weight, and that this is the ordinary assumption of the book rather than a concession in it. In a world where formal instruction was a male business, Proverbs takes it for granted that half of what a young man knows he will have learned from a woman, and requires him to keep it.

Then the reason, and it is not the reason a modern parent would give. Not because I said so, and not because it will keep you out of trouble, but because these things are a graceful garland for your head and pendants for your neck. A garland was what you wore at a wedding; a pendant was worn where everyone could see it. The father’s argument is that obedience is attractive, and that a well-formed life is a good-looking thing.

Say that plainly, because Christian instruction is so often defended as safe rather than beautiful. The father here is not offering his son protection from life. He is offering him a way of being alive that other people will want to look at.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent. If they say, "Come with us, let us lie in wait for blood; let us ambush the innocent without reason; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent. The whole of the next ten verses hangs on that if, and the father does not pretend it is unlikely. He knows the invitation is coming, he knows it will be attractive, and he says so before it arrives — which is the single most useful thing a parent can do.

In Hebrew the refusal is one short word. There is no reasoning attached to it, and that is deliberate. The father does not tell his son to weigh the offer carefully. He tells him to say no, because the decisive moment in this kind of temptation is almost never the moment of decision; by the time you are considering it, most of the work has already been done on you.

Then he lets the enticers speak for themselves, and the first word out of their mouths is the one that does the damage. Come with us. Not here is money. Not here is excitement. Come with us — the offer of belonging, made to a young man at exactly the age when belonging is the loudest hunger he has.

That is the mechanism, and it has not changed in three thousand years. Almost nobody is recruited into a bad life by the badness of it. They are recruited by a group that seemed glad they had arrived. Ask why a young man joined, and the honest answer is rarely that he wanted to hurt anybody; it is that on a particular evening these were the people who had a place for him.

And the father tells us what the place actually is: let us lie in wait for blood; let us ambush the innocent without reason. Without reason. The victim has done nothing. He is simply the man who has what they want, and the warmth of the invitation and the coldness of the plan are in the same sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: like Sheol let us swallow them alive, and whole, like those who go down to the pit; we shall find all precious goods, we shall fill our houses with plunder; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Listen to how the gang talks about itself. Like Sheol let us swallow them alive, and whole, like those who go down to the pit. Sheol is the grave, the place of the dead, and it is Hebrew’s image for the appetite that is never satisfied. These men are not describing a robbery. They are comparing themselves to death.

That is the grandiosity of evil, and it should be recognised because it is always part of the recruitment. Wickedness never advertises itself as small, shabby and likely to end badly. It presents itself as large — unstoppable, inevitable, a force. The young man is not being offered a crime. He is being offered a way of feeling enormous.

Then, immediately, the economics: we shall find all precious goods, we shall fill our houses with plunder. Notice that the father does not weaken the argument in order to answer it. He lets them make their best case, and their best case is a good one — this works, there is money in it, and the houses really do get filled.

Any parent, preacher or friend who wants to be useful should mark that. The father does not tell his son that sin is unrewarding. He tells him where the reward ends up, which is a different and far more honest argument, and he saves it for v. 19. Pretending that the wrong road has no pleasures is the surest way to be disbelieved by somebody who can see that it does.

verseByVerse.quote: throw in your lot among us; we will all have one purse"— my son, do not walk in the way with them; hold back your foot from their paths, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The offer reaches its climax and it is, of all things, a pension scheme. Throw in your lot among us; we will all have one purse. One purse — shared risk, shared reward, nobody left short. It is the language of a family, used by men who have just finished describing an ambush.

This is why the passage is not really about crime. Strip out the violence and the sales pitch is one a decent young man hears constantly: these people will look after you, you will be inside something, you will not have to face things alone. The counterfeit is effective precisely because the thing it counterfeits is good. Men are made for a common purse. The question is whose.

The father’s answer is not an argument, and that is the striking thing. He does not say do not agree with them or do not admire them. He says do not walk in the way with them; hold back your foot from their paths. The issue is geography, not opinion.

He knows something about how people change that we usually get backwards. We imagine a man decides what he believes and then chooses his company to match. In fact he chooses his company and his beliefs follow it, slowly, and he will experience the change as having thought his way there. Whoever you are walking beside next year is very largely who you will be next year, which is why Proverbs keeps returning to it (13:20; 22:24-25).

Hence the strange concreteness of hold back your foot. Not your heart, not your mind. Your foot. The father is asking for a decision that can be taken on a Tuesday evening, about where the body goes.

verseByVerse.quote: for their feet run to evil, and they make haste to shed blood. For in vain is a net spread in the sight of any bird, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the father gives his verdict on the men who made the offer, and it turns on speed. Their feet run to evil, and they make haste to shed blood. They are not walking. Haste is a mark of folly all through this book, because hurry is what removes the gap in which a man might think again — and every one of these invitations depends on being accepted quickly.

Then a proverb dropped in like a stone: in vain is a net spread in the sight of any bird. The picture is a fowler laying his net in the open while the birds watch him do it. No bird is fool enough to fly into that. Even a creature with no capacity for reflection has enough sense not to walk into a trap it has seen being set.

And that is the sting, because in the next verse these men will do exactly what the bird refuses to do. The comparison is not flattering and it is not meant to be. Kidner catches the irony well: the very eagerness of evil is part of its self-defeat — speed that outstrips judgment is speed toward the cliff.

There is a practical use for this. When something must be decided tonight, when the offer expires if you think about it, when the person pressing you cannot say why the hurry — that pressure is itself information. Wisdom has never yet been damaged by a week’s delay, and almost every ruinous decision a person makes was made faster than it needed to be.

verseByVerse.quote: but these men lie in wait for their own blood; they set an ambush for their own lives. Such are the ways of everyone who is greedy for unjust gain; it takes away the life of its possessors. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the reversal the whole speech has been building toward, and it lands in one line: these men lie in wait for their own blood; they set an ambush for their own lives. Word for word it is what they said in v. 11 about somebody else. The trap is the same trap. Only the occupant has changed.

This is the structural claim of the book of Proverbs, and it needs stating clearly because it governs everything that follows. Folly is not punished from outside as an afterthought. Folly is self-consuming. God has not bolted penalties onto a neutral world to discourage sin; he has made a world in which certain ways of living destroy the person who lives them, the way a fire destroys the house it is warming.

Then the summary, and it widens the target considerably. Such are the ways of everyone who is greedy for unjust gain. Everyone. The Hebrew word behind unjust gain is betsa‘, and it means profit got by cutting — gain that takes a slice out of somebody. A man does not need a knife to qualify. He needs only an arrangement in which his increase is somebody else’s loss and he has decided not to look too closely at whose.

And the last clause is the one to carry away: it takes away the life of its possessors. The gain does not merely fail to satisfy. It feeds on the man who owns it. Jesus said the same thing in five words, and about the same trade: all who take the sword will perish by the sword (Matthew 26:52).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–33 — Wisdom's Street Sermon: The Cost of Rejection
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Lady Wisdom appears for the first time—not in a private classroom but in the public square, at the busiest intersection, crying aloud to all who pass. Her sermon is a prophetic rebuke followed by a conditional promise: turn at my reproof and I will pour out my spirit; refuse and I will not answer when calamity comes. The section is the most urgent passage in Proverbs 1–9: wisdom is available, free, and publicly offered—but it will not always be available.
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom is personified as a woman throughout Proverbs 1–9, reaching its climax in chapter 8 where she is present at creation. This personification is not merely literary but theological: wisdom is not an abstract principle but a relational offer from God himself. To reject Wisdom is to reject God; to receive Wisdom is to receive God's own self-revelation. Waltke identifies Wisdom as a hypostasis of the divine attribute—God's wisdom made accessible and personal.
verseByVerse.examples: The tone of vv. 26–28 is shocking by any standard: Wisdom laughs at calamity, mocks at panic. This is not cruelty but the consequence of rejected love: when every appeal has been refused and judgment arrives, there is nothing left to offer. The passage anticipates the parable of the ten virgins (Matt 25:1–13): 'Lord, Lord, open to us'—and the door is shut. The urgency of the invitation is matched by the finality of its deadline.

verseByVerse.quote: Wisdom cries aloud in the street, in the markets she raises her voice; at the head of the noisy streets she cries out; at the entrance of the city gates she speaks: (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scene changes completely. The father stops speaking, and a woman starts — Wisdom herself, and she is not in a classroom. Wisdom cries aloud in the street, in the markets she raises her voice; at the head of the noisy streets she cries out; at the entrance of the city gates she speaks.

Look at where she has gone. The street, the market, the busiest corner, and the gate — which in an Israelite town was the courthouse, the exchange and the meeting place all at once. These are the four loudest places available, and she has chosen every one of them. Wisdom is not whispering in a library to people who have already made time for her. She is shouting over traffic.

That settles something about God that people are slow to believe. The reason a man does not have wisdom is not that God has hidden it and set a puzzle. Waltke says it well: God has posted wisdom at every intersection, and the question is never whether it can be found but whether the passer-by will stop. The tragedy of this chapter is not obscurity. It is indifference in broad daylight.

And the picture is not finished in the Old Testament. On the last day of the feast, in the most crowded place in Jerusalem, a man stood up and cried out — if anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37). Wisdom went out into the street and raised her voice, and at length Wisdom took a body and did it in person. He is the wisdom of God, and he did not wait in the temple for the qualified to come to him. He went to the road, and the market, and the gate, and shouted over the noise, and was crucified within sight of a public highway so that nobody could say the offer had been made quietly.

verseByVerse.quote: "How long, O simple ones, will you love being simple? How long will scoffers delight in their scoffing and fools hate knowledge? If you turn at my reproof, behold, I will pour out my spirit to you; I will make my words known to you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her sermon opens with an exasperated question, and she names three men in the crowd. How long, O simple ones, will you love being simple? How long will scoffers delight in their scoffing and fools hate knowledge?

Three kinds, and they are not three degrees of the same thing. The simple is the open man of v. 4, still fixable — but notice the verb: he has begun to love being simple, because ignorance is restful and knowing things obliges you to act. The scoffer has found a technique. He does not argue with wisdom, he makes it faintly ridiculous, and a raised eyebrow has ended more conversations than any argument ever did. The fool has gone furthest: he does not neglect knowledge, he hates it, because it will not leave him alone.

How long is prophetic language (cf. Jeremiah 4:14), and it is the sound of somebody who has been calling for a long time already. But the exasperation is not the point of the verse; the next line is. If you turn at my reproof, behold, I will pour out my spirit to you.

One condition, and it is a small one — turn. Not understand, not qualify, not clean yourself up first. And the promise is out of all proportion to it: not a course of lessons but a pouring out, the language used later of the Spirit poured out on all flesh (Joel 2:28; Acts 2:17). Wisdom does not offer to sell what she has. She offers to hand it over.

Hold that still for a moment. Every person in that street is being scolded and offered everything in the same breath, by somebody they have been ignoring for years, at no charge, on a condition anybody can meet. That is what God is like, and it is why the rest of the chapter is so serious: an offer this generous can only be refused deliberately.

verseByVerse.quote: Because I have called and you refused to listen, have stretched out my hand and no one has heeded, because you have ignored all my counsel and would have none of my reproof, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the tone hardens, and the reason for it is set out with painful care. Because I have called and you refused to listen, have stretched out my hand and no one has heeded, because you have ignored all my counsel and would have none of my reproof.

Four verbs, and every one of them is hers. She called. She stretched out her hand. She counselled. She reproved. Whatever is about to happen in this passage, the record shows a God who moved first and kept moving, and a street that went on walking past.

The stretched-out hand is the image to stay with, because it is not the gesture of a teacher. It is what you do at a station platform, or from a riverbank. Hands are stretched out to people who are going somewhere they should not go, by people who are prepared to be pulled in themselves.

And it is exactly the picture the Lord reaches for over Jerusalem, in a sentence that should be read slowly: how often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing (Matthew 23:37). The Son of God stood in sight of the city that would kill him within the week and wept over its refusal. Not annoyed at being disobeyed. Grieved at what they were doing to themselves, and going anyway to the place where the hand would be stretched out for the last time and nailed there.

Which means the judgment that follows in this chapter is not the outburst of an offended deity. It is the last chapter of a long story in which every earlier chapter was an appeal.

verseByVerse.quote: I also will laugh at your calamity; I will mock when terror strikes you, when terror strikes you like a storm and your calamity comes like a whirlwind, when distress and anguish come upon you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then the hardest sentence in the chapter. I also will laugh at your calamity; I will mock when terror strikes you. There is no use softening it, and no honest reader gets past it quickly.

Two things need saying, and the first is what the laughter is not. It is not pleasure in suffering. The God of this book takes no delight in the death of the wicked and says so under oath (Ezekiel 33:11), and the same Wisdom who laughs here was weeping two verses ago. Whatever this is, it is not sadism.

What it is, is the ancient way of stating that a warning has been vindicated. To laugh at a thing, in this idiom, is to be entirely unthreatened by it and entirely unsurprised — the response of the one person in the story who said all along that this was where the road went. The laughter is not aimed at pain. It is aimed at the argument that there would be no pain.

The second thing is the imagery, and it is chosen with care: like a storm… like a whirlwind. Both arrive from a clear sky. That is how the collapse of a badly-founded life actually happens — not by slow visible decline, which could be noticed and corrected, but by years of nothing at all followed by a single afternoon. The structure was being eaten the whole time. The failure is sudden; the weakness was not.

Which is the mercy hidden in a passage that does not sound merciful. It was printed in advance, in a book anybody may open, by a Wisdom who stood in the street and shouted it. Nobody who reaches the whirlwind will be able to say they were not told what weather this road runs into.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they will call upon me, but I will not answer; they will seek me diligently but will not find me. Because they hated knowledge and did not choose the fear of the LORD, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they will call upon me, but I will not answer; they will seek me diligently but will not find me. This verse has frightened people who had no business being frightened by it, so it must be handled carefully and plainly.

Start with what it says. The people described here are not seeking Wisdom. They are seeking rescue. They want the whirlwind to stop, and they have discovered that Wisdom is useful, which is a completely different thing from wanting her. The next line gives their history in one clause: they hated knowledge and did not choose the fear of the LORD. Hated. Not missed, not never encountered — hated, over years, while she stood in the street calling.

Now the pastoral point, and it is the reason for the care. If you are afraid that you have crossed a line and God will no longer hear you, that fear is itself evidence that you are not the person in this verse. The people in v. 28 are not anxious about God; they are anxious about consequences, and there is no sign anywhere in the passage that they want him. A man troubled about whether God will receive him has already been given the one thing this crowd never had — a desire for God himself — and that desire is not something a hardened heart manufactures. It is the beginning of the work of God in a person, not the proof of his absence.

Set beside this verse the promise that stands over the whole Bible, and let it settle the question: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37). Never. Not the man who left, not the man who wasted twenty years, not the one who has been in the street ignoring the voice since he was nineteen. The door in Proverbs 1 closes on people who never once tried it. It has never yet closed on somebody pushing.

And did not choose is the phrase to carry away. The fear of the LORD is not absorbed from a Christian culture, a Christian family, or a lifetime of attendance. It is chosen, and it has to be chosen again on Monday.

verseByVerse.quote: would have none of my counsel and despised all my reproof, therefore they shall eat the fruit of their way, and have their fill of their own devices. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The indictment finishes — would have none of my counsel and despised all my reproof — and then the sentence is passed, and it is a strange one. Therefore they shall eat the fruit of their way, and have their fill of their own devices.

Notice the shape of that. God does not import a punishment from somewhere else. He serves them their own cooking. The sentence for a life of self-direction is a full plate of self-direction, and the terrible word in the verse is fill: they get as much as they wanted, which is precisely the problem. Waltke puts it exactly — God allows them to have what they chose, and what they chose destroys them.

Paul says the same thing three times over in Romans 1, and it is the most chilling refrain in the New Testament: God gave them up (Romans 1:24, 26, 28). Not struck them down. Gave them up — to themselves, which turned out to be enough.

So the image of eating is exact, and it should be taken personally. What a man consumes he becomes. A steady diet of one’s own opinion, one’s own excuses and one’s own account of every disagreement will, over twenty years, produce a person shaped entirely by it — and he will not be able to see this, because the only instrument he has for assessing himself is the thing that has been feeding him.

Which is the whole case for reproof, and why this book keeps pressing it. There is no way out of that loop from inside it. Somebody has to come from outside and tell you the truth, and the only question is whether you have anyone left who is allowed to.

verseByVerse.quote: For the simple are killed by their turning away, and the complacency of fools destroys them; but whoever listens to me will dwell secure and will be at ease, without dread of disaster." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends by putting the two roads side by side, and the first of them kills by a route nobody fears. The simple are killed by their turning away, and the complacency of fools destroys them.

Complacency is shalvah — ease, untroubledness, the state of a man for whom nothing is currently urgent. It is not rebellion. Nobody in this half of the verse has shaken a fist at God; they have simply never found the matter pressing, and Proverbs says that this is what does the killing. Not the scoffer’s contempt. The comfortable man’s quiet postponement.

Then the other road, and the promise on it is precisely worded: whoever listens to me will dwell secure and will be at ease, without dread of disaster. Read carefully. It does not say that disaster will not come. It says there will be no dread of it — which is a promise about the man, not about his circumstances. Wisdom does not offer a life with no storms in it. It offers a house that is still standing when the storm has passed (cf. Matthew 7:24-25).

And that is where the chapter finally lands. It began with a father who had one son and limited time, and it ends with an open offer to whoever listens — anyone at all, from any street, on the sole condition of stopping to hear.

He is the Wisdom of God, and the security this verse promises was not cheap. He stood in the noisy street and called, and was ignored; he stretched out his hand, and it was nailed down; he ate the fruit of a way that was not his own, so that those who listen to him should never have to. The house that stands in the whirlwind stands on him, and it will not be moved.
