5.title: Proverbs 5 — The Forbidden Woman and the Joy of Covenant Marriage

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Bitter End of the Seductive Path
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 5 is the father's most extended warning against the 'forbidden woman' (zarah, the strange or foreign woman—not necessarily foreign by ethnicity but foreign to the covenant community by her behavior). The chapter moves through three stages: the initial attractiveness (honey and oil, vv. 3–4), the actual destination (death, Sheol, vv. 5–6), and the devastating personal consequences for the man who falls (vv. 7–14). The final image is the man at the end of his life groaning in anguish, remembering when he could have listened.
verseByVerse.theology: The structure of the seduction—sweet promises, bitter consequences—is the template for all temptation in Proverbs and beyond. The mouth of the forbidden woman 'drips honey and her speech is smoother than oil'—maximum attractiveness. But 'in the end she is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a two-edged sword'—maximum destruction. The trajectory runs from pleasure to pain, from sweetness to bitterness, from life to death. Every temptation follows this structure; wisdom is the ability to project forward to the end before the beginning is entered.
verseByVerse.examples: Verses 12–14 are among the most poignant in Proverbs: the man who failed to listen says, 'How I hated discipline, and my heart despised reproof! I did not listen to the voice of my teachers... I am at the brink of utter ruin in the assembled congregation.' The assembled congregation—the covenant community—is the witness to his destruction. What he thought was private has become public; what he thought was pleasurable has become his ruin.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, be attentive to my wisdom; incline your ear to my understanding, that you may keep discretion, and your lips may guard knowledge. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The father opens as he always does — be attentive to my wisdom; incline your ear to my understanding — and the familiarity of it should not disguise what is coming. Of all the dangers in these nine chapters, this is the one he will spend three chapters on.

But the aim in v. 2 is not what a reader expects at the head of a chapter about adultery. That you may keep discretion, and your lips may guard knowledge. The lips. Not the eyes, not the hands — the mouth, which is a strange organ to fortify against this particular danger.

It is not strange once the chapter is read. The seduction that follows is entirely verbal. It is not the woman’s appearance that is described in v. 3; it is her lips and her speech. So the father arms his son at the point where the attack will actually come, and what he asks for is a man whose own mouth is under orders — because a conversation takes two, and almost every one of these disasters could have been ended by one person declining to say the next thing.

A word before the chapter proper, since the subject makes people flinch. Proverbs is not squeamish, it is not sneering at desire, and it is emphatically not going to end with a prohibition. It is going to end with a better invitation. Anybody who reads this chapter as a warning against pleasure has read it exactly backwards; the father’s argument, from first verse to last, is that his son is being offered a counterfeit of something he already has access to, at a price he has not been told.

verseByVerse.quote: For the lips of a forbidden woman drip honey, and her speech is smoother than oil, but in the end she is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a two-edged sword. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the lips of a forbidden woman drip honey, and her speech is smoother than oil. The father does not begin by saying she is dangerous. He begins by admitting she is lovely, and every honest reader should notice how rare that is in moral instruction.

Honey and oil are not chosen at random. Honey is the sweetest thing in the ancient world, and oil is what removed friction — the substance you rubbed on skin, on hinges, on anything that was catching. So her speech is described as sweet and frictionless: nothing in the conversation snags.

And that is the accurate description. What she offers is not primarily a body. It is being listened to. It is a person who finds him interesting at a point in his life when the people at home have long since stopped asking. Almost every affair begins in a conversation that both parties would have described, truthfully, as innocent.

Then the hinge of the verse, and it turns on two words: in the end. The Hebrew is aharit, the outcome, the way a thing finishes.

Because the reversal is total, and the father states it in the same sensory terms. Sweet becomes bitter as wormwood — a plant so bitter its name is a byword. Smooth becomes sharp as a two-edged sword. The very qualities that drew him are the ones that turn, and they turn into their exact opposites.

Here, then, is the whole skill the chapter is trying to teach, and it can be put in one sentence: wisdom is the ability to taste the end of a thing at its beginning. Folly is not a failure to know that adultery is wrong. It is a failure of imagination — the inability, at the moment when the honey is actually on the tongue, to taste the wormwood that is attached to it.

verseByVerse.quote: Her feet go down to death; her steps follow the path to Sheol; she does not ponder the path of life; her ways wander, and she does not know it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her feet go down to death; her steps follow the path to Sheol. The father is now describing not what she offers but where she is going, and the second half of v. 6 is the most unexpectedly compassionate line in the chapter.

She does not ponder the path of life; her ways wander, and she does not know it.

Set that against 4:26, where the son was commanded to ponder the path of your feet. She has not done it. She is not presented here as a strategist running a campaign against young men; she is presented as somebody lost, on a road she has never examined, and the closing clause is the saddest in the chapter — she does not know it.

That changes the tone of the passage in a way that matters. The predator in Proverbs 5 is herself a casualty. She is not the enemy so much as the wreckage of the same folly, still moving. Any reading of this chapter that leaves a man feeling superior to the woman in it has missed the verse.

And the word wander deserves attention, because it names the mechanism. Her ways are not aimed at death; they meander toward it. That is how this kind of ruin actually happens to people. Nobody sets a destination of Sheol. They drift, one unexamined step at a time, each of which felt like nothing — and the terrible mercy of a straight road to destruction is that a man can see it and turn. A wandering one gives him no such warning.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, O sons, listen to me, and do not depart from the words of my mouth. Keep your way far from her, and do not go near the door of her house, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep your way far from her, and do not go near the door of her house.

Read the counsel carefully, because it is not the counsel most people would give. The father does not say do not commit adultery. He does not even say do not enter her house. He says keep your way far, and do not go near the door.

He is fighting the battle two streets earlier than his son thinks it is being fought, and he does so because he understands where a man’s strength actually lies. Nobody wins this at the door. At the door the honey and the oil are working at full strength, the sentences are already smooth, and a man’s judgment is being asked to perform under conditions in which it has never once performed well.

So the practical counsel of this chapter is unheroic and concrete, and it is about geography and calendars rather than resolve. Which conversations are continued after they should have stopped. Which route home. Which app is on the phone. Which colleague gets told things that his wife has not been told. Whether a man is ever alone in a house where he should not be alone. None of that is glamorous, and all of it is the actual fight.

Joseph is the model, and what he did was not admirable in the usual way. Faced with a woman who had him by the coat, he did not reason, negotiate, or explain his convictions. He left the coat and ran (Genesis 39:12) — and looked, for that moment, ridiculous. Paul gives exactly the same instruction with no more sophistication than Joseph showed: flee from sexual immorality (1 Corinthians 6:18). There are sins a Christian is told to stand and fight. This is one he is told to run from, and the running is not cowardice. It is the only tactic that has ever worked.

verseByVerse.quote: lest you give your honor to others and your years to the merciless, lest strangers take their fill of your strength, and your labors go to the house of a foreigner, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the father does something a modern preacher would hesitate over: he appeals to self-interest, and he itemises the bill. Lest you give your honour to others and your years to the merciless, lest strangers take their fill of your strength, and your labours go to the house of a foreigner.

Four losses, and the striking thing about all four is that they are things the man gives. He is not robbed. He hands them over, and the passage watches them go across the table one at a time.

Your honour — the standing he spent twenty years building, which can be spent in an evening and cannot be re-earned by the same means. Your years — and the word beside it is the cruel one, to the merciless. There is no mercy in this transaction. Time handed over does not come back on compassionate grounds, and a man of fifty who has burned a decade has burned a decade.

Your strength, which is the capacity he had for work, for children, for building something — consumed by others. And your labours, going to a house that is not his: the money, the property, the things he made, ending up somewhere he never intended and cannot follow.

The father is not being mercenary. He is doing something more useful than moralising: he is filling in the part of the transaction that temptation never mentions. Every offer of this kind is presented as an addition to a life — something gained, on the side, at no apparent cost. The verse simply reads out the price, in advance, in the currencies a man actually cares about.

verseByVerse.quote: and at the end of your life you groan, when your flesh and body are consumed, and you say, "How I hated discipline, and my heart despised reproof! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now the chapter does the thing that makes it unforgettable. The father stops arguing and takes his son forward forty years, and lets him listen to himself.

At the end of your life you groan, when your flesh and body are consumed, and you say: How I hated discipline, and my heart despised reproof!

Notice first the timing. At the end. Not next month. This is the answer to the one objection every young man raises, which is that he knows plenty of people who did this and nothing happened to them. Nothing has happened to them yet. The bill in this chapter is not presented at the point of sale.

Then the sound. The word is groan — not weeping, not argument. The noise a person makes when speech is no longer any use.

And then the words themselves, which are the most terrible in the chapter, because of what they contain and what they leave out. How I hated discipline. He is not blaming the woman. He is not blaming God, or his upbringing, or the man who introduced them. At the end of his life, with everything gone, he has arrived at complete clarity about one thing: he was offered correction and he could not stand it.

That clarity is the tragedy. He is not saying anything he was not told. It is the same information he had at nineteen, in the same words — and the whole difference is that it is now too late to be of any use.

Which is precisely why the father is telling his son this today. The lament is printed in advance so that it need not be spoken. A man may have these words for nothing now, or pay everything he has for them later. There is no third option, and the only variable is when.

verseByVerse.quote: I did not listen to the voice of my teachers or incline my ear to my instructors. I am at the brink of utter ruin in the assembled congregation." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lament continues, and it becomes specific. I did not listen to the voice of my teachers or incline my ear to my instructors.

The plurals matter. Not one voice — teachers, instructors. This was not a man who lacked input. He had a father, a mother, older men in the assembly, and presumably a friend or two who said something once and was not thanked for it. He was surrounded by people who told him the truth, and the whole apparatus made no difference at all, because there is no quantity of good counsel that can compensate for an unwillingness to receive any of it.

Then the last line, and it locates the ruin somewhere no reader expects. I am at the brink of utter ruin in the assembled congregation.

In the congregation. Among the gathered people of God. Everything in this affair was arranged to be private — the discretion, the deleted messages, the second life kept carefully apart from the first — and it ends in the one place he most wanted it never to reach. That is the consistent testimony of Scripture and of pastoral experience alike: what is done in secret does not stay secret. It merely accumulates interest while it waits.

And there is a word here for the church that gathers, and it cuts the other way. This congregation is described as watching a man’s ruin, and it is the same congregation whose counsel he refused. A community that will only ever be present at the collapse has not finished its work. The place to be involved in a brother’s life is upstream of v. 14, in the years when the involvement is unwelcome, mildly awkward, and could still make a difference.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–23 — The Alternative: Covenant Marriage as the Proper Spring
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Against the forbidden woman, the father places the wife of one's youth—not as a lesser alternative but as the genuine article. The water imagery is deliberate: the forbidden woman is a contaminated spring that poisons; the wife of one's youth is your own cistern, your own well, from which pure and sustaining water flows. The joy of covenant marriage is presented as the proper, God-ordained, and fully satisfying alternative to adultery.
verseByVerse.theology: Verses 18–19 are the most positive and explicit description of sexual joy within marriage in Proverbs. 'Rejoice in the wife of your youth... let her breasts fill you at all times with delight; be intoxicated always in her love.' The language is uninhibited: delight, intoxication, always. The covenant relationship is not a restrained alternative to the excitement of forbidden love; it is the place where genuine, unbounded, God-blessed erotic joy is intended to flourish. Song of Solomon develops this theology at full length.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter closes with the theological grounding of all sexual ethics: 'the LORD sees' (v. 21). Human sexuality is not a private domain into which God does not look; it is a domain he created and governs. The man who wonders why he should remain faithful to his wife when no one is watching does not understand that the covenant was made before the God who sees everything. His iniquities ensnare him (v. 22) and he dies for lack of discipline (v. 23) not because God is a spoilsport but because sexual faithlessness carries structural consequences that God has woven into the fabric of reality.

verseByVerse.quote: Drink water from your own cistern, flowing water from your own well. Should your springs be scattered abroad, streams of water in the streets? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now the chapter turns, and everything changes. Drink water from your own cistern, flowing water from your own well.

The father has spent fourteen verses on a road that ends in a groan. He does not finish there, and he does not finish with a rule. He finishes with an invitation, and the change of imagery is the argument: from honey and oil, which are sweeteners, to water, which is what a man dies without.

In a dry country a cistern was the difference between a household living and a household leaving. It was cut out of rock by hand, sealed, and filled slowly. It was not exciting. It was everything.

Two words in the picture do the work. Your own — this is his, by covenant, with nobody else’s claim on it. And flowing, which distinguishes a living spring from stored rainwater; the second half of the verse insists that what he has at home is not stagnant.

Then v. 16 poses the question the other way round: should your springs be scattered abroad, streams of water in the streets? Water in the street is water lost. It is not being drunk by anybody; it is running away between the stones — and that is the father’s verdict on a life dispersed. Not wicked so much as wasted. Everything that was meant to feed one household, poured out where it feeds nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: Let them be for yourself alone, and not for strangers with you. Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let them be for yourself alone, and not for strangers with you. Exclusivity is being defended, and the modern reader should be clear about what is being claimed. Marriage in this book is not primarily a restriction on a man; it is a possession given to him. The fence is not around a wilderness. It is around a well.

Then the sentence that changes the whole tone of the chapter: let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth.

Rejoice is a command, and it is one of the most practical in Scripture, because it says that delight in a marriage is not merely a feeling that arrives or fails to. It is something a man is told to do, which means it can be neglected, and which means it can be cultivated.

Almost nobody wakes up one morning wanting somebody else. What happens first is a long slow stopping — the compliments that dried up, the questions no longer asked, the shared laughter that migrated somewhere else, the appreciation that turned to inventory. A man who has stopped rejoicing in his wife has already begun the journey of this chapter without leaving the house, and the woman in v. 3 will not have to work very hard when she arrives.

And the phrase the wife of your youth is doing quiet, tender work. It is the same phrase Malachi uses when God says he hates divorce, and it is chosen to make a man remember (Malachi 2:14-15). She is not merely his wife. She is the girl he chose, and who chose him, when both of them had nothing — and everything they now have between them, they built.

verseByVerse.quote: a lovely deer, a graceful doe. Let her breasts fill you at all times with delight; be intoxicated always in her love. Why should you be intoxicated, my son, with a forbidden woman and embrace the bosom of an adulteress? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Scripture says something that has embarrassed the church far more than it ever embarrassed Scripture. A lovely deer, a graceful doe. Let her breasts fill you at all times with delight; be intoxicated always in her love.

This is in the Bible, spoken by a father to a son, as instruction. It is not a concession to human weakness and it is not a euphemism. The word rendered intoxicated means to reel, to be carried away — the word you would use of a man who has had too much wine — and it is being commanded, of a husband, about his wife, always.

The reason for the vividness is strategic, and it is the whole argument of the chapter. The father is not asking his son to choose duty over pleasure. He is telling him that the pleasure is on the other side, and that the forbidden road is not the exciting option but the impoverished one — a counterfeit of a thing he can have without the wormwood.

Hence the rhetorical question of v. 20: why should you be intoxicated, my son, with a forbidden woman? It is not a demand for a reason to be faithful. It is genuine bewilderment. Why would a man with a well go and drink from the street?

Two pastoral things must be said, or this passage will wound the people who most need it. First, it is written to a husband about his own marriage, and it is not a standard by which to grade a wife. A man reading it as a description of what he is owed has turned the verse round to face the wrong way; every command in it is addressed to him.

Second, many marriages are not like this, and some are painfully far from it. Illness, exhaustion, grief, age, a history nobody chose — there are a hundred honest reasons, and none of them is a failure. The verse is not a measurement to be failed. It is a direction to be walked in, at whatever pace two people can manage; and a couple facing toward each other in a hard season is nearer to Proverbs 5 than a couple with nothing wrong who have simply stopped trying.

verseByVerse.quote: For a man's ways are before the eyes of the LORD, and he ponders all his paths. The iniquities of the wicked ensnare him, and he is held fast in the cords of his sin. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
For a man’s ways are before the eyes of the LORD, and he ponders all his paths. And here at last is the reason underneath every argument the chapter has made.

The word ponders is the same verb the son was given at 4:26 and the woman was said to neglect at 5:6. Man is commanded to weigh his path; she does not; God does. That is the shape of the whole chapter in one word.

And notice what this does to the idea of a private life. Every affair depends on a belief in secrecy — not a theological belief, a working assumption that a locked drawer is actually locked. This verse simply removes the assumption. There has never been a moment in any relationship in this chapter that was not fully attended.

Then v. 22, and the image is a snare: the iniquities of the wicked ensnare him, and he is held fast in the cords of his sin. Not God’s cords. His own. The trap is described as self-manufactured and self-baited, which is exactly what habitual sin feels like from inside — a man who could have stopped at any of a hundred points, discovering that he now cannot stop at all, and unable to name the moment when the rope became a knot.

But the eyes in v. 21 are not only the eyes of a judge, and the chapter cannot be left there. The God who sees everything is the God who came and looked. He looked at a woman caught in the very act and had the only clean hand in the courtyard, and he did not throw anything (John 8:7-11). He looked at a woman at a well with five husbands behind her, and what he offered her was water she would never have to come back for. The eyes that miss no path are the eyes that went looking for people on the worst of them.

verseByVerse.quote: He dies for lack of discipline, and because of his great folly he is led astray. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
He dies for lack of discipline, and because of his great folly he is led astray. The chapter ends on a death, and on a passive verb.

Led astray. Not goes astray. The man who began by choosing has stopped choosing; something else has the reins. That is the last and truest word about this road — it is entered as an act of freedom and it ends with a man being taken somewhere.

And the cause is given as lack of discipline, which returns to what he said in v. 12: how I hated discipline. The two verses lock together, and between them they tell the whole story. He hated the correction, so he had none; having none, he was not held; not being held, he was led.

Now a word to the reader for whom this is not a warning but a description. Some who read this chapter have already done what it describes, and the chapter has just ended in death with no exit offered. That is not because there is none. It is because Proverbs is a book of observation and it is telling the truth about the road; it was never the book that had the last word.

So let the last word be said plainly. There is no sin in this chapter that is beyond the blood of Christ. David committed the adultery, arranged the murder to hide it, and was forgiven and left to us the psalm he wrote about it (Psalm 51). The woman of John 8 walked out of that courtyard with no charge against her. The verdict of Proverbs 5 stands — this road ends in death, exactly as it says — and the gospel does not contradict it. It reports that somebody else went to the end of it.

For the whole story of Scripture is a marriage, and it is not the story of a faithful bride. God took a people to himself, and she went after other lovers, and he described what she had done in language more explicit than anything in this chapter (Ezekiel 16). And he did not divorce her. He went into the far country after her, and paid the price of her adultery in his own body, and called her his own, and will yet present her to himself without a single spot — the bride who was the adulteress, in white, at his side, forever (Ephesians 5:25-27). He was led astray for the folly that was not his, and died for the lack of a discipline he never lacked, so that the wanderers might be brought home.

5.text: <sup>1</sup>My son, be attentive to my wisdom; incline your ear to my understanding,<sup>2</sup>that you may keep discretion, and your lips may guard knowledge.<sup>3</sup>For the lips of a forbidden woman drip honey, and her speech is smoother than oil,<sup>4</sup>but in the end she is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a two-edged sword.<sup>5</sup>Her feet go down to death; her steps follow the path to Sheol;<sup>6</sup>she does not ponder the path of life; her ways wander, and she does not know it.<sup>7</sup>And now, O sons, listen to me, and do not depart from the words of my mouth.<sup>8</sup>Keep your way far from her, and do not go near the door of her house,<sup>9</sup>lest you give your honor to others and your years to the merciless,<sup>10</sup>lest strangers take their fill of your strength, and your labors go to the house of a foreigner,<sup>11</sup>and at the end of your life you groan, when your flesh and body are consumed,<sup>12</sup>and you say, "How I hated discipline, and my heart despised reproof!<sup>13</sup>I did not listen to the voice of my teachers or incline my ear to my instructors.<sup>14</sup>I am at the brink of utter ruin in the assembled congregation."<sup>15</sup>Drink water from your own cistern, flowing water from your own well.<sup>16</sup>Should your springs be scattered abroad, streams of water in the streets?<sup>17</sup>Let them be for yourself alone, and not for strangers with you.<sup>18</sup>Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth,<sup>19</sup>a lovely deer, a graceful doe. Let her breasts fill you at all times with delight; be intoxicated always in her love.<sup>20</sup>Why should you be intoxicated, my son, with a forbidden woman and embrace the bosom of an adulteress?<sup>21</sup>For a man's ways are before the eyes of the LORD, and he ponders all his paths.<sup>22</sup>The iniquities of the wicked ensnare him, and he is held fast in the cords of his sin.<sup>23</sup>He dies for lack of discipline, and because of his great folly he is led astray.

6.title: Proverbs 6 — Surety, Sloth, Trouble-Making, and the Forbidden Woman

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–19 — Three Warnings: Rash Vows, Laziness, and Moral Corruption
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 6 opens with three distinct wisdom warnings before returning to the theme of the forbidden woman. The first (vv. 1–5) warns against pledging surety for another's debt—not because generosity is wrong but because reckless financial commitments enslave. The second (vv. 6–11) is the famous rebuke of the sluggard via the ant—the most industrious creature teaches the laziest person. The third (vv. 12–19) describes the troublemaker and culminates in the seven things God hates.
verseByVerse.theology: The seven abominations of vv. 16–19 form a theological center: haughty eyes, lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, a heart devising wicked plans, feet quick to run to evil, a false witness, and one who sows discord among brothers. The list moves from internal attitude (eyes, heart) through action (hands, feet) to speech (tongue, witness) and social impact (sowing discord). The abomination is not merely the acts but the character they express: a person oriented against the grain of God's ordered, truthful, peaceable creation.
verseByVerse.examples: The sluggard passage (vv. 6–11) is the most memorable in Proverbs because of its rhetorical strategy: not command but observation. 'Go to the ant, O sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise.' The sluggard is not berated but redirected: look at what you have been too proud to look at. The ant has no leader, no overseer, no ruler—and yet she prepares her food in summer and gathers in harvest. The contrast with the sluggard who needs constant external motivation is devastating. The ant's self-directed industry is natural wisdom; the sluggard's self-inflicted poverty is unnatural folly.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, if you have put up security for your neighbor, have given your pledge for a stranger, if you are snared in the words of your mouth, caught in the words of your mouth, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter opens on something entirely practical, and it catches most readers off guard: a warning about co-signing a loan. My son, if you have put up security for your neighbour, have given your pledge for a stranger.

To stand surety was to promise a creditor that if the borrower failed, you would pay. It was not a donation and it was not a loan; it was the assumption of somebody else’s liability, with no ceiling on it and no control over the outcome. And notice the drift across the line: security for a neighbour, a pledge for a stranger. Somebody you know has asked you to stand behind somebody you do not.

Then v. 2, and the diagnosis is the one this book keeps returning to: you are snared in the words of your mouth, caught in the words of your mouth. Said twice, in almost the same words, because the trap is the same trap and it was made of language.

Nothing was signed under duress. What happened is that a man was in a room, and a request was made, and the atmosphere was warm, and saying no would have been awkward for about four seconds. So he said yes to a stranger’s debt in order to avoid four seconds of discomfort, and Proverbs uses the word snared — because a snare is precisely a thing that costs nothing to step into.

A guard, because this must not be turned into an excuse for meanness. Proverbs is emphatic elsewhere that the generous man is blessed and that whoever is kind to the poor lends to the LORD (19:17; 22:9). The warning is not against giving. It is against a particular structure — open-ended liability for a debt you cannot see and a decision you will not be making — and the difference between the two is simple enough to test. Give what you can afford to lose, and the matter is closed. Guarantee what you cannot afford to lose, and you have handed a stranger the keys to your household.

verseByVerse.quote: then do this, my son, and save yourself, for you have come into the hand of your neighbor: go, hasten, and plead urgently with your neighbor. Give your eyes no sleep and your eyelids no slumber; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the counsel, and it is remarkable both for its urgency and for its complete absence of comfort. Then do this, my son, and save yourself, for you have come into the hand of your neighbour: go, hasten, and plead urgently with your neighbour.

Three verbs stacked on each other. Go. Hasten. Plead. And the phrase that explains the panic is you have come into the hand of your neighbour — a hand, in Hebrew, being the standing image for power over somebody. He is not in difficulty. He is in somebody’s hand.

The word rendered plead urgently is a strong one, with the flavour of storming at a man, and it takes the son’s pride away entirely. He is told to humble himself in front of the person he was trying to look generous to a fortnight ago, and to say the thing nobody wants to say: I should not have done this, and I am asking you to release me.

Then v. 4 sets the level of effort: give your eyes no sleep and your eyelids no slumber. Do not sleep until it is dealt with.

Underneath the specific case is a rule about mistakes in general, and it is one of the most useful things in this book. When a man has done something foolish, the instinct is to wait — to hope it resolves, to let a week pass, to avoid the conversation. Wisdom says the opposite, and says it about every kind of error: the cost of a foolish commitment is lowest on the first morning and rises every day afterward. There is no situation of this kind that improves by being left alone.

verseByVerse.quote: save yourself like a gazelle from the hand of the hunter, like a bird from the hand of the fowler. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Save yourself like a gazelle from the hand of the hunter, like a bird from the hand of the fowler.

Two pictures, and both are of animals in the moment when the trap closes. Neither of them negotiates. There is no gradual withdrawal, no partial escape, no strategy of managing the hunter. There is one movement, made instantly, with everything the creature has.

The father is describing what such a moment costs, and it is not dignity that is preserved by it. A gazelle bolting is not graceful; it is frantic, and it does not care who is watching. Which is exactly the point, because the reason most people do not get out of a bad commitment is not that they cannot. It is that getting out would require looking foolish in front of somebody, and they would rather be slowly ruined than briefly embarrassed.

And there is a wider principle in it that reaches beyond money. Scripture has two different instructions for two different dangers. Some things a Christian is told to stand and resist — the devil, when he is resisted, flees (James 4:7). Other things he is told to run from, without argument and without a backward look: sexual immorality, the love of money, youthful passions (1 Corinthians 6:18; 1 Timothy 6:11; 2 Timothy 2:22). Confusing the two lists has cost people a great deal. There are traps that cannot be reasoned with, and the only wise response to them has feathers and no plan.

And there is one more thing to say about surety before the chapter leaves it, because the New Testament picks the word up and does something startling with it. To stand surety is to put your name to a stranger’s debt with no ceiling on the liability, which Proverbs regards as an act of folly — and it is precisely the word used of Christ. He has become the guarantor of a better covenant (Hebrews 7:22): the same office, the same open-ended exposure, entered deliberately and with his eyes open. He gave his pledge for strangers. He was snared by the words of his own mouth, and he did not go, or hasten, or plead to be released; he was taken into the hand of the creditor, and he paid the whole of it, and the goods of his house were emptied to the last. The chapter warns a man not to do this for a stranger. He did it for enemies.

verseByVerse.quote: Go to the ant, O sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise. Without having any chief, officer, or ruler, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go to the ant, O sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise.

Notice the method before the message. The father does not tell the lazy man to work harder; he sends him outside to look at something. That is a shrewder approach than a lecture, because a sluggard has heard every lecture and has an answer ready for all of them. He has no answer prepared for an ant.

And what he is told to consider is small enough to be humiliating. Not an ox, not a lion. An insect he could stand on without noticing.

Then the observation, and it lands where the sluggard actually lives: without having any chief, officer, or ruler. Three words for supervision, piled up, because that is the whole comparison. The ant has nobody standing over her.

The sluggard, by contrast, is a man who works — when watched. He is not incapable, and he is very often likeable. What he lacks is any engine of his own: he needs a deadline, a boss, a crisis, or somebody’s disappointment to get him moving, and remove all four and he stops. Kidner’s line on it is exact: the ant does instinctively what the sluggard requires a sermon to attempt.

So the diagnostic in this verse is not how hard a man works. It is what happens on the days when nobody would ever know. That is where the ant and the sluggard finally part company, and every man can answer it privately in about ten seconds.

verseByVerse.quote: she prepares her bread in summer and gathers her food in harvest. How long will you lie there, O sluggard? When will you arise from your sleep? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
She prepares her bread in summer and gathers her food in harvest. The ant’s second quality, and it is the one the sluggard finds hardest, because it has nothing to do with effort.

It is timing. The ant works when the work is available rather than when the need is felt, and those are two entirely different calendars. Nobody in summer is hungry. The whole of her industry is directed at a season she is not currently in — which is a definition of wisdom as good as any in the book, and the exact faculty this chapter has been calling discretion: the ability to see Thursday from Monday.

Then the father turns and speaks to the man directly, and for the first time there is exasperation in it. How long will you lie there, O sluggard? When will you arise from your sleep?

Two questions, and the second is the honest one. Not will you arise — the sluggard fully intends to. When. He is not a man who has decided against getting up. He is a man who has been about to get up for eleven years, and the gap between his intentions and his mornings has never once been examined.

Before going further a real guard is needed here, because these verses have been used to beat people they were never aimed at. A man flattened by depression is not a sluggard. A woman worn out by chronic illness, by caring for a dying parent, by grief that has taken her legs away, is not being addressed in this passage. Scripture knows the difference exactly: it tells the idle to work, and it tells the weary that he gives his beloved sleep (Psalm 127:2), and the God of Elijah, finding his prophet lying under a tree wanting to die, did not rebuke him. He let him sleep, and fed him twice, before he said anything at all (1 Kings 19:5-8).

verseByVerse.quote: A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest, and poverty will come upon you like a robber, and want like an armed man. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest. Three times a little, and the whole verse is built to sound reasonable — because it is quoting the sluggard, and everything he says is reasonable.

This is the most accurate sentence in Scripture about how people actually fail. Nobody decides to waste a life. What happens is a series of individually defensible small concessions, each of which really is small, and not one of which would look like anything if you examined it on its own. That is the whole art of it: the decision is never large enough to be worth resisting.

And the folding of the hands is a lovely detail, because it is such a comfortable gesture. It is not collapse. It is a man settling.

Then v. 11, and the change of register is deliberately violent: poverty will come upon you like a robber, and want like an armed man.

The reasonableness stops. After all that gentle language, ruin arrives with a weapon in its hand — and the point is the suddenness. The sluggard does not experience his decline as a decline. Every individual morning was fine. What happens is that the accumulated consequence arrives one day, all at once, in a form that cannot be negotiated with: the letter, the diagnosis, the conversation with the manager, the moment the account is refused.

He never saw a robber coming, and he was right not to. It was not outside the house. It was assembling quietly inside it, out of the mornings.

verseByVerse.quote: A worthless person, a wicked man, goes about with crooked speech, winks with his eyes, signals with his feet, points with his finger, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A worthless person, a wicked man, goes about with crooked speech. The Hebrew behind worthless is beliyya‘al — literally something like without profit, a man from whom no good comes — and the word is dark enough that the New Testament eventually uses it as a name for the evil one himself (2 Corinthians 6:15).

Then the portrait, and it is one of the most observant passages in the Bible. Winks with his eyes, signals with his feet, points with his finger.

Not one word is spoken. Everything in that verse is gesture — a look across a table, a nudge, a slight movement of a hand while somebody else is talking. And that is precisely how this particular man operates: he communicates entirely in things that cannot be quoted back at him.

Anyone who has been in a church meeting or an office where this is happening knows the feeling and usually cannot name it. Nothing was said. Nobody made an accusation. But the room turned, and a person left it diminished, and if you tried afterwards to write down what had actually occurred you would have almost nothing on the page — a raised eyebrow, a pause before a name, a sentence that trailed off.

That deniability is the whole design. He is not a bad arguer; he never argues. He arranges for the damage to be done by other people’s inferences, so that when the wreckage is examined his hands are visibly clean — and it is exactly this that Proverbs calls crooked. Not the falsehood of what he says. The bentness of how he says it.

verseByVerse.quote: with perverted heart devises evil, continually sowing discord; therefore calamity will come upon him suddenly; in a moment he will be broken beyond healing. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
With perverted heart devises evil, continually sowing discord. Now the source is named, and it is not the winking eye. It is a heart that is turned the wrong way round, and the eye is only reporting what is inside.

The phrase to sit with is continually sowing discord. Sowing is a farmer’s word, which means this is not a man who occasionally causes trouble. It is his crop. He works at it in season, and he expects a yield, and — this is the sinister part — he will be somewhere else when it comes up. A sower is never standing in the field at harvest. He is three fields away, and the trouble that appears in a church or a family months later has no visible connection to the conversation that planted it.

Then the verdict, and it is the most abrupt in the chapter. Therefore calamity will come upon him suddenly; in a moment he will be broken beyond healing.

The punishment matches the crime with some precision. He worked by indirection, in increments nobody could trace; his own ruin arrives in one piece, immediately, with no increments at all. He broke things quietly over years; he is broken in a moment.

And beyond healing is a phrase Proverbs uses very sparingly. It is not saying God cannot forgive such a man — the whole Bible stands against that reading, and Paul, who had approved a killing, is the standing refutation of it. It is saying that this particular kind of damage does not repair itself, and that the fracture, once it comes, will not be patched by the means the man has spent his life using. He cannot hint his way out of it.

verseByVerse.quote: There are six things that the LORD hates, seven that are an abomination to him: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
There are six things that the LORD hates, seven that are an abomination to him. The numerical form — six, and then seven — is a device found all over the ancient world, and it does one thing: it tells the listener to wait for the last item. The seventh is the one the whole list has been built to deliver.

But before the list, look at the verb, because it is not the one people expect in Scripture. Hates. Not disapproves, not is displeased by. And the second word, abomination, is to‘ebah — the language of physical revulsion, of a thing that cannot be in the room.

Some readers are made uneasy by this, having been taught that God is love and assuming that love is a temperature rather than a commitment. But hatred of this kind is not the opposite of love; it is love’s reflex. A man who loves his children hates whatever is destroying them, and the intensity of the second feeling is a direct measure of the first. A God who could look at the seven things in this list without revulsion would not be kind. He would be indifferent.

Then the list begins, and it begins at the top of a man and works down. Haughty eyes — literally lifted-up eyes, and pride comes first because everything else in the list requires it. Nothing else here is possible in a man who genuinely believes he is one creature among others.

A lying tongue — because a society runs on the assumption that words correspond to things, and every lie spends a little of a currency it did not earn. And hands that shed innocent blood, the first of the seven that anybody would have thought to put on the list, arriving third.

verseByVerse.quote: a heart that devises wicked plans, feet that make haste to run to evil, a false witness who breathes out lies, and one who sows discord among brothers. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list continues inward and then outward. A heart that devises wicked plans — and devises is a craftsman’s word, the same root used of a man designing something in metal. This is not a heart that stumbles into evil. It is a workshop.

Feet that make haste to run to evil — and the haste is deliberate, set against the ant who works in the right season and against the wise man of 4:26 who ponders the path of his feet. Evil is consistently in a hurry in this book, for the plain reason that its proposals do not survive being thought about.

Then a false witness who breathes out lies. Note the verb: breathes. Lying is no longer an act he performs but the air he moves in — as involuntary and as constant as respiration, so that he no longer notices he is doing it. And a false witness is the specific sin of destroying a man in the one place he cannot defend himself, the court, which in Israel was the last protection of the poor.

And then the seventh, the one the whole numerical device has been holding back: one who sows discord among brothers.

That is startling company. It stands in the same list as murder and perjury, and it is placed last, in the position of climax. The man who sets brothers against each other is weighed here beside the man who sheds innocent blood.

Which ought to be read slowly by anybody who has ever enjoyed a piece of news about a person in his own congregation. This is a sin with no obvious victim, no visible weapon and, in most churches, no consequence at all. It is often committed by people of unimpeachable reputation, in low voices, with genuine concern in their faces. And God, whose one great work in the world is to make a divided humanity into a single family, puts the man who quietly unmakes it at the top of the list of things he cannot bear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–35 — The Forbidden Woman: Why the Cost Is Absolute
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter's final section returns to the forbidden woman but now develops the economic and social consequences of adultery with unprecedented specificity. The thief who steals to eat is condemned but not destroyed; the adulterer who takes another man's wife destroys himself utterly—wounds, dishonor, and a husband's implacable jealousy that no amount of payment can satisfy. The comparison is deliberately asymmetric: theft can be compensated; adultery cannot.
verseByVerse.theology: The argument moves from the lamp-and-light value of parental instruction (vv. 20–23) through the danger of the forbidden woman's beauty (vv. 24–25) to the comparative analysis of theft versus adultery (vv. 26–35). The logic is relentless: can you carry fire without burning yourself? Can you walk on coals without scorching your feet? Then how can you commit adultery without destruction? The physical impossibilities are used to demonstrate the moral inevitability: adultery always destroys.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 26—'A prostitute reduces you to a loaf of bread'—is one of the most economically precise verses in Proverbs. The prostitute takes money; the adulteress takes your entire life. The comparison between hiring a prostitute (which reduces a wealthy man to penury) and committing adultery (which reduces him to nothing at all) is not an endorsement of prostitution but a warning about the infinite cost of adultery. The husband's jealousy (vv. 34–35) is beyond any economic resolution: no bribe, no restitution, no payment can satisfy it. This is a warning, not a prediction of deserved violence.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, keep your father's commandment, and forsake not your mother's teaching. Bind them on your heart always; tie them around your neck. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The father returns to the theme he cannot leave alone, and he begins where he always does: keep your father’s commandment, and forsake not your mother’s teaching.

Which is a strange way to open a warning about adultery, and the strangeness is the strategy. He does not begin with the woman. He begins with what his son already has, because the man who is full is much harder to tempt than the man who is merely warned.

Then two verbs of attachment: bind them on your heart always; tie them around your neck. Both are about fastening something so it cannot be put down and cannot be mislaid. And the picture behind them is probably the phylactery — the small case of Scripture that Israel bound to the body in obedience to Deuteronomy 6:8 — though what the father asks for goes considerably further in. Not on the arm. On the heart.

The word to notice is always. A man does not know in advance which Tuesday the conversation will happen on. Wisdom is either fastened on before he leaves the house or it is not available on the day, and that is the entire reason for a discipline that looks excessive on the three hundred and sixty-four days when nothing occurs.

verseByVerse.quote: When you walk, they will lead you; when you lie down, they will watch over you; and when you awake, they will talk with you. For the commandment is a lamp and the teaching a light, and the reproofs of discipline are the way of life, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you walk, they will lead you; when you lie down, they will watch over you; and when you awake, they will talk with you.

Three times of day, three different services, and the third is the surprising one.

Walking, wisdom leads — it goes in front while a man is making decisions. Lying down, it watches over him, which is what you say of a sentry, or a nurse, or a parent at a bedside; something is awake while he is not. And when he wakes, it talks with him.

Pause on that last one, because it names an experience most Christians have had without connecting it to a verse. There is a particular quality to the first minutes of consciousness, before the day has arranged itself, when whatever is really in a man surfaces on its own. Fear talks then. So does resentment. So, if it is there, does Scripture — which is why what a person puts into himself deliberately at eleven at night is very often what speaks to him uninvited at six.

Then v. 23 gives the reason: the commandment is a lamp and the teaching a light. And a lamp in the ancient world was a small clay dish with a wick — enough to see the next few feet of floor, and not one step more. That is exactly the promise Scripture makes about itself. Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path (Psalm 119:105). Not a floodlight over the whole road. A lamp at the feet, which is all a man needs to take the next step and never as much as he would like.

verseByVerse.quote: to preserve you from the evil woman, from the smooth tongue of the adulteress. Do not desire her beauty in your heart, and do not let her capture you with her eyelashes; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The purpose of the lamp is now given: to preserve you from the evil woman, from the smooth tongue of the adulteress. Once again it is the tongue, not the face, and the chapter has already told us why — a man who is being properly talked to at home is much harder to talk to elsewhere.

Then the command that decides the whole matter: do not desire her beauty in your heart.

The battlefield has moved. Not do not touch her, not do not go to her house — in your heart. Proverbs locates the sin at the point of desire, before anything has been done and while a man could still truthfully say that nothing has happened.

Which is precisely where Jesus put it, in a sentence that has troubled every honest reader since: everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart (Matthew 5:28). He was not raising the standard. He was quoting the standard, from here, and refusing to let anybody keep the outside of the law while the inside was doing as it liked.

And then the last clause, which is almost tender in its precision: do not let her capture you with her eyelashes. The whole disaster of this chapter — the wounds, the dishonour, the disgrace that is never wiped away — is traced back to a glance held half a second too long. That is where it starts. Not in a decision, in a look that was returned.

verseByVerse.quote: for the price of a prostitute is only a loaf of bread, but a married woman hunts down a precious life. Can a man carry fire next to his chest and his clothes not be burned? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the price of a prostitute is only a loaf of bread, but a married woman hunts down a precious life.

The Hebrew here is genuinely compressed and older versions pull two ways: it may mean that a prostitute reduces a man to his last loaf, or that her price is merely a loaf while the adulteress costs a life. The ESV takes the second, and it fits the chapter’s argument, which from here to the end is a comparison of costs.

Neither reading is any kind of endorsement. The point is arithmetic, and it is brutal: one transaction costs a man money; the other costs him everything he is. And the verb is hunts down — the language of tracking an animal, patient and deliberate, over ground the quarry does not know is being watched.

Then the father abandons argument altogether and asks two questions no one can answer. Can a man carry fire next to his chest and his clothes not be burned?

Look at how the picture is built. He is not throwing fire at somebody. He is carrying it — holding it in against himself, in the fold of his robe, which is how a man carried something he wanted to keep. It is the posture of protecting a thing, not of attacking with it.

That is the truest image of a secret affair in Scripture. He does not think of himself as setting anything alight. He thinks he is holding something precious, close, carefully — and the cloth is burning the entire time, and there is no version of the story in which a man holds fire against his chest and the fabric decides not to catch.

verseByVerse.quote: Or can one walk on hot coals and his feet not be scorched? So is he who goes in to his neighbor's wife; none who touches her will go unpunished. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or can one walk on hot coals and his feet not be scorched? The second question raises the stakes on the first. Fire in the robe burns cloth, and cloth can be replaced. Coals under the feet burn the man himself, and now he cannot walk away from the injury because the injury is in the part of him that walks.

Then the conclusion, and it is the flattest and most absolute sentence in the chapter: so is he who goes in to his neighbour’s wife; none who touches her will go unpunished.

None. Proverbs is a book of general observation and it hedges a great deal, but it does not hedge here. The claim is not that this is usually discovered, or that it tends to end badly. It is that the consequence is built into the structure of things, exactly as burning is built into fire, and no amount of care in the handling alters it.

The obvious objection is that people plainly do get away with it, and the objection misreads what is being promised. The verse does not say a man will be found out; it says he will not go unpunished. Much of the burning happens in a place nobody can see — in what a man becomes while he manages it: the practised lying, the two selves, the incapacity for intimacy with anybody at all because intimacy now requires an account of where he has been. A man may keep this hidden for thirty years and never once escape it. He is not getting away with it. He is carrying it.

And his neighbour’s wife is a phrase that will not let go of the third party. There is always a man in this story who did nothing at all, and whose house is on fire.

verseByVerse.quote: People do not despise a thief if he steals to satisfy his appetite when he is hungry, but if he is caught, he will pay sevenfold; he will give all the goods of his house. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the father does something unexpected: he defends a thief. People do not despise a thief if he steals to satisfy his appetite when he is hungry.

Not that theft is permitted — the very next line has him paying sevenfold. But the community understands him. A man who takes bread because he has none has done a wrong thing for a reason every person in the room can feel, and nobody spits when he passes. There is a kind of sympathy available to him.

Then v. 31 refuses to let the sympathy do too much work: but if he is caught, he will pay sevenfold; he will give all the goods of his house. Sevenfold is the language of completeness rather than a legal tariff, and the second clause explains it — everything in the house. Understanding a man’s motive does not cancel the debt.

And here is where the comparison is going, and why it is set up so carefully. Even at his worst, the thief has two things going for him: a motive people can respect, and a debt that can be paid. Everything he took had a price on it, and when the price is met the matter is genuinely closed. He can walk out of the house with nothing and be, in the only sense that counts, square.

Hold that against what is coming in the next verses, because the whole force of the passage is in the contrast: the adulterer has neither. No hunger to plead, and nothing he can hand over.

verseByVerse.quote: He who commits adultery lacks sense; he who does it destroys himself. He will get wounds and dishonor, and his disgrace will not be wiped away. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who commits adultery lacks sense. The Hebrew says he lacks heart — lev, the organ that governs a man — and the phrase is not an insult about his intelligence. It is a statement that the steering has gone. Something is doing the driving, and it is not the part of him that makes decisions.

Then the phrase that separates this from the thief: he who does it destroys himself. Not risks himself. Destroys. And it is reflexive — nobody is doing it to him.

Then the bill, in three items. Wounds — real ones, in a world where an angry husband was a physical fact. Dishonour — the loss of standing in a community where a man’s name was most of what he owned. And then the third, which is the one that outlasts the others: his disgrace will not be wiped away.

The verb is the one used of erasing writing from a surface. The thief’s debt could be paid, and the ledger cleaned. This cannot be rubbed out. Long after the affair is over, long after the man is genuinely and thoroughly repentant, the thing sits in a family’s history where anybody can see it. That is not vindictiveness; it is simply what this sin does. It writes on people who did not consent to be written on.

And so the chapter arrives, without meaning to, at the exact place where the gospel becomes necessary rather than merely comforting. Proverbs says the disgrace cannot be wiped away, and Proverbs is right; there is no human mechanism that does it. But the New Testament reaches for that same image and uses that same kind of verb, and says that God has done what the ledger could not: he cancelled the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands, nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:14). The record was not misplaced, and it was not excused. It was taken off the wall, and driven through with a nail, into the hands of somebody else.

verseByVerse.quote: For jealousy makes a man furious, and he will not spare when he takes revenge. He will accept no compensation; he will refuse though you multiply gifts. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
For jealousy makes a man furious, and he will not spare when he takes revenge. He will accept no compensation; he will refuse though you multiply gifts.

The chapter ends inside the head of the man nobody has mentioned: the husband. And the first thing to say is that his jealousy is not presented here as a character flaw. Scripture uses the same word of God himself, who calls himself a jealous God (Exodus 34:14) — because jealousy, properly understood, is not the fear of losing a possession. It is the response of a covenant love to the violation of that covenant, and a man who felt nothing at all in these circumstances would not be admirable. He would simply not have loved her.

Then the point the whole second half of the chapter has been driving toward, laid out in commercial terms: he will accept no compensation. The thief could pay sevenfold and be finished. Here there is no figure. Multiply the gifts as high as you like and the answer does not change, because nothing was taken that has a price.

That is the final argument of Proverbs 6, and it is not a threat about an angry man. It is a statement about the kind of thing a marriage is. Some things in the world can be compensated; they are the things that were quantities in the first place. A person is not a quantity. What was broken here was not an asset but a bond, and no amount of anything can be exchanged for a bond, which is precisely what makes it worth having.

And yet the chapter’s last word is not the last word, because there is one place in Scripture where an unappeasable jealousy was appeased and an uncompensatable debt was paid. God took a bride and she went after other lovers, and there was no gift she could multiply and nothing she could bring. So the offended husband paid it himself. He did not accept compensation; he provided it, out of his own body, and bought back the very wife who had wronged him — not because the debt was small, but because he would rather bear it than lose her.
