verseByVerse.quote: Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets, but he who is trustworthy in spirit keeps a thing covered. Where there is no guidance, a people falls, but in an abundance of counselors there is safety. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets'—the slanderer trades in others' vulnerabilities; every private confidence betrayed is a small act of social destruction. 'He who is trustworthy in spirit keeps a thing covered'—keeping confidences is a form of love; the trustworthy person becomes a shelter for others. 'In an abundance of counselors there is safety'—the lone decision-maker is vulnerable to blind spots; wisdom seeks multiple perspectives. Waltke: this is the anti-authoritarian strand in Proverbs—even a king needs advisers.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever puts up security for a stranger will surely suffer harm, but he who hates striking hands in pledge is secure. A gracious woman gets honor, and violent men get riches. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever puts up security for a stranger'—financial co-signing for someone unknown is folly, not generosity; wisdom requires knowing who you are trusting with your resources. 'A gracious woman gets honor'—hen (grace, favor) is covenant love expressed in bearing; the gracious woman's character is her lasting legacy. 'Violent men get riches'—Proverbs does not deny that wickedness sometimes succeeds in the short term; it insists that what they get is not what they think it is, and that honor is the superior acquisition.

verseByVerse.quote: A man who is kind benefits himself, but a cruel man hurts himself. The wicked earns deceptive wages, but one who sows righteousness gets a sure reward. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A man who is kind benefits himself'—kindness is not self-sacrifice at the expense of the self but the form of life that produces the most flourishing. 'A cruel man hurts himself'—cruelty is self-destructive; the brutal person hardens his own soul and destabilizes the relationships he needs. 'The wicked earns deceptive wages'—the Hebrew is 'wages of deceit': what wickedness offers as pay turns out to be counterfeit. Keller: sin always overpromises and underdelivers. 'A sure reward'—righteousness produces a return that does not evaporate.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever is steadfast in righteousness will live, but he who pursues evil will die. Those of crooked heart are an abomination to the LORD, but those of blameless ways are his delight. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Steadfast in righteousness will live'—the Hebrew for 'steadfast' suggests a firm, established orientation rather than a momentary decision. Life is attached to righteousness as its proper fruit. 'He who pursues evil will die'—the active pursuit of evil is self-annihilation. 'Those of crooked heart are an abomination'—the word for 'crooked' describes a twisted, devious inner life; God's revulsion is directed not at bad behavior in isolation but at the distorted character that produces it. 'His delight'—blameless ways actually please God; sanctification is not God tolerating us but God enjoying what he is making.

verseByVerse.quote: Be assured, an evil man will not go unpunished, but the offspring of the righteous will be delivered. Like a gold ring in a pig's snout is a beautiful woman without discretion. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'An evil man will not go unpunished'—'be assured' is literally 'hand to hand,' the language of a guarantee; Proverbs puts its full weight behind this. Justice may be slow but not absent. 'The offspring of the righteous will be delivered'—righteousness blesses not only the individual but his household; the covenant promises of God travel through families. 'A gold ring in a pig's snout'—one of Proverbs' most vivid images: beauty without discretion is not merely wasted but actively incongruous. Kidner: physical beauty is a gift; character is what makes it inhabitable.

verseByVerse.quote: The desire of the righteous ends only in good, but the hope of the wicked in wrath. One person gives freely, yet gains even more; another withholds unduly, but comes to poverty. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The desire of the righteous ends only in good'—the telos of righteous desire is aligned with reality; what the righteous person wants is what God has purposed to give. 'One person gives freely, yet gains even more'—the economics of the kingdom invert natural expectation. Generosity is not philanthropy that depletes the giver but participation in God's own economy of abundance. Keller: the gospel logic is always dying and rising—what you release, God multiplies; what you hoard, you lose.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever brings blessing will be enriched, and one who waters will himself be watered. The people curse him who holds back grain, but a blessing is on the head of him who sells it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever brings blessing will be enriched'—the generous soul becomes the conduit for blessing and is enriched by being the channel. This is not prosperity-gospel transactionalism but the pattern of a God who says 'give, and it will be given to you' (Luke 6:38). 'He who holds back grain'—hoarding in a time of need is a moral failure, not merely an economic one. The man who sells grain rather than hoarding it is blessed—he participates in sustaining life. Waltke: ownership is stewardship; what we hold we hold on behalf of others.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever diligently seeks good seeks favor, but evil comes to him who searches for it. Whoever trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous will flourish like a green leaf. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever diligently seeks good seeks favor'—what you seek shapes what you find and who you become; the seeker of good becomes a person upon whom favor rests. 'Whoever trusts in his riches will fall'—wealth is not inherently evil (Proverbs celebrates the fruit of diligence) but trust in wealth is misplaced; wealth cannot sustain what only God can sustain. 'Flourish like a green leaf'—the image of organic vitality; the righteous are not merely not-dead but actively alive, growing, productive. Sproul: the Christian life is not maintenance but growth.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever troubles his own household will inherit the wind, and the fool will be servant to the wise of heart. The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and whoever captures souls is wise. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Troubles his own household will inherit the wind'—domestic dysfunction destroys the troubler himself; what he acquires by his folly is insubstantial, vapor, nothing. 'The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life'—the image of Eden restored: the righteous person's life produces the fruit of the tree of life, sustaining and healing others. 'Whoever captures souls is wise'—the Hebrew means 'takes lives' in a positive sense: the wise person who calls others to wisdom is doing the most life-giving work possible. Keller: this is the missionary impulse built into wisdom itself.

verseByVerse.quote: If the righteous is repaid on earth, how much more the wicked and the sinner! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'If the righteous is repaid on earth'—even the righteous face consequences for their sins in this life; the discipline of God is real. 'How much more the wicked and the sinner!'—if God does not overlook even minor failures in his own children, he will surely not overlook the gross wickedness of those who reject him. Peter quotes this verse (1 Pet. 4:18) to urge perseverance under suffering: if judgment begins with God's household, the ungodly have cause for serious alarm. Kidner: the verse is not a threat but a call to sober self-examination and joyful dependence on grace.

11.theology: Generosity as creation ethics. The paradox of verses 24–25 — give freely and grow richer; withhold and suffer want — is not merely social observation but theological claim. It reflects the character of the God who "gives generously to all without reproach" (Jas 1:5) and who does not become less by giving. The created order reflects the Creator's generosity: the sun gives its light and is not diminished; the spring gives its water and is not exhausted; the tree gives its fruit and produces more. The person who lives generously is living in harmony with the grain of a world made by the generous God. The person who hoards is living against that grain, and creation — and its Maker — pushes back. The New Testament makes the theological grounding explicit: "God so loved the world that he gave" (John 3:16). Generosity is Trinitarian ethics applied to human life.
11.examples:
Then: The false balance of verse 1 was not an abstract ethical problem in the ancient world; it was the everyday reality of the marketplace, where the temptation to cheat was constant and the detection of cheating was difficult. Leviticus 19:35–36 and Deuteronomy 25:13–16 prohibit the false weight explicitly; Amos 8:5 condemns it as a form of oppression of the poor. Proverbs frames it not as a violation of law but as an abomination to the LORD himself — which is a stronger and more personal condemnation. The business person who cheats their customers does not merely break a regulation; they revolt God.

Now: "In an abundance of counselors there is safety" (v. 14) is the wisdom text for governance, leadership, and organisational culture. The leader — whether of a family, a business, a church, or a nation — who surrounds themselves with people who agree with them, who dismisses challenge and criticism, who mistakes confidence for competence, is setting themselves up for the fall that pride always brings (v. 2). The cultivating of honest, diverse, wise counsel is not a sign of weakness; it is the most important leadership discipline Proverbs knows.

12.title: The Righteous and the Wicked
12.text: <sup>1</sup>Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge, but he who hates reproof is stupid. <sup>4</sup>An excellent wife is the crown of her husband, but she who brings shame is like rottenness in his bones. <sup>10</sup>Whoever is righteous has regard for the life of his animal, but the mercy of the wicked is cruel. <sup>15</sup>The way of a fool is right in his own eyes, but a wise man listens to advice. <sup>17</sup>Whoever speaks the truth gives honest evidence, but a false witness speaks deceitfully. <sup>18</sup>There is one whose rash words are like sword thrusts, but the tongue of the wise brings healing. <sup>22</sup>Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, but those who act faithfully are his delight. <sup>25</sup>Anxiety in a man's heart weighs him down, but a good word makes him glad.
12.overview:
Chapter 12 continues the pattern of antithetical proverbs, with particular attention to two themes: the contrast between the righteous and the wicked (seen in their relationship to discipline, speech, and truthfulness), and the power of words to wound or heal. The chapter opens with the blunt observation that loving discipline is inseparable from loving knowledge (v. 1) — a truth that most people resist — and closes with the beautiful pastoral insight that "a good word makes him glad" (v. 25).

The speech proverbs of this chapter (vv. 17–22) form a cluster of particular moral and pastoral weight. Words are not neutral — they are "like sword thrusts" or they "bring healing"; they are "an abomination to the LORD" (lying) or his "delight" (faithfulness). The God who spoke the world into existence and whose word is truth is the God who holds human words to the highest possible standard. Every lie is a mimicry of the father of lies (John 8:44); every true and healing word is a participation in the truth of the one who is the Word (John 1:1).

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 12 — Wisdom and Folly in Work, Words, and Character
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 12 pairs wisdom and folly in their effects on marriage, work, speech, and reputation. The upright woman (v.4) and the excellent wife contrast with destructive company; the diligent hand (v.24) versus the slack hand; truthful lips versus lying lips. Waltke: Proverbs 12 is a portrait gallery where every portrait is a binary—two paths, two outcomes, one choice.
verseByVerse.theology: Speech is the most prominent theme: truthful lips (v.17), lying tongue (v.19), rash words (v.18), healing words (v.18), the mouth of the righteous (v.6), lips that are the delight of kings (v.22). What we say reveals who we are and shapes who others become. The tongue is the gauge of the heart.
verseByVerse.examples: The excellent wife of v.4 echoes the explicit praise of ch.31. The proverb about the righteous caring for animals (v.10) grounds ethics in a comprehensive view of creation—stewardship of life at every level. The connection between word and deed, character and consequence, runs through every verse.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge, but he who hates reproof is stupid. A good man obtains favor from the LORD, but a man of evil devices he condemns. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge'—discipline is not punishment but the formation of character through correction; to embrace it is to choose growth over comfort. 'He who hates reproof is stupid'—the Hebrew word for stupid (ba'ar) means brutish, animal-like: to refuse correction is to operate below the level of human rationality. 'A good man obtains favor from the LORD'—favor is not earned by performance but flows naturally to the person whose character aligns with God's own goodness. Keller: grace and character are not opposites; grace produces the character that attracts further grace.

verseByVerse.quote: No one is established by wickedness, but the root of the righteous will never be moved. An excellent wife is the crown of her husband, but she who brings shame is like rottenness in his bones. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The root of the righteous will never be moved'—wickedness produces no foundation; righteousness produces one that endures. The root-metaphor emphasizes hiddenness: what is most important is underground, invisible. 'An excellent wife is the crown of her husband'—crown language is royal; she confers dignity and honor on him, adding to his stature in the community. 'Like rottenness in his bones'—the contrast is visceral: a shameful wife doesn't just embarrass but hollows out from within. Waltke: marriage is either the crown of a man's life or its slow destruction.

verseByVerse.quote: The thoughts of the righteous are just; the counsels of the wicked are deceitful. The words of the wicked lie in wait for blood, but the mouth of the upright delivers them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The thoughts of the righteous are just'—character shapes cognition; the righteous person's inner life is rightly ordered, and this produces just plans rather than self-serving ones. 'The counsels of the wicked are deceitful'—deceit is not an occasional tool of the wicked but their habitual mode. 'The words of the wicked lie in wait for blood'—speech as ambush; words that destroy lives before a physical blow is struck. 'The mouth of the upright delivers them'—righteous speech rescues; this is the positive power of words wielded by truthful people.

verseByVerse.quote: The wicked are overthrown and are no more, but the house of the righteous will stand. A man is commended according to his good sense, but one of twisted mind is despised. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The house of the righteous will stand'—permanence is attached to righteousness. The wicked may flourish temporarily, but they are not building anything that lasts. 'A man is commended according to his good sense'—public reputation ultimately tracks with genuine wisdom; culture may celebrate the clever fool for a season, but lasting commendation follows discernment. 'Twisted mind is despised'—the community's judgment eventually aligns with moral reality. Kidner: reputation is the public face of character; character eventually breaks through whatever mask is worn.

verseByVerse.quote: Better to be lowly and have a servant than to play the great man and lack bread. Whoever is righteous has regard for the life of his animal, but the mercy of the wicked is cruel. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Better to be lowly and have a servant'—Proverbs consistently prefers authentic modest wellbeing over pretentious poverty; the person who lives within his means is genuinely better off than the person who performs a prosperity he doesn't possess. 'Whoever is righteous has regard for the life of his animal'—one of Scripture's clearest statements about animal welfare. The righteous person's justice extends to every creature under his care. 'The mercy of the wicked is cruel'—even their best intentions produce harm; without righteousness as the foundation, good intentions are not enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread, but he who follows worthless pursuits lacks sense. Whoever is wicked covets the spoil of evildoers, but the root of the righteous bears fruit. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever works his land will have plenty'—the connection between diligent work and material provision is one of Proverbs' most consistent themes. This is not prosperity gospel but creational reality: God built provision into the pattern of faithful labor. 'He who follows worthless pursuits lacks sense'—'worthless' is the word for emptiness, vanity, vapor; chasing empty things is the definition of foolishness. 'The root of the righteous bears fruit'—vitality and production are the natural outcomes of righteousness, not accidental byproducts.

verseByVerse.quote: An evil man is ensnared by the transgression of his lips, but the righteous escapes from trouble. From the fruit of his mouth a man is satisfied with good, and the work of a man's hand comes back to him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Ensnared by the transgression of his lips'—the evil person is caught in his own words: every lie requires another, every false claim creates a web. 'The righteous escapes from trouble'—not because he is clever at evasion but because his words create no traps. 'From the fruit of his mouth a man is satisfied'—righteous speech produces the speaker's own satisfaction; there is an intrinsic reward to truthful, helpful, constructive words. 'The work of a man's hand comes back to him'—labor and word both operate on the boomerang principle: what you send out returns to you.

verseByVerse.quote: The way of a fool is right in his own eyes, but a wise man listens to advice. The vexation of a fool is known at once, but the prudent man ignores an insult. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Right in his own eyes'—self-referential certainty is the hallmark of folly; the fool has no external standard to check himself against, so he is always right and always in danger. 'A wise man listens to advice'—the willingness to hear correction is a defining attribute of wisdom in Proverbs (counsel appears dozens of times). 'The vexation of a fool is known at once'—the fool's anger is immediately visible: reactive, unfiltered, undisciplined. 'The prudent man ignores an insult'—not from weakness but from the strength to choose which battles matter. Kidner: the wise person knows that reacting to every provocation is itself a form of being controlled by others.

verseByVerse.quote: An honest witness tells the truth, but a false witness utters deceit. There is one whose rash words are like sword thrusts, but the tongue of the wise brings healing. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'An honest witness tells the truth'—in a legal context, truthful testimony is a moral obligation; false witness is a capital offense in the Torah (Deut. 19:18–19). 'Rash words are like sword thrusts'—the Hebrew for rash means 'spoken without thought,' but the damage is real and deep. Words wound as surely as blades. 'The tongue of the wise brings healing'—the positive power of speech: words can repair what rash words destroy. Sproul: one of the Holy Spirit's most needed works in the believer's life is the sanctification of the tongue (James 3:1–12).

verseByVerse.quote: Truthful lips endure forever, but a lying tongue is but for a moment. Deceit is in the heart of those who devise evil, but those who plan peace have joy. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Truthful lips endure forever'—truth has a permanence that corresponds to reality itself; a lie is a distortion of what is and cannot outlast what is. 'A lying tongue is but for a moment'—however successful the deception, it is temporary; reality reasserts itself. 'Those who plan peace have joy'—the Hebrew shalom-planner's inner life is characterized by joy. Waltke: peace-making is not passive but active—it requires planning, intention, constructive effort—and it rewards the planner with the very shalom he creates for others.

verseByVerse.quote: No ill befalls the righteous, but the wicked are filled with trouble. Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, but those who act faithfully are his delight. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'No ill befalls the righteous'—not a naïve denial of suffering (Job, the Psalms, Jesus himself are counterexamples) but a statement about ultimate orientation: no real, lasting, destroying harm can befall the person whom God is for. 'Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD'—God hates lying not because it violates a rule but because he is the God of truth; every lie is an offense against his character. 'Those who act faithfully are his delight'—faithfulness mirrors God's own covenant fidelity; when a human being acts faithfully, God recognizes himself in it.

verseByVerse.quote: A prudent man conceals knowledge, but the heart of fools proclaims folly. The hand of the diligent will rule, while the slothful will be put to forced labor. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A prudent man conceals knowledge'—not deception but discernment: knowing when to speak and when not to. The prudent person does not display everything he knows. 'The heart of fools proclaims folly'—the fool has no internal editor; what is in the heart comes immediately to the mouth. 'The hand of the diligent will rule'—diligence produces leadership. Work creates capacity, and capacity creates authority. 'The slothful will be put to forced labor'—the idle person ends up working under compulsion, having forfeited the freedom that diligence would have produced. Kidner: laziness is not freedom but a path to servitude.

verseByVerse.quote: Anxiety in a man's heart weighs him down, but a good word makes him glad. One who is righteous is a guide to his neighbor, but the way of the wicked leads them astray. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Anxiety in a man's heart weighs him down'—the Hebrew for weighs down suggests bowing the head, physical heaviness. Anxiety is a reality Proverbs does not deny. 'A good word makes him glad'—the antidote to anxiety is often a word from another person; this is the social function of pastoral speech. 'One who is righteous is a guide to his neighbor'—the righteous person does not merely know the right path but leads others onto it. 'The way of the wicked leads them astray'—the wicked are not merely lost but leading others into lostness. Influence is moral.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever is slothful will not roast his game, but the diligent man will get precious wealth. In the path of righteousness is life, and in its pathway there is no death. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever is slothful will not roast his game'—the lazy person cannot complete even what he starts; the hunt succeeds but the cooking never happens. Energy without follow-through produces nothing. 'In the path of righteousness is life'—the final verse of the chapter is a thesis statement: righteousness and life are inseparable. 'In its pathway there is no death'—death does not travel the road of righteousness. This is not immortality-by-moralism but the orientation of an entire life toward the Life-giver. Sproul: the path of righteousness is not the path we build by our effort but the path blazed by Christ into which we enter by faith.

12.theology: The image of God and the ethics of speech. Chapter 12's speech proverbs (vv. 17–22) are grounded in the theology of the image of God. Human beings are made in the image of the God who spoke the world into existence, whose word is truth, and whose name is faithful. When human beings speak truly, they reflect their Maker; when they lie, they distort the image and align themselves with the one Jesus calls "a liar and the father of lies" (John 8:44). The seriousness with which Proverbs treats truthfulness — "an abomination to the LORD" for lying, "his delight" for faithfulness — reflects this theological grounding. Speech is not neutral; it is one of the primary arenas in which the image of God is either honoured or defaced.
12.examples:
Then: "Whoever is righteous has regard for the life of his animal" (v. 10) is one of Proverbs' most unexpected ethical observations. Animal welfare is a sign of righteousness — the capacity for care extends beyond the human community to the creatures entrusted to human stewardship. This is creation ethics in miniature: the righteous person treats their animals with the same kind of regard that the Creator has for his creation. The wicked person's "mercy" — even their attempts at kindness — is described as "cruel," because cruelty is what happens when you imitate mercy without the character that makes mercy real.

Now: "A good word makes him glad" (v. 25) is the pastoral charter for encouragement as a spiritual discipline. In a culture of criticism — online and offline — where the easy response to anything is scepticism, cynicism, or complaint, the deliberate cultivation of the encouraging word is an act of wisdom and love. Keller points to this as an application of the gospel: the person who knows they are loved and welcomed by God is freed to give away the good words that others need. Encouragement is not flattery; it is the truthful affirmation of what is genuinely good in a person, offered at the moment when the weight of anxiety needs a word to lift it.

13.title: Hope Deferred
13.text: <sup>1</sup>A wise son hears his father's instruction, but a scoffer does not listen to rebuke. <sup>7</sup>One pretends to be rich, yet has nothing; another pretends to be poor, yet has great wealth. <sup>10</sup>By insolence comes nothing but strife, but with those who take advice is wisdom. <sup>12</sup>Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life. <sup>16</sup>In everything the prudent acts with knowledge, but a fool flaunts his folly. <sup>20</sup>Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm. <sup>22</sup>A good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children, but the sinner's wealth is laid up for the righteous. <sup>24</sup>Whoever spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him is diligent to discipline him.
13.overview:
Chapter 13 touches on themes of wealth and poverty (both real and pretended), the long view of wisdom, the power of association, and the nature of parental love. At its emotional centre is one of the most universally resonant verses in Proverbs: "Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life" (v. 12). This proverb is not an instruction or a command; it is a diagnosis — a precise and compassionate observation about the inner experience of waiting, disappointment, and eventual fulfilment.

The chapter also contains two of Proverbs' most important social and relational observations: "Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise" (v. 20) — the wisdom of chosen community — and "whoever spares the rod hates his son" (v. 24) — the love that disciplines. Together these proverbs describe the two primary environments in which wisdom is formed: the community of the wise that shapes us by association, and the family of love that shapes us by discipline. Neither is optional; both are forms of love in action.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 13 — Discipline, Hope, and the Intergenerational Stakes of Wisdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 13 is preoccupied with consequences that extend across time: hope deferred and hope fulfilled (v.12), a good man leaving an inheritance (v.22), the rod of discipline and the child's future (v.24). Wealth and poverty appear in multiple angles—honest gain, fraudulent gain, the wealth of the diligent, the ruin of the sluggard. Every proverb is a small window into the long-game nature of wisdom.
verseByVerse.theology: Proverbs 13 insists that parental discipline is an act of love (v.24)—one of the most countercultural claims in the book. The culture says love means giving children what they want; Proverbs says love means shaping children into what they should be. The parent who withholds discipline hates the child; the parent who applies it loves.
verseByVerse.examples: Hope deferred as heart-sickness (v.12) is one of Scripture's most psychologically accurate descriptions. Every counselor recognizes it: the patient who has longed for something good and been repeatedly disappointed. The gospel addresses hope deferred not by promising quick fulfillment but by providing an anchor (Heb. 6:19) that holds even when fulfillment is delayed.

verseByVerse.quote: A wise son hears his father's instruction, but a scoffer does not listen to rebuke. From the fruit of his mouth a man eats what is good, but the desire of the treacherous is for violence. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A wise son hears his father's instruction'—the opening contrast revisits the central pedagogical relationship of chapters 1–9: the son who listens is the son who becomes wise. The father's instruction is the vehicle of wisdom through time. 'A scoffer does not listen to rebuke'—the scoffer is the consummate unteachable person; he has pre-decided that external correction has nothing to offer him. 'From the fruit of his mouth a man eats what is good'—words have consequences for the speaker; righteous speech produces good outcomes that the speaker himself enjoys. Speech and consequence are joined.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever guards his mouth preserves his life; he who opens wide his lips comes to ruin. The soul of the sluggard craves and gets nothing, while the soul of the diligent is richly supplied. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever guards his mouth preserves his life'—the mouth is the critical vulnerability; unguarded speech is one of the most common paths to self-destruction. 'He who opens wide his lips comes to ruin'—the image of the widely opened mouth suggests uninhibited, careless, unfiltered speech that pours out without wisdom. 'The soul of the sluggard craves and gets nothing'—desire without discipline produces nothing. The sluggard wants the outcome but refuses the process. 'The diligent is richly supplied'—desire plus discipline produces abundance. Kidner: appetite alone accomplishes nothing; appetite yoked to effort changes the world.

verseByVerse.quote: The righteous hates falsehood, but the wicked brings shame and disgrace. Righteousness guards him whose way is blameless, but sin overthrows the wicked. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The righteous hates falsehood'—not merely avoids but hates; the moral formation of the righteous person produces a visceral aversion to deception. This is how character works: it is not only behavioral restraint but transformed desire. 'Brings shame and disgrace'—the wicked person is his own shame, not merely the object of others' disapproval. 'Righteousness guards him'—righteousness functions as a protector; the blameless person has a defense that is not his own cleverness or strength. Waltke: God's character, as we share in it through wisdom, becomes our shelter.

verseByVerse.quote: One pretends to be rich, yet has nothing; another pretends to be poor, yet has great wealth. The ransom of a man's life is his wealth, but a poor man hears no threat. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'One pretends to be rich, yet has nothing'—the performance of prosperity conceals genuine poverty; the pretense is not sustainable. 'Another pretends to be poor, yet has great wealth'—the wealthy person who presents as poor: perhaps from wisdom (avoiding envy), perhaps from miserliness. Proverbs does not condemn either without context but notes both as realities. 'The ransom of a man's life is his wealth'—the wealthy person can be threatened: kidnappers target the rich. 'A poor man hears no threat'—poverty has an ironic protection from a particular kind of danger. No one extorts someone who has nothing to give.

verseByVerse.quote: The light of the righteous rejoices, but the lamp of the wicked will be put out. By insolence comes nothing but strife, but with those who take advice is wisdom. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The light of the righteous rejoices'—light as vitality, direction, joy; the righteous person is characterized by an inner luminosity that expresses itself outward. 'The lamp of the wicked will be put out'—the wick runs out of oil; wickedness cannot self-sustain. 'By insolence comes nothing but strife'—insolence (pride, arrogance) is the generator of conflict; wherever you find chronic strife, you will find a proud person who refuses to yield. 'With those who take advice is wisdom'—the opposite posture: teachability is the path to wisdom, not an alternative to it.

verseByVerse.quote: Wealth gained hastily will dwindle, but whoever gathers little by little will increase it. Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Wealth gained hastily will dwindle'—quick acquisition by questionable means has no root system; it dissipates as quickly as it came. 'Whoever gathers little by little will increase it'—patient, incremental, honest accumulation builds genuine wealth. The principle is organic growth rather than speculation. 'Hope deferred makes the heart sick'—one of Scripture's most psychologically true observations. The prolonged gap between longing and fulfillment produces literal sickness of spirit. 'A desire fulfilled is a tree of life'—when the longed-for thing finally comes, it gives life to the whole person. This is why the gospel's 'already' is so important: hope is not only future but partially present.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever despises the word brings destruction on himself, but he who reveres the commandment will be rewarded. The teaching of the wise is a fountain of life, that one may turn away from the snares of death. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever despises the word brings destruction on himself'—to dismiss God's word is not neutral; it is active self-harm. 'He who reveres the commandment will be rewarded'—reverence for divine instruction is rewarded, not because God is transactional but because the commandment describes the grain of reality, and moving with the grain produces good outcomes. 'A fountain of life'—Proverbs presents wisdom as a spring that never runs dry, producing life continuously rather than in one-time doses. 'Snares of death'—the dangers are real; wisdom is not optional decoration but survival equipment.

verseByVerse.quote: Good sense wins favor, but the way of the treacherous is their ruin. Every prudent man acts with knowledge, but a fool flaunts his folly. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Good sense wins favor'—the prudent person's reputation grows as his judgment proves reliable. Favor follows competence with wisdom. 'The way of the treacherous is their ruin'—treachery is self-destroying; every betrayal costs the betrayer something he cannot recover. 'Every prudent man acts with knowledge'—action and knowledge are linked in wisdom; the prudent person does not act impulsively but from accumulated, tested understanding. 'A fool flaunts his folly'—the fool is unaware that his display of folly is a display; he thinks he is impressive. This self-deception is the essence of the fool's condition.

verseByVerse.quote: A wicked messenger falls into trouble, but a faithful envoy brings healing. Poverty and disgrace come to him who ignores instruction, but whoever heeds reproof is honored. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A faithful envoy brings healing'—the messenger is not only a carrier of information but a representative of integrity; the faithful one can be trusted with sensitive communication and thus becomes a reconciling force. 'Poverty and disgrace come to him who ignores instruction'—the consequences of refusing wisdom are material (poverty) and relational (disgrace). Both are real. 'Whoever heeds reproof is honored'—the willingness to hear correction is one of the most consistently honored qualities in Proverbs. It signals teachability, humility, and the wisdom to recognize one's limits.

verseByVerse.quote: A desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, but to turn away from evil is an abomination to fools. Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul'—Proverbs does not denigrate desire; legitimate desire fulfilled is one of God's good gifts to humans. 'To turn away from evil is an abomination to fools'—the fool finds repentance repulsive; the moral turnaround required by wisdom offends him. This is the deepest sign of foolishness: not ignorance but refusal. 'Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise'—formation happens by proximity; the character of companions shapes the character of the person. 'Companion of fools will suffer harm'—the negative version: fools' influence is contagious and destructive. Choose your companions carefully.

verseByVerse.quote: Disaster pursues sinners, but the righteous are rewarded with good. A good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children, but the sinner's wealth is laid up for the righteous. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Disaster pursues sinners'—the image of pursuit: sin does not merely have consequences, it hunts. 'The righteous are rewarded with good'—good, not as payment but as the natural return on righteousness. 'A good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children'—the long-term orientation of wisdom; the righteous person builds for the third generation, not just his own lifetime. This is the opposite of consumerism. 'The sinner's wealth is laid up for the righteous'—the transfer of wealth across generations ultimately follows righteousness, not wickedness. Providence is the longest game of all.

verseByVerse.quote: The fallow ground of the poor would yield much food, but it is swept away through injustice. Whoever spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him is diligent to discipline him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Fallow ground of the poor would yield much food, but swept away through injustice'—a lament about structural evil: the poor have resources that are systematically taken from them by the unjust powerful. Proverbs is not naive about socioeconomic injustice. 'Whoever spares the rod hates his son'—Proverbs' most striking claim about parenting: to withhold discipline is a form of hatred, not kindness. 'He who loves him is diligent to discipline'—the diligence emphasizes constancy: this is not an occasional intervention but a sustained, attentive, intentional formation of character. Love acts for the child's long-term flourishing, not his immediate comfort.

verseByVerse.quote: The righteous has enough to satisfy his appetite, but the belly of the wicked suffers want. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The righteous has enough to satisfy his appetite'—satisfaction, not excess; wisdom produces sufficiency rather than endless accumulation. The righteous person knows when enough is enough. 'The belly of the wicked suffers want'—want (lack) as the end of wickedness; no amount of acquisition fills the void that is not a material problem. Keller: the stomach of the wicked is a metaphor for the insatiability of disordered desire. Only the righteous, whose deepest appetite is for God himself, can be genuinely satisfied—because God is genuinely satisfying.

13.theology: Hope, eschatology, and the tree of life. Proverbs 13:12 — "hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life" — carries eschatological weight that the original context only hints at. The "tree of life" is a deliberate echo of Genesis 2–3 and an anticipation of Revelation 22:2. Human longing for the desire finally fulfilled — for the hope that does not defer indefinitely — is the deepest longing of the creature for the Creator, for the restoration of the relationship and the world that sin destroyed. Every earthly experience of a desire fulfilled, every moment when the long-deferred hope finally arrives, is a shadow of the ultimate fulfilment: the face-to-face knowledge of God in the new creation, the tree of life available to all, the heart-sickness of waiting finally resolved. The gospel is the announcement that the desire has been fulfilled in Christ — and that the full experience of that fulfilment awaits the consummation of all things.
13.examples:
Then: "A good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children" (v. 22) sets a multigenerational horizon for wisdom and faithfulness. The wise person does not merely plan for their own flourishing but for the flourishing of their grandchildren — which requires the kind of long-term thinking, patient investment, and deferred gratification that Proverbs consistently commends. The contrast with "the sinner's wealth laid up for the righteous" reflects the reversal of fortunes that Proverbs sees in the long run: the unjust accumulation of the wicked ultimately benefits the righteous, whether through inheritance, restitution, or the simple working of providential justice.

Now: "Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise" (v. 20) is the wisdom text for mentorship, spiritual direction, and the deliberate cultivation of community. Keller observes that the modern tendency toward therapeutic individualism — the assumption that growth is primarily an internal, private process — runs counter to Proverbs' social understanding of wisdom formation. We are shaped by our communities; the question is not whether we will be formed by others but which others will form us. The wise person chooses their community with the same intentionality that they choose their work, their diet, or their reading — because the community is forming them whether they are aware of it or not.

14.title: The Way That Seems Right
14.text: <sup>4</sup>Where there are no oxen, the manger is clean, but abundant crops come by the strength of the ox. <sup>12</sup>There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death. <sup>20</sup>The poor is disliked even by his neighbor, but the rich has many friends. <sup>23</sup>In all toil there is profit, but mere talk leads only to poverty. <sup>26</sup>In the fear of the LORD one has strong confidence, and his children will have a refuge. <sup>29</sup>Whoever is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a hasty temper exalts folly. <sup>31</sup>Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker, but he who is generous to the needy honors him. <sup>34</sup>Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people.
14.overview:
Chapter 14 contains one of the most sobering verses in Proverbs — "there is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death" (v. 12) — and one of the most theologically charged — "whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker" (v. 31). Together these two proverbs capture two dimensions of the book's wisdom: epistemological humility (I cannot fully trust my own judgment about what is right) and social theology (how I treat the poor is how I treat the one who made them).

The chapter also contains one of Proverbs' most unsentimental economic observations: "Where there are no oxen, the manger is clean, but abundant crops come by the strength of the ox" (v. 4). Risk, mess, and the management of difficult resources are the price of productivity. The clean manger is the achievement of the person who has avoided all complexity and produced nothing. This is the wisdom of entrepreneurship, leadership, and any endeavour that requires investment: there is no abundant harvest without the ox, and no ox without the mess.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 14 — The Wise Woman, False Witness, and the Fear of the Lord
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 14 opens with the wise woman who builds her house and the fool who tears it down, and closes with the king who honors God by caring for the poor. Between those bookends: the danger of false witness, the deceitfulness of the heart, the fear of the Lord as the only reliable fountain of life. Waltke notes that ch.14 has a particularly high concentration of fool-sayings, as if Proverbs is pressing the reader toward a decision.
verseByVerse.theology: The fear of the LORD appears explicitly in vv.2 and 26-27: it is the foundation of integrity, the fortress of the faithful, and the only reliable protection against the snares of death. Everything else in the chapter—wise speech, honest witness, care for the poor, measured anger—flows from this root. Fear of God is not a feeling but a comprehensive orientation of the person toward the real world as God governs it.
verseByVerse.examples: The poor appear twice (vv.20-21, 31): those who despise the neighbor sin, but those who are kind to the needy honor God. The social ethics of Proverbs are grounded in theology: the poor bear the image of their Maker, and how we treat them reveals how we actually regard him.

verseByVerse.quote: The wisest of women builds her house, but folly with her own hands tears it down. Whoever walks in uprightness fears the LORD, but he who is devious in his ways despises him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The wisest of women builds her house'—wisdom is creative, constructive; she makes something permanent and good. 'Folly with her own hands tears it down'—folly is destructive but also ironic: the foolish woman destroys with the same hands that could build. Self-destruction is active, not passive. 'Whoever walks in uprightness fears the LORD'—the connection is immediate: walking straight IS fearing God; they are not two separate things. 'Devious in his ways despises him'—the devious person's crookedness is theological: it implies that God either does not see or does not matter. Crooked living is practical atheism.

verseByVerse.quote: By the mouth of a fool comes a rod for his back, but the lips of the wise will preserve them. Where there are no oxen, the manger is clean, but abundant crops come by the strength of the ox. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'By the mouth of a fool comes a rod for his back'—his words earn him punishment; the fool's speech is his own undoing. 'The lips of the wise will preserve them'—wisdom of speech is self-protective; thoughtful words keep their speaker out of trouble. 'Where there are no oxen, the manger is clean'—a memorable economic proverb: a clean stall means no animals, which means no work, which means no harvest. The mess of productive life is the cost of fruitfulness. Kidner: the proverb is an argument for accepting inconvenience and complexity as the price of productivity. Sterility is not cleanliness.

verseByVerse.quote: A faithful witness does not lie, but a false witness breathes out lies. A scoffer seeks wisdom in vain, but knowledge comes easily to a man of understanding. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A faithful witness does not lie'—trustworthiness in testimony is not heroic but definitional: to be a faithful witness simply IS not to lie. 'A false witness breathes out lies'—'breathes out' suggests that lying is as natural and constant as breathing for the false witness; it is not an occasional failure but a character state. 'A scoffer seeks wisdom in vain'—the scoffer cannot find what he refuses to receive; his posture of contempt closes the door to wisdom. 'Knowledge comes easily to a man of understanding'—the teachable person finds the door already open; reception is the key.

verseByVerse.quote: Leave the presence of a fool, for there you do not meet words of knowledge. The wisdom of the prudent is to discern his way, but the folly of fools is deceiving. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Leave the presence of a fool'—not cruelty but self-protection; prolonged exposure to foolishness shapes the listener. The fool is contagious. 'For there you do not meet words of knowledge'—the fool has nothing to offer the seeker of wisdom; his company is an intellectual and moral dead end. 'The wisdom of the prudent is to discern his way'—wisdom applied to navigation: the prudent person reads situations, reads character, reads the road ahead. 'The folly of fools is deceiving'—the fool deceives himself most of all; his self-deception is primary, his deception of others secondary.

verseByVerse.quote: Fools mock at the guilt offering, but the upright enjoy acceptance. The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares its joy. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Fools mock at the guilt offering'—to mock the sacrifice for sin is to deny the reality of sin and of the need for atonement. This is the fool's defining characteristic: he treats the most serious thing lightly. 'The upright enjoy acceptance'—the one who takes sin seriously receives the reconciliation that the fool dismisses. 'The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares its joy'—one of Proverbs' most psychologically profound observations: inner life has a privacy that no outsider fully penetrates. The deepest joys and the deepest griefs are not fully communicable. Keller: this is why we need both community and personal communion with God—community sustains us but cannot reach what only God can reach.

verseByVerse.quote: The house of the wicked will be destroyed, but the tent of the upright will flourish. There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The house of the wicked will be destroyed'—permanence, again, is attached to character, not to the appearance of solidity. 'The tent of the upright will flourish'—even a tent, the most temporary of dwellings, flourishes when righteousness inhabits it. 'There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death'—one of Proverbs' most quoted and most sobering proverbs. Internal approval is an unreliable guide; the feeling of rightness is not the same as being right. Sproul: conscience must be calibrated by Scripture or it will endorse what God condemns. The road to destruction is paved with sincere conviction.

verseByVerse.quote: Even in laughter the heart may ache, and the end of joy may be grief. The backslider in heart will be filled with the fruit of his ways, and a good man will be filled with the fruit of his ways. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Even in laughter the heart may ache'—Proverbs does not flatten human experience into simple cause-and-effect; grief and joy can coexist in the same moment. The laughing surface can conceal the aching depth. 'The end of joy may be grief'—not every joy leads somewhere good; pleasures with no future can tip into sorrow. 'The backslider in heart will be filled with the fruit of his ways'—the backslider is the one who turns away from wisdom; his own choices produce what fills him. 'A good man will be filled with the fruit of his ways'—the same principle, applied in both directions: we are filled by what we choose.

verseByVerse.quote: The simple believes everything, but the prudent gives thought to his steps. One who is wise is cautious and turns away from evil, but a fool is reckless and careless. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The simple believes everything'—credulity as a form of naivety; the simple person has no discernment filter. This is dangerous in an age of deception. 'The prudent gives thought to his steps'—deliberation is characteristic of wisdom; the prudent person does not react but reflects before acting. 'One who is wise is cautious and turns away from evil'—caution and moral separation are linked: the wise person does not merely recognize evil but moves away from it. 'A fool is reckless and careless'—'reckless' means overconfident, unaware of danger. Kidner: the fool's carelessness is not a personality trait but a spiritual posture—he does not believe that danger is real.

verseByVerse.quote: A man of quick temper acts foolishly, and a man of evil devices is hated. The simple inherit folly, but the prudent are crowned with knowledge. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A man of quick temper acts foolishly'—the connection between anger and foolishness is causal: reactive anger bypasses judgment and produces foolish actions. The quick-tempered person is reliably foolish because reliable wisdom requires time he refuses to take. 'A man of evil devices is hated'—the schemer, by contrast, is cold and calculated; both quick temper and cold scheming produce hatred, but by different routes. 'The simple inherit folly'—what you are, you accumulate more of. 'The prudent are crowned with knowledge'—knowledge is not merely held but worn; it becomes the defining feature, the mark of the person.

verseByVerse.quote: The evil bow down before the good, the wicked at the gates of the righteous. The poor is disliked even by his neighbor, but the rich has many friends. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The evil bow down before the good'—a statement of long-term trajectory; ultimately righteousness achieves what wickedness pursues (status, honor, deference). 'The wicked at the gates of the righteous'—the gates are where supplication happens. 'The poor is disliked even by his neighbor'—a clear-eyed observation about social reality: poverty is socially isolating; those with nothing to offer are avoided. Proverbs does not endorse this; it observes it as a feature of fallen human community. 'The rich has many friends'—whose friendship is worth examining. This verse pairs with v.21 to challenge the reader's response to poverty.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever despises his neighbor is a sinner, but blessed is he who is generous to the poor. Do they not go astray who devise evil? Those who devise good meet steadfast love and faithfulness. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever despises his neighbor is a sinner'—the contempt that the natural man feels for those beneath him is identified plainly as sin. The poor person is the neighbor of v.21, and contempt for him is not a social failure but a moral one. 'Blessed is he who is generous to the poor'—generosity to the poor is a path of blessing, not an obligation that costs the giver. 'Those who devise good meet steadfast love and faithfulness'—hesed and emet, the covenant attributes of God himself, meet those who plan good for others. To plan good for your neighbor is to walk in the way of the God who plans good for his people.

verseByVerse.quote: In all toil there is profit, but mere talk tends only to poverty. The crown of the wise is their wealth, but the folly of fools brings folly. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In all toil there is profit'—a sweeping affirmation of the value of work. Every legitimate labor produces something. 'Mere talk tends only to poverty'—words without corresponding work deplete rather than produce. The distinction is between speech that leads to action and speech that substitutes for it. 'The crown of the wise is their wealth'—wisdom's crown is not just spiritual; it includes material flourishing. The fool's crown, by contrast, is more folly: what the fool gains is not advancement but deeper entrenchment in folly's cycle.

verseByVerse.quote: A truthful witness saves lives, but one who breathes out lies is deceitful. In the fear of the LORD one has strong confidence, and his children will have a refuge. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A truthful witness saves lives'—in the legal context of the ancient Near East, honest testimony was literally life-saving. But the principle extends: truthful people are socially life-giving. 'In the fear of the LORD one has strong confidence'—the source of genuine confidence is not self-assurance but theocentric certainty: the person who fears God knows that ultimate reality is on his side. 'His children will have a refuge'—the fear of God extends protection intergenerationally. The parents' theological faithfulness creates a shelter for the next generation. Waltke: covenantal faithfulness is the most durable legacy a parent can leave.

verseByVerse.quote: The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life, that one may turn away from the snares of death. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life'—the fear of God is generative: it produces life rather than merely constraining behavior. A fountain flows constantly; fear of God is not a periodic religious exercise but a continuous source of vitality. 'The snares of death'—death is not passive but actively snaring; the world is full of traps that the God-fearer can see and avoid. Keller: the Christian who does not practice conscious dependence on God is not spiritually self-sufficient—he is unarmed. The fear of God arms you with the wisdom to see what others walk into blindly.

verseByVerse.quote: In a multitude of people is the glory of a king, but without people a prince is ruined. Whoever is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a hasty temper exalts folly. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In a multitude of people is the glory of a king'—population was the measure of a king's power and success in the ancient world; a depleted people meant a depleted kingdom. The leader's greatness is not separable from his people's flourishing. 'Whoever is slow to anger has great understanding'—the link between emotional regulation and intellectual capacity: it takes genuine understanding to pause before reacting. 'He who has a hasty temper exalts folly'—the angry person inadvertently promotes folly; every outburst is a public demonstration of foolishness. The self-controlled person promotes wisdom by the same logic.

verseByVerse.quote: A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh, but envy makes the bones rot. Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker, but he who is generous to the needy honors him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh'—inner peace has a physical dimension; the person at peace with God and neighbors is physically healthier. 'Envy makes the bones rot'—envy is self-corrosive; it eats the envier from inside while the envied person suffers no harm. 'Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker'—the poor person bears the image of God; to oppress him is to commit an offense against the Creator whose image he bears. 'He who is generous to the needy honors him'—generosity to the poor is worship. Social ethics and theology are inseparable in Proverbs; how we treat the poor is how we treat God.

verseByVerse.quote: The wicked is overthrown through his evildoing, but the righteous finds refuge in his death. Wisdom rests in the heart of a man of understanding, but it makes itself known even in the midst of fools. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The righteous finds refuge in his death'—one of Proverbs' most hopeful statements: for the righteous, death is not disaster but refuge. This anticipates the fuller revelation that for the believer, to die is gain (Phil. 1:21). The wicked are overthrown by what they trusted; the righteous are sheltered by what they trusted even through death. 'Wisdom rests in the heart of a man of understanding'—wisdom is at home there; it is not forced or performed but organic. 'Makes itself known even in the midst of fools'—wisdom cannot ultimately be suppressed; it surfaces even in unlikely contexts because it corresponds to reality.

verseByVerse.quote: Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people. A servant who deals wisely has the king's favor, but his wrath falls on one who acts shamefully. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people'—perhaps the most famous political proverb in the book: the health of nations is ultimately a moral question. Calvin cited this verse frequently: the public good and private virtue are inseparable. No political structure, no economic system, no diplomatic achievement can compensate for the moral corrosion that sin produces at the national level. 'A servant who deals wisely has the king's favor'—competent, wise service is noticed and rewarded at every level of society. The faithful employee who brings wisdom to his work builds a reputation that eventually reaches the highest levels.

14.theology: Epistemological humility and the way that seems right. Proverbs 14:12 is the wisdom literature's most explicit warning against the fundamental human epistemological problem: we cannot fully trust our own moral perception. The fall has distorted not only our wills but our minds — we rationalise, justify, and self-deceive with remarkable sophistication. Reformed theology calls this the noetic effects of sin: the corruption of human reason by the fall. The antidote Proverbs prescribes is not the exercise of more careful reason but the submission of reason to the word of God: "trust in the LORD with all your heart and do not lean on your own understanding" (3:5). The way that seems right is diagnosed by the standard of the one whose ways are always right — and that standard is available in Scripture, received by the humble, and applied by the fear of the LORD.
14.examples:
Then: "Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker" (v. 31) had immediate and specific application in the economic realities of ancient Israel: the wealthy landowner who withheld wages, the merchant who used false weights, the judge who took bribes — all were doing theology, whether they knew it or not. The prophetic tradition (Amos, Isaiah, Micah) hammers on exactly this point: social injustice is theological offence. Proverbs frames it as wisdom: the person who grasps this truth — that the poor person is God's image-bearer — will treat them accordingly, not merely out of compassion but out of reverence.

Now: "The way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death" (v. 12) is the most important verse in Proverbs for an age that has made individual moral intuition the supreme ethical authority. "Seems right to me" has become the clinching argument in contemporary moral discourse. Proverbs' response is not to deny the importance of moral intuition but to insist that it is fallible — fallen, distorted, self-serving — and requires the correction of a standard outside itself. The fear of the LORD, received through Scripture, is that standard. The person who submits their "seems right" to God's word is practising the deepest form of epistemological humility.

15.title: A Soft Answer
15.text: <sup>1</sup>A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. <sup>3</sup>The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good. <sup>8</sup>The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD, but the prayer of the upright is his delight. <sup>13</sup>A glad heart makes a cheerful face, but by sorrow of heart the spirit is crushed. <sup>16</sup>Better is a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble with it. <sup>17</sup>Better is a dinner of herbs where love is than a fattened ox and hatred with it. <sup>22</sup>Without counsel plans fail, but with many advisers they succeed. <sup>23</sup>To make an apt answer is a joy to a man, and a word in season, how good it is! <sup>29</sup>The LORD is far from the wicked, but he hears the prayer of the righteous. <sup>33</sup>The fear of the LORD is instruction in wisdom, and humility comes before honor.
15.overview:
Chapter 15 is rich in speech proverbs, "better than" comparisons, and observations about God's active engagement with human life. It opens with one of the most practically powerful proverbs in the book — "a soft answer turns away wrath" — and closes with the thesis of the entire wisdom tradition: "the fear of the LORD is instruction in wisdom, and humility comes before honor." The chapter consistently chooses quality of life over quantity: a little with the fear of the LORD over great treasure and trouble; a dinner of herbs where love is over a fattened ox with hatred.

The "better than" proverbs of this chapter (vv. 16–17) represent one of Proverbs' most important rhetorical strategies: the deliberate revaluation of what the world considers valuable. Great treasure, fattened oxen, grand feasts — these are the markers of success that every culture celebrates. Proverbs does not deny that they are good; it insists that they are less good than the things that money cannot buy: the fear of the LORD, love, peace, and the presence of God. The person who has learned to prefer the genuinely better over the apparently better has taken a long step toward wisdom.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 15 — Soft Words, Watchful God, and the Discipline That Leads to Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 15 opens with the most famous proverb on speech ('a soft answer turns away wrath') and closes with the fear of the LORD as the path to life. In between: the LORD who watches everywhere (v.3), the glad heart that makes a cheerful face (v.13), the value of the multitude of counselors (v.22), and the discipline that leads to the honored life (v.33). The chapter is a sustained meditation on what it means to live before the watching God.
verseByVerse.theology: God's omniscience (v.3) is not abstract theology but a pastoral reality: the eyes of the LORD are everywhere, watching evil and good. This should produce honest speech, careful conduct, and the joyful sobriety of knowing that you are never unwatched. The person who internalizes this lives differently—not in anxiety but in the freedom that comes from consistent accountability.
verseByVerse.examples: The cheerful heart and glad face (vv.13-15) are not commanded but produced: they are the fruit of wisdom, not its prerequisite. The person who fears God and walks in wisdom acquires a disposition of joy as a byproduct. Discipline (vv.31-33) is the path, not an obstacle—those who receive reproof inhabit wisdom.

verseByVerse.quote: A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. The tongue of the wise commends knowledge, but the mouths of fools pour out folly. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A soft answer turns away wrath'—the most power-reversing proverb in the book: the gentle response de-escalates what force would inflame. The person who answers softly is not weak but strategically powerful. 'A harsh word stirs up anger'—the same dynamic in reverse: harsh words are not merely ineffective but counterproductive; they multiply the anger they were meant to defeat. 'The tongue of the wise commends knowledge'—commend means 'makes beautiful, presents attractively.' The wise person presents knowledge in a form that makes others want it. 'Mouths of fools pour out folly'—unfiltered, undiscriminating, unedited. The wise speak carefully; the fool's mouth is an open spigot.

verseByVerse.quote: The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good. A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but perverseness in it breaks the spirit. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The eyes of the LORD are in every place'—divine omniscience is stated without qualification: no transaction, no bedroom, no boardroom, no hidden corner is unobserved. This is not presented as threat but as fact. The person who understands this lives in a completely different moral universe from the person who assumes God is distant or inattentive. Waltke: the watching God is simultaneously the God who cares enough to watch and the God whose watching is itself a form of governance. 'A gentle tongue is a tree of life'—the fourth occurrence of 'tree of life' in Proverbs (3:18; 11:30; 13:12); every occurrence points to Eden restored. Gentle speech is life-giving. 'Perverseness breaks the spirit'—the twisted tongue crushes the inner person.

verseByVerse.quote: A fool despises his father's instruction, but whoever heeds reproof is prudent. In the house of the righteous there is much treasure, but trouble is in the income of the wicked. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A fool despises his father's instruction'—the educational relationship that structures chapters 1–9 appears again; the fool's defining move is to dismiss what the father offers. 'Whoever heeds reproof is prudent'—the teachable person becomes the prudent person; prudence is not an innate gift but the result of having accepted correction over time. 'In the house of the righteous there is much treasure'—the household of the righteous accumulates genuinely; righteousness and abundance go together in the long run. 'Trouble is in the income of the wicked'—what the wicked earns is contaminated by the method of earning it; their income carries a hidden cost.

verseByVerse.quote: The lips of the wise spread knowledge; not so the hearts of fools. The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD, but the prayer of the upright is his delight. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The lips of the wise spread knowledge'—the wise person's speech is productive, reproductive; knowledge moves from the speaker to the listener and multiplies. 'Not so the hearts of fools'—the heart of the fool is where the problem is rooted; the fool's speech is a symptom of a disordered interior. 'The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD'—religious performance without righteousness of life is not merely unhelpful but offensive to God (cf. Isa. 1:13; Amos 5:21). 'The prayer of the upright is his delight'—prayer from a righteous life is not merely tolerated but enjoyed by God. Keller: God is not indifferent to our prayers; he delights in communion with those who walk uprightly.

verseByVerse.quote: The way of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD, but he loves him who pursues righteousness. There is severe discipline for him who forsakes the way; whoever hates reproof will die. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'He loves him who pursues righteousness'—God's love is covenantal and directional: it is particularly expressed toward those who are actively pursuing righteousness. This is not works-righteousness but the dynamic of the responsive heart. 'There is severe discipline for him who forsakes the way'—the stakes of abandonment are high; this is not simply about consequences but about the loving severity of God toward those who turn back. 'Whoever hates reproof will die'—the refusal of correction is the most diagnostic sign of fatal foolishness. Sproul: the person who cannot be corrected has made himself unteachable by God himself, which is the most dangerous condition possible.

verseByVerse.quote: Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the LORD; how much more the hearts of the children of man! A scoffer does not like to be reproved; he will not go to the wise. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the LORD'—if the deepest realm of death and destruction is transparent to God, the human heart certainly is. The argument is from greater to lesser: if the cosmic realm of death holds no secrets from God, how could your private thoughts? 'How much more the hearts of the children of man!'—the implication is that self-deception before God is categorically impossible. 'A scoffer does not like to be reproved'—the scoffer's aversion to correction is not merely personal preference but a closed system: he will not go to those who could help him precisely because their help would require him to change.

verseByVerse.quote: A glad heart makes a cheerful face, but by sorrow of heart the spirit is crushed. The heart of him who has understanding seeks knowledge, but the mouths of fools feed on folly. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A glad heart makes a cheerful face'—the exterior reflects the interior; genuine inner joy surfaces on the face without effort. This is not manufactured cheerfulness but the overflow of a heart at peace. 'By sorrow of heart the spirit is crushed'—grief is real and heavy; Proverbs does not minimize it. 'The heart of him who has understanding seeks knowledge'—the insatiable appetite for wisdom characterizes the understanding person; he is always moving toward greater knowledge, not resting in what he already has. 'The mouths of fools feed on folly'—the fool's appetite is also insatiable but directed toward what destroys rather than what builds.

verseByVerse.quote: All the days of the afflicted are evil, but the cheerful of heart has a continual feast. Better is a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble with it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'All the days of the afflicted are evil'—the subjective experience of the person crushed by circumstances is that every day is bad. Proverbs observes this honestly. 'The cheerful of heart has a continual feast'—the inner disposition transforms external circumstances; what is materially a little becomes experientially abundant when the heart is joyful. 'Better is a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble with it'—the comparative better-than is a characteristic Proverbs form. The fear of God transfigures small material resources; great wealth burdened by anxiety is worse than poverty accompanied by peace. Keller: the soul's orientation is the multiplier that makes all the difference.

verseByVerse.quote: Better is a dinner of herbs where love is than a fattened ox and hatred with it. A hot-tempered man stirs up strife, but he who is slow to anger quiets contention. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Better is a dinner of herbs where love is'—the second better-than in two verses: simple food in a loving home is genuinely preferable to a luxurious feast in an atmosphere of hatred. Proverbs is remarkably clear that relational quality outweighs material abundance. 'A hot-tempered man stirs up strife'—the angry person is a social disturbance; wherever he goes, conflict follows. 'He who is slow to anger quiets contention'—the emotionally regulated person has a calming effect on social systems. Patience is not passivity but an active, socially creative force. The church needs more people who quiet contention than those who win arguments.

verseByVerse.quote: The way of a sluggard is like a hedge of thorns, but the path of the upright is a level highway. A wise son makes a glad father, but a foolish man despises his mother. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The way of a sluggard is like a hedge of thorns'—the sluggard experiences obstacles everywhere; his path is impenetrable not because the world is cruel but because he has not maintained the road. The diligent person's path is clear because he has done the work of clearing it. 'The path of the upright is a level highway'—the diligent find that the way gets easier as they progress; wisdom builds its own infrastructure. 'A wise son makes a glad father'—the joy of the parent in the child's wisdom is one of the most repeated refrains in Proverbs. It is the fulfillment of the entire pedagogical project of chapters 1–9.

verseByVerse.quote: Folly is a joy to him who lacks sense, but a man of understanding walks straight ahead. Without counsel plans fail, but with many advisers they succeed. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Folly is a joy to him who lacks sense'—the fool enjoys his foolishness; this is not a minor problem but a profound one. He does not suffer from his condition, which means he has no motivation to change it. 'A man of understanding walks straight ahead'—purpose and direction; the wise person does not meander but pursues his course. 'Without counsel plans fail, but with many advisers they succeed'—the second appearance of the multitude-of-counselors principle (cf. 11:14). Wisdom is not isolated; it is communal, dialogical, tested by multiple perspectives. Waltke: the wise person is humble enough to know that his own judgment has limits.

verseByVerse.quote: To make an apt answer is a joy to a man, and a word in season, how good it is! The path of life leads upward for the prudent, that he may turn away from Sheol beneath. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'To make an apt answer is a joy to a man'—finding exactly the right word for the moment is one of wisdom's deepest pleasures. The well-spoken word satisfies the speaker and the hearer. 'A word in season, how good it is!'—the right word at the right moment is not merely clever but deeply good: it sustains the weary (cf. Isa. 50:4). 'The path of life leads upward for the prudent'—wisdom's direction is upward and forward; it moves away from death. 'That he may turn away from Sheol beneath'—the contrast is vertical and moral: wisdom's trajectory is life-and-God-ward; folly's trajectory is death-ward. Every step of wisdom is a step away from destruction.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD tears down the house of the proud but maintains the widow's boundaries. The thoughts of the wicked are an abomination to the LORD, but gracious words are pure. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The LORD tears down the house of the proud'—God is actively engaged in the demolition of pride; pride is not merely punished but targeted. 'Maintains the widow's boundaries'—the widow in ancient Israel had no male protector to defend her land claims; God himself is her defender (cf. Prov. 23:10-11). The God who brings down the proud takes up the cause of the powerless. 'The thoughts of the wicked are an abomination to the LORD'—God's revulsion extends to the inner life, not only external acts. 'Gracious words are pure'—gracious speech is ceremonially clean in God's sight; the right word is an act of worship.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever is greedy for unjust gain troubles his own household, but he who hates bribes will live. The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer, but the mouth of the wicked pours out evil things. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever is greedy for unjust gain troubles his own household'—the bribe-taker or corrupt official brings the curse home with him; the household suffers for the individual's corruption. 'He who hates bribes will live'—integrity is not merely morally superior but practically life-sustaining. 'The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer'—the interior work before speech; the righteous person does not immediately reach for words but thinks. 'The mouth of the wicked pours out evil things'—no pondering, no pause, no filter. The contrast is between speech rooted in a reflective heart and speech vomited from an unreflective one.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is far from the wicked, but he hears the prayer of the righteous. The light of the eyes rejoices the heart, and good news refreshes the bones. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The LORD is far from the wicked'—relational distance, not metaphysical distance: God is omnipresent but covenantally near only to those in right relationship with him. 'He hears the prayer of the righteous'—hears in the full biblical sense: attends to, responds to, acts upon. Not that only perfect people can pray, but that righteous life clears the channel of prayer. 'The light of the eyes rejoices the heart'—the face lit up with good news communicates joy before words do; the body carries the soul's response. 'Good news refreshes the bones'—the deepest level of the physical person is renewed by joy. The gospel is, literally, good news—and it does exactly this.

verseByVerse.quote: The ear that listens to life-giving reproof will dwell among the wise. Whoever ignores instruction despises himself, but he who listens to reproof gains heart. (ESV)
