Which is why the injuries that go deepest are almost never inflicted by enemies. An enemy can reach your reputation. Only somebody who loves you can reach the place a sentence lands and stays for twenty years.

And note the direction of the second image: bars of a castle. Bars keep people out, and they also keep people in. The wronged brother has locked the gate, and he is now inside it with the grievance, which is the least comfortable place in the building. Nobody is enjoying this arrangement, including the man who built it.

The practical counsel Proverbs gives by implication is uncomfortable but plain. Since the fortification goes up quickly and comes down slowly, the time to act is absurdly early — before the tone has hardened, while the thing is still one awkward conversation rather than a siege.

Almost everybody waits, and the waiting is always defended by the same reasoning: it will look like I am making too much of it. Given a year, it will not look like too much. It will look like a wall.

Then v. 20, and the metaphor is deliberately physical: from the fruit of a man’s mouth his stomach is satisfied. Not his conscience, not his reputation. He eats what he says.

That is the chapter’s recurring argument in its plainest form. Words are not vapour that dissipates once the noise stops; they are seed, they produce a crop, and the person who planted it is the one who has to live on what comes up.

Take it personally in one specific direction. The man who has spent years speaking about his wife with a mild, funny contempt has not merely described a marriage. He has been growing one, and he is eating it now.

And the promise runs the other way with equal force, which is where the two verses meet. The brother in v. 19 was lost by something said. Verse 20 says the harvest belongs to whoever does the sowing — which means the man who put the wall up is also, still, the man best placed to say the sentence that starts taking it down.

verseByVerse.quote: Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruits. He who finds a wife finds a good thing and obtains favor from the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything in this chapter has been climbing to v. 21. Seventeen verses of lips and mouths and whispers and answers, and now the principle underneath them all, stated without qualification: death and life are in the power of the tongue. James takes the same line up and puts it more alarmingly still — the tongue sets on fire the entire course of life (James 3:6) — and neither writer is speaking loosely. Then v. 22, which arrives without any obvious link to what precedes it and needs careful handling, because a proverb about finding a wife is read by people in every possible marital condition and Proverbs is not in the business of ranking them.

The Hebrew of v. 21 is more physical than the English. Death and life are in the hand of the tongue. A small organ with no bones in it is given a fist.

And notice the order, because Proverbs is not being decorative. Death comes first. The book has spent seventeen verses on what speech does, and when it finally states the principle it leads with the damage.

Be specific about what death means here, since nobody reading this has talked anybody into a grave. It is the sentence said to a nine-year-old that he is still repeating to himself at fifty-two. It is the assessment offered in a meeting that quietly ended a man’s standing and was never revisited. It is the remark about a body, made once, in front of others, twenty years ago.

And life is just as concrete. Somebody once said a sentence to you that you have never lost — that you were good at this, that they were glad you existed, that they forgave you. You could probably quote it. It cost the speaker about four seconds.

Which is the test, and it takes a minute. Name one of each. Almost everyone can produce the killing sentence immediately and has to think a little longer for the life-giving one — and both of them are still working, decades after the air went still.

Then ask why speech should carry that kind of weight at all, because the answer is not psychology. It is creation. God spoke, and there was light; the universe exists because a word was said. And human beings are made in the image of that God, which means our words are not noise made by animals with opinions. They are a creaturely echo of the thing by which everything was made.

That is why the stakes in this proverb are life and death rather than manners. To use speech to destroy a person is not merely unkind; it is a distortion of the image. And to use it to tell the truth, to encourage, to name grace over somebody — that is a small participation in the work of the one who is himself the Word.

This verse has been badly abused, and the abuse needs naming. It is not teaching that your words create reality, that you must never voice a fear in case you summon it, or that speaking a thing aloud makes it so. That is a superstition, and it puts a burden on the sick and the frightened that Scripture never puts there.

Our words are derivative and creaturely. They shape people — which is quite enough to be going on with — but they do not command outcomes, and a Christian who is afraid to say I am struggling has been taught something this verse does not say.

Verse 22 then arrives, and it needs handling with care, because read flatly it hands out a verdict to two kinds of reader who do not deserve one.

Proverbs speaks in generalisations about how life normally runs. It is not issuing a promise to every individual, and this book of all books knows it — the same collection says it is better to live in a corner of the housetop than in a shared house with a quarrelsome wife (21:9). A writer who can say that is not being naive twenty-seven chapters earlier. Some ancient versions even read a good wife here, which suggests early readers already felt the tension.

So to the man who is single: this verse is not a scoreboard, and it does not mean the favour of the LORD has passed you by. Paul thought singleness a gift with genuine advantages (1 Corinthians 7:7-8), and the wisest man who ever lived never married at all.

And to the man whose marriage is hard: it is not a verdict on you either, or a suggestion that you chose wrongly and have forfeited something. The proverb celebrates a gift. It does not audit your household.

What it does do is refuse the modern instinct to treat a spouse as an achievement — something located, earned, and deserved. Finds and obtains favour are both words for receiving. The man in this verse did not win anything. He was given somebody.

verseByVerse.quote: The poor use entreaties, but the rich answer roughly. A man of many companions may come to ruin, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two last observations, one about speech and one about friendship, which have been the chapter’s twin subjects since v. 1. Verse 23 is speech under the pressure of power: what a man can afford to sound like depends on who needs whom. Verse 24 is friendship under the pressure of trouble, and it finds that numbers are no help — a man may have companions in quantity and be ruined all the same, because a crowd is not a covenant. Then, at the very end of a chapter full of mouths that wound and walls that go up, a single line about somebody who stays.

Verse 23 reports and does not comment, and the restraint is doing work. The proverb simply puts the two speeches side by side — pleading and roughness — and lets the reader supply the verdict, which is a far harder thing to argue with than a rebuke.

And the roughness it describes is not usually shouting. Today it is the email left unanswered for three weeks. The single-word reply. The meeting shortened because you had somewhere to be, to a person who had nowhere else to go.

Which yields a rather exposing measurement. In almost any exchange, power can be read off the length of the replies. The one who needs the other less is the one who can afford to be brief.

So the test is simply to watch your own answers this week as a function of who is asking. Notice who gets sentences and who gets three words; whose message you answer within the hour and whose sits until it is convenient. Nobody has to admit to contempt for the pattern to be legible.

The verse is not saying that the wealthy are wicked. It is describing what power does to speech — and everybody is on the rich side of some room. You have someone who needs something from you and cannot easily go elsewhere, and how you speak to that person, when nothing obliges you to be gracious, is the most accurate thing about you that anybody could measure.

Then v. 24, and honesty requires admitting that the first line is difficult in Hebrew; the older versions pull between a man of many companions coming to ruin and a man of many companions being broken to pieces. Either way the point stands, and it is about arithmetic: quantity is not the same as depth, and a great many acquaintances can leave a person less supported rather than more.

That lands with unusual force now, when the number of people who know your name has never been higher and the number who could describe your inner life has probably never been lower. The contacts list is long. The question is not how many people you know. It is who you would ring on the worst night of your life, and whether they would come.

Then the second half, and the verb is the striking thing. Sticks closer is dabaq — the same word Genesis uses when it says a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife (Genesis 2:24). The word for the deepest human covenant is the word chosen here for a friend.

So the friendship being described is not warmth or long acquaintance. It is covenant-grade loyalty: the kind that has decided in advance, before it knows what it will cost, that it is not leaving.

And Keller is right that this is finally about Christ — but it matters how, because the evidence is not sentimental. He was given the title as an insult — a friend of tax collectors and sinners — and he never once corrected it. He told the disciples plainly, no longer do I call you servants… I have called you friends (John 15:15).

And then the test of it came, and the result should be stated plainly. When the crisis arrived, his friends did not stick closer than brothers. They ran. Every one of them. The friendship in that garden was entirely one-directional — and he went to the cross with it still holding.

Now look back at where this chapter began. Verse 1: whoever isolates himself seeks his own desire. A man closing a door from the inside. Twenty-three verses later the chapter ends on a friend who cannot be shut out, and the arrangement of it is not accidental.

One last guard, so this does not become a disappointment. The verse does not promise you a David and Jonathan; many faithful Christians have been very lonely, and pretending otherwise would be cruel. What is guaranteed is the friend of the second line, not a supply of the first.

But that is not a consolation prize, and the chapter has already told you where he can be found. The strong tower of v. 10 turned out to be a name. The crushed spirit of v. 14 turned out to have somebody nearest to it. And the friend of v. 24 is the same person, who does not leave when the crisis deepens because leaving is the one thing he has never done.

18.theology: The theology of speech: death and life in the tongue. Proverbs 18:21 — "death and life are in the power of the tongue" — is the most theologically weighty speech proverb in the book. It grounds the speech ethics of Proverbs not in social convention or reputation management but in the deepest realities of human existence: life and death. This is possible because human beings are made in the image of the God who spoke creation into existence and whose word is the source of all life. When we speak, we are exercising a capacity that reflects our Maker — which means that the misuse of speech is not merely rude or unkind but a distortion of the image of God. And the use of speech to give life — to encourage, to tell the truth, to speak the gospel — is a participation in the creative, life-giving work of the one who is the Word.
18.examples:
Then: "The name of the LORD is a strong tower" (v. 10) was not abstract theology for Israel; it was the daily reality of a nation surrounded by enemies, dependent on God's protection in a way that the great empires were not. The person who ran to the LORD's name was the person who, in the absence of a strong army or a fortified city, had discovered that the LORD himself was stronger than any alternative. The refugee who arrives at the tower breathless and trembling is not demonstrating weakness; they are demonstrating the wisdom that knows where safety actually resides.

Now: "A fool takes no pleasure in understanding, but only in expressing his opinion" (v. 2) has never been more relevant than in the age of social media, where the primary mode of engagement is the public declaration of one's views, and where the discipline of genuine understanding — of reading carefully, listening fully, considering the other perspective — is systematically discouraged by algorithms that reward strong expression over patient comprehension. Keller's observation that wisdom requires the humility to be genuinely interested in understanding applies with particular force to digital discourse: the wisest person in any online conversation is probably the one saying the least.

19.title: Poverty, Wealth, and the LORD
19.text: <sup>1</sup>Better is a poor person who walks in his integrity than one who is crooked in speech and is a fool. <sup>3</sup>When a man's folly brings his way to ruin, his heart rages against the LORD. <sup>11</sup>Good sense makes one slow to anger, and it is his glory to overlook an offense. <sup>14</sup>House and wealth are inherited from fathers, but a prudent wife is from the LORD. <sup>17</sup>Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed. <sup>20</sup>Listen to advice and accept instruction, that you may gain wisdom in the future. <sup>21</sup>Many are the plans in the mind of a man, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will stand. <sup>23</sup>The fear of the LORD leads to life, and whoever has it rests satisfied; he will not be visited by harm.
19.overview:
Chapter 19 ranges across poverty and wealth, marriage, generosity to the poor, the sovereignty of God, and the fear of the LORD as the foundation of the satisfied life. It opens with one of Proverbs' "better than" comparisons — the poor person of integrity is better than the foolish person who is crooked in speech — and closes with the settled confidence of the one who fears the LORD: "he will not be visited by harm."

Two of the chapter's most important proverbs address the relationship between human plans and divine purpose (v. 21 — a companion to 16:9) and generosity to the poor (v. 17 — one of the most striking economic proverbs in the book). Verse 17 frames generosity as lending to God himself: the one who is generous to the poor has the LORD as their debtor, and the repayment is guaranteed. This is not a transaction but a theological statement: care for the poor is care for the God who made them and identifies himself with them.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 19 — Integrity, Anger, and the Lord Who Watches the Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 19 returns repeatedly to the poor: how the poor are treated by their former friends (v.4,7), how the wise son relates to his father (v.13,26,27), how the LORD cares for the poor (v.17). Integrity and folly are compared across social contexts—the poor person of integrity versus the fool, the rich man with false friends versus the genuine friend in adversity. Anger appears twice (vv.11,19) as a force that must be governed or it governs.
verseByVerse.theology: The LORD lends to those who are kind to the poor (v.17)—one of Proverbs' most striking economic claims. Generosity to the poor is re-framed as a loan to God himself. This is not metaphorical but theological: the poor person mediates the claim of the God who identifies with the poor (cf. Matt. 25:40). To give to the poor is to give to God, and God repays.
verseByVerse.examples: Patience and anger management (vv.11,19) are recurrent Proverbs themes. The slow-to-anger person is consistently praised as wise; the uncontrolled angry person consistently produces his own destruction. Self-mastery is the first requirement of social wisdom because without it, no social skill can be consistently deployed.

verseByVerse.quote: Better is a poor person who walks in his integrity than one who is crooked in speech and is a fool. Desire without knowledge is not good, and whoever makes haste with his feet misses his way. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Better is a poor person who walks in his integrity than one who is crooked in speech and is a fool'—the poor person of integrity beats the wealthy fool. Character, not economic status, determines actual worth. 'Desire without knowledge is not good'—zeal without wisdom is dangerous; enthusiasm for a good end through foolish means produces bad outcomes. 'Whoever makes haste with his feet misses his way'—speed and direction are both necessary; hurrying without wisdom leads away from the goal. Waltke: the combination of desire and knowledge, urgency and direction, is the practical form of wisdom in action.

verseByVerse.quote: When a man's folly brings his way to ruin, his heart rages against the LORD. Wealth brings many new friends, but a poor man is deserted by his friend. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'When a man's folly brings his way to ruin, his heart rages against the LORD'—remarkable psychological accuracy: the person whose own foolishness has destroyed him blames God. Self-deception projects responsibility outward. 'Wealth brings many new friends, but a poor man is deserted by his friend'—the social magnetism of wealth and the social isolation of poverty. Fair-weather friendship tracks financial status; the prosperous person cannot know whether his friends love him or his resources. The poor person discovers who his real friends are by discovering who has abandoned him.

verseByVerse.quote: A false witness will not go unpunished, and he who breathes out lies will not escape. Many seek the favor of a generous man, and everyone is a friend to a man who gives gifts. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A false witness will not go unpunished'—the certainty is absolute; Proverbs states the outcome as a guaranteed consequence of the character of God who is the Lord of justice. 'Many seek the favor of a generous man'—the generous person has no shortage of attention and relationship; generosity is social currency. 'Everyone is a friend to a man who gives gifts'—the sober observation behind the positive appearance: if everyone becomes your friend when you give gifts, you have no way of knowing which friendships are real. Kidner: affluence creates the paradox of having many friends and few genuine ones.

verseByVerse.quote: All a poor man's brothers hate him; how much more do his friends go far from him! He pursues them with words, but does not have them. Whoever gets sense loves his own soul; he who keeps understanding will discover good. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'All a poor man's brothers hate him'—the starkest social observation in this cluster: the poor person is abandoned even by family. 'He pursues them with words, but does not have them'—the saddest image: he runs after people who are already walking away, calling to them with words that produce no return. 'Whoever gets sense loves his own soul'—getting wisdom is an act of self-love: the person who acquires understanding genuinely values his own life enough to invest in its improvement. 'He who keeps understanding will discover good'—wisdom retained, internalized, and practiced produces good outcomes.

verseByVerse.quote: A false witness will not go unpunished, and he who breathes out lies will perish. It is not fitting for a fool to live in luxury, much less for a slave to rule over princes. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A false witness will not go unpunished, and he who breathes out lies will perish'—the intensification from v.5 ('not escape') to 'will perish'; the stakes of false witness are ultimate. 'It is not fitting for a fool to live in luxury'—the mismatch between character and privilege: luxury without wisdom is not merely unfortunate but unfitting, like a crown on a pig. 'Much less for a slave to rule over princes'—the compounded mismatch of authority without character or preparation. Proverbs affirms social order not as permanent but as reflecting the wisdom that character should precede responsibility.

verseByVerse.quote: Good sense makes one slow to anger, and it is his glory to overlook an offense. A king's wrath is like the growling of a lion, but his favor is like dew on the grass. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Good sense makes one slow to anger'—understanding produces patience: the person who understands human frailty, including his own, is not shocked or outraged when people fail. 'His glory to overlook an offense'—overlooking is not weakness but strength; the person strong enough not to need to retaliate demonstrates genuine confidence. 'A king's wrath is like the growling of a lion'—the growl before the strike: royal anger is preceded by warning but followed by overwhelming force. 'His favor is like dew on the grass'—morning dew in the Levant is life-sustaining, arriving silently and refreshing everything it touches. Royal favor quietly transforms what it touches.

verseByVerse.quote: A foolish son is ruin to his father, and a wife's quarreling is a continual dripping of rain. House and wealth are inherited from fathers, but a prudent wife is from the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A foolish son is ruin to his father'—ruin, not inconvenience; the stakes of the son's folly are total. 'A wife's quarreling is a continual dripping of rain'—the persistent, unrelenting quality of chronic domestic strife; not a storm that ends but a drip that never stops. 'House and wealth are inherited from fathers'—material inheritance follows natural channels. 'A prudent wife is from the LORD'—but wisdom in a spouse is not inherited or purchased; it is a divine gift. The man who has a prudent wife has received something from God's own hands. Waltke: this proverb elevates the prudent wife to the category of divine grace, not human achievement.

verseByVerse.quote: Slothfulness casts into a deep sleep, and an idle person will suffer hunger. Whoever keeps the commandment keeps his life; he who despises his ways will die. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Slothfulness casts into a deep sleep'—the sluggard's characteristic posture: not merely resting but sunk in a torpor that is increasingly difficult to escape. 'An idle person will suffer hunger'—the direct consequence; in an agricultural economy, not working means not eating. 'Whoever keeps the commandment keeps his life'—obedience to God's instruction is life-preserving; the commandment describes the grain of reality, and moving with the grain sustains life. 'He who despises his ways will die'—despising the path of wisdom is not neutral but actively life-ending. Every step away from wisdom is a step toward death.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed. Discipline your son, for there is hope; do not set your heart on putting him to death. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed'—one of the most striking economic-theological claims in the whole Bible. The poor person is the medium through whom God receives and promises repayment. This is not a fund-raising device but a theological reality: God identifies with the poor so thoroughly that to give to them is to give to him (cf. Matt. 25:40). 'Discipline your son, for there is hope'—the urgency and optimism of the call to parental formation: while there is still time, there is hope. 'Do not set your heart on putting him to death'—by failing to discipline, you are not showing mercy but enabling destruction.

verseByVerse.quote: A man of great wrath will pay the penalty; for if you deliver him, you will only have to do it again. Listen to advice and accept instruction, that you may gain wisdom in the future. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A man of great wrath will pay the penalty'—uncontrolled anger has consequences that cannot be avoided. 'If you deliver him, you will only have to do it again'—the unaddressed pattern repeats; rescuing the angry person from the consequences of his anger without addressing the anger only enables the next episode. 'Listen to advice and accept instruction, that you may gain wisdom in the future'—teachability is an investment in the future; the person who receives instruction now accumulates wisdom for the challenges ahead. Sproul: the disciple is precisely the person who places himself under instruction consistently and over time.

verseByVerse.quote: Many are the plans in the mind of a man, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will stand. What is desired in a man is steadfast love, and a poor man is better than a liar. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Many are the plans in the mind of a man, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will stand'—human planning is prolific but not ultimate; God's purpose is singular, fewer, and absolutely certain. This is comfort and correction together: comfort because God's good purposes will not be thwarted; correction because our many plans must be held loosely. 'What is desired in a man is steadfast love'—the most desirable human quality is hesed, covenant love; more than cleverness, wealth, or eloquence. 'A poor man is better than a liar'—the familiar economic reversal: poverty plus honesty beats wealth plus dishonesty.

verseByVerse.quote: The fear of the LORD leads to life, and whoever has it rests satisfied; he will not be visited by harm. The sluggard buries his hand in the dish and will not even bring it to his mouth again. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The fear of the LORD leads to life, and whoever has it rests satisfied'—satisfaction is the fruit of the fear of God; the God-fearer does not experience the insatiability of disordered desire. 'He will not be visited by harm'—not an absolute promise of physical safety but the orientation of the God-fearing life toward life rather than harm. 'The sluggard buries his hand in the dish and will not even bring it to his mouth again'—one of Proverbs' most mordant comic images: the lazy person has gotten as far as putting his hand in the food and still cannot complete the action. Kidner: the sluggard's problem is not laziness in the abstract but the accumulated habit of not finishing what he starts.

verseByVerse.quote: Strike a scoffer, and the simple will learn prudence; reprove a man of understanding, and he will gain knowledge. He who does violence to his father and chases away his mother is a son who brings shame and reproach. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Strike a scoffer, and the simple will learn prudence'—the scoffer is himself unteachable, but his punishment instructs the watching simple person. Public accountability has social pedagogical effects. 'Reprove a man of understanding, and he will gain knowledge'—the contrast is about receptivity: the understanding person learns from a word; the scoffer cannot learn from a blow. 'He who does violence to his father and chases away his mother'—the violence against parents is extreme folly; those who gave him life are driven away by the son whose life they gave. The shame and reproach are proportional to the ingratitude and rebellion.

verseByVerse.quote: Cease to hear instruction, my son, and you will stray from the words of knowledge. A worthless witness mocks at justice, and the mouth of the wicked devours iniquity. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Cease to hear instruction, my son, and you will stray from the words of knowledge'—the warning about the moment of disengagement: once you stop listening, drift has already begun. The process of going astray does not begin with a dramatic rebellion but with the quiet decision to stop attending to wisdom. 'A worthless witness mocks at justice'—not merely commits perjury but makes a mockery of the whole system of justice; false witness destroys the social institution that protects everyone. 'The mouth of the wicked devours iniquity'—the wicked person's appetite is for wickedness; he swallows it eagerly.

verseByVerse.quote: Condemnation is ready for scoffers, and beating for the backs of fools. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Condemnation is ready for scoffers, and beating for the backs of fools'—'ready' suggests that the judgment is already prepared, waiting only for the appointed moment of its application. The scoffer and the fool are not going to escape by cleverness or luck; their consequences have been set. Proverbs does not say when, but it says certainly. Kidner: the certainty of judgment is not a threat to terrorize the fearful but a word of sanity to those who might be tempted to envy the apparent success of the wicked. Wait—and watch.

19.theology: The poor, the LORD, and the economics of grace. Proverbs 19:17 — "whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD" — is the wisdom literature's most direct statement of what might be called the economics of grace: the system of exchange that operates in the kingdom of God, where generosity to the vulnerable is generosity to God himself. This is consistent with the theology of the image of God (14:31 — oppressing the poor insults the Maker) and with the prophetic tradition (Amos, Micah, Isaiah — care for the poor is the litmus test of genuine covenant faithfulness). And it is confirmed by Jesus, who in Matthew 25 makes the treatment of the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the naked, and the imprisoned the criterion by which the nations are judged: what is done or not done to the least is done or not done to him. Generosity to the poor is not optional philanthropy; it is covenantal faithfulness to the LORD who identifies himself with them.
19.examples:
Then: "When a man's folly brings his way to ruin, his heart rages against the LORD" (v. 3) was recognisable to every ancient Israelite who had seen the pattern in their own community: the person who made bad decisions (foolish financial risks, sexual unfaithfulness, dishonest dealings) and then, when the consequences arrived, complained that God was being unfair. This is not a modern phenomenon; it is the timeless human instinct to attribute to God what we ourselves have caused. The wisdom tradition's insistence on honest self-examination is the antidote.

Now: "A prudent wife is from the LORD" (v. 14) is the wisdom perspective on the pursuit of a spouse. In a culture that approaches marriage as a matter of personal preference, strategic compatibility, and market dynamics, Proverbs insists that the most important qualities in a spouse — wisdom, character, prudence, faithfulness — are ultimately gifts of God rather than achievements of searching. This does not mean passivity in the search but a posture of dependence and gratitude: the wisdom to recognise a genuine gift when it is offered, and the humility to receive it as from the LORD rather than as a personal achievement.

20.title: Wine Is a Mocker
20.text: <sup>1</sup>Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise. <sup>5</sup>The purpose in a man's heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out. <sup>7</sup>The righteous who walks in his integrity — blessed are his children after him! <sup>9</sup>Who can say, "I have made my heart clean; I have been pure from my sin"? <sup>12</sup>The hearing ear and the seeing eye, the LORD has made them both. <sup>18</sup>Plans are established by counsel; by wise guidance wage war. <sup>22</sup>Do not say, "I will repay evil"; wait for the LORD, and he will deliver you. <sup>24</sup>A man's steps are from the LORD; how then can man understand his own way? <sup>27</sup>The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all his innermost parts.
20.overview:
Chapter 20 is one of the more theologically reflective chapters in the Solomonic collection, with several proverbs that press beneath the surface of behaviour to the deeper questions of human nature and divine governance. "Who can say, 'I have made my heart clean; I have been pure from my sin'?" (v. 9) is one of the most important rhetorical questions in the Old Testament — an implicit answer that anticipates the universal sinfulness that Paul will articulate in Romans 3. And "the spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all his innermost parts" (v. 27) is a remarkable statement about divine omniscience and human self-knowledge.

The chapter also contains an important observation about deep motivation: "the purpose in a man's heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out" (v. 5). Human motivation is rarely transparent — people do not always know why they do what they do, and neither do the people around them. The person of understanding has the patient, empathetic skill to draw out what is hidden — to hear beneath the stated reason to the actual reason, to see beneath the presenting behaviour to the deeper desire or fear that drives it.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 20 — Sobriety, Integrity, and the Lamp That Searches the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 20 begins with wine as a mocker (v.1) and ends with the human spirit as a lamp of the LORD (v.27). Between those poles: the lazy man at harvest (v.4), the mystery of who is truly pure (v.9), the divine sovereignty over hearing and sight (v.12), the danger of hasty vows (v.25), and the sanctity of honest weights. The chapter is a sustained call to self-examination before a God who sees everything.
verseByVerse.theology: The lamp of the LORD searches the spirit (v.27)—one of the most searching statements in Proverbs about divine knowledge of the inner life. God does not observe behavior from the outside but illuminates the innermost person. Nothing is hidden from this light. This should produce both awe and freedom: awe because all pretense is futile; freedom because we need not pretend.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 9 ('Who can say, I have made my heart pure?') is one of Proverbs' most honest moments: even after wisdom's formation, no one can claim moral purity. The awareness of remaining corruption is itself a mark of wisdom; only the fool thinks himself clean. This humility drives the believer back to the gospel, the only true cleansing.

verseByVerse.quote: Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise. The terror of a king is like the growling of a lion; whoever provokes him to anger forfeits his life. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler'—the intoxicants are personified as troublemakers: wine mocks (undermines dignity, produces ridicule), strong drink brawls (produces aggression, violence). 'Whoever is led astray by it is not wise'—not a statement about moderate use but about being 'led astray': the person who surrenders his judgment to alcohol has chosen a fool as his master. 'The terror of a king is like the growling of a lion'—the king's anger is not merely personal displeasure but an expression of royal authority backed by lethal force. Provoking it is a life-or-death miscalculation.

verseByVerse.quote: It is an honor for a man to keep aloof from strife, but every fool will be quarreling. The sluggard does not plow in the autumn; he will seek at harvest and have nothing. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'It is an honor for a man to keep aloof from strife'—walking away from conflict is not weakness but genuine honor; the person who can disengage demonstrates a form of strength the quarreling fool lacks. 'Every fool will be quarreling'—the quarrelsome person is identified as a fool; chronic conflict is diagnostic of character. 'The sluggard does not plow in the autumn; he will seek at harvest and have nothing'—the lag between cause and consequence: the moment of decision (plowing or not plowing) comes long before the moment of consequence (harvest). The sluggard's problem is not feeling lazy at harvest time but not feeling urgent enough at plowing time.

verseByVerse.quote: The purpose in a man's heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out. Many a man proclaims his own steadfast love, but a faithful man who can find? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The purpose in a man's heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out'—human motivation is hidden and deep; it takes wisdom and patient questioning to bring it to the surface. The man of understanding does not take surface declarations at face value but draws out what is really there. 'Many a man proclaims his own steadfast love'—self-advertisement of loyalty is cheap and common. 'A faithful man who can find?'—the rhetorical question implies scarcity: genuine covenant faithfulness, tested by time and adversity, is rare. Keller: this is why the gospel's announcement of God's absolutely reliable hesed is such astonishing news—it offers what human faithfulness cannot reliably provide.

verseByVerse.quote: The righteous who walks in his integrity—blessed are his children after him! A king who sits on the throne of judgment winnows all evil with his eyes. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The righteous who walks in his integrity—blessed are his children after him!'—the blessing of integrity is intergenerational; the children of a righteous parent inherit a foundation they did not build. Kidner: the most durable inheritance a parent can leave is not property but character modeled faithfully across years. 'A king who sits on the throne of judgment winnows all evil with his eyes'—the ideal king's discernment functions like the winnowing fan: separating what is true from what is false, driving out evil with the penetrating power of judicial wisdom. This is the king Proverbs hopes for and Christ perfectly fulfills.

verseByVerse.quote: Who can say, “I have made my heart pure; I am clean from my sin”? Unequal weights and unequal measures are both alike an abomination to the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Who can say, I have made my heart pure; I am clean from my sin?'—the rhetorical question expects 'no one.' This is one of Proverbs' most honest theological moments: after all the instruction in wisdom, no one can claim moral self-sufficiency. The awareness of remaining impurity is itself a mark of wisdom. 'Unequal weights and unequal measures are both alike an abomination to the LORD'—the commercial applications of divine justice; the marketplace is not a morality-free zone but a space where God's character is either honored or defiled by every transaction.

verseByVerse.quote: Even a child makes himself known by his acts, by whether his conduct is pure and upright. The hearing ear and the seeing eye, the LORD has made them both. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Even a child makes himself known by his acts'—character is visible even in the young; the parent who watches carefully can discern the trajectory of the child's life early. Acts are character made visible. 'The hearing ear and the seeing eye, the LORD has made them both'—a profound epistemological statement: the capacities by which we acquire wisdom (hearing, seeing) are divine gifts. No human being generated his own capacity to learn; every insight depends on faculties that God made. Waltke: this should produce gratitude for every moment of understanding and humility about the limits of our perception.

verseByVerse.quote: Love not sleep, lest you come to poverty; open your eyes, and you will have plenty of bread. “Bad, bad,” says the buyer, but when he goes away, then he boasts. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Love not sleep, lest you come to poverty'—the love of sleep—the excessive preference for rest over work—is a form of sloth that impoverishes. 'Open your eyes, and you will have plenty of bread'—wakefulness and alertness are practical conditions of sufficiency. '“Bad, bad,” says the buyer, but when he goes away, then he boasts'—a moment of commercial comedy: the buyer disparages the merchandise to drive the price down, then brags to his friends about his acquisition. Proverbs notes this negotiating tactic without quite condemning it, but it is an example of the daily small dishonesty that erodes integrity in commerce.

verseByVerse.quote: There is gold and abundance of costly stones, but the lips of knowledge are a precious jewel. Take a man's garment when he has put up security for a stranger, and hold it in pledge when he puts up security for foreigners. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The lips of knowledge are a precious jewel'—wisdom in speech exceeds gold and precious stones in value; the rarity and worth of genuinely knowledgeable counsel surpasses any material treasure. 'Take a man's garment when he has put up security for a stranger'—practical advice about financial exposure: when someone has co-signed for an unknown person, secure yourself. The wisdom here is not heartlessness but prudence; co-signing with unknown parties is so risky that protecting yourself is justified.

verseByVerse.quote: Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be full of gravel. Plans are established by counsel; by wise guidance wage war. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be full of gravel'—the temporal sequence: the initial sweetness of dishonest gain gives way to something indigestible and painful. Proverbs tracks consequences through time rather than stopping at the moment of pleasure. 'Plans are established by counsel; by wise guidance wage war'—the same wisdom principle about counsel (cf. 11:14; 15:22) applied to the highest-stakes context: military strategy. Even in war, the multitude of counselors is the path to success. Waltke: no domain of life is exempt from the need for wisdom.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets; therefore do not associate with a simple babbler. If one curses his father or his mother, his lamp will be put out in utter darkness. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets'—the slanderer is defined by his willingness to betray confidences; this is his essential character, not an occasional failure. 'Do not associate with a simple babbler'—the person who cannot keep a confidence is not a safe companion; proximity to him makes you vulnerable. 'If one curses his father or his mother, his lamp will be put out in utter darkness'—the fifth commandment violated; to curse the parents who gave life is to strike at the source of one's own being. 'Lamp put out in utter darkness'—the most complete image of extinction; not diminished but eliminated.

verseByVerse.quote: An inheritance gained hastily in the beginning will not be blessed in the end. Do not say, “I will repay evil”; wait for the LORD, and he will deliver you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'An inheritance gained hastily in the beginning will not be blessed in the end'—quick acquisition without the proper process or time lacks the blessing that comes with rightful inheritance. 'Do not say, “I will repay evil”'—the command against personal vengeance; the impulse to retaliate is natural but must be resisted. 'Wait for the LORD, and he will deliver you'—the alternative to vengeance is not passive resignation but active trust in God's justice. Sproul: Romans 12:19 ('vengeance is mine, I will repay') quotes this impulse; the believer's role is to get out of God's way and let him be the judge. This requires more faith than taking matters into one's own hands.

verseByVerse.quote: Unequal weights are an abomination to the LORD, and false scales are not good. A man's steps are from the LORD; how then can man understand his way? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Unequal weights are an abomination to the LORD, and false scales are not good'—third occurrence of the dishonest-scales condemnation (cf. 11:1; 20:10); the repetition signals how seriously Proverbs takes commercial integrity. 'A man's steps are from the LORD; how then can man understand his way?'—the deepest limitation on self-knowledge: if God directs our steps, our self-understanding is always partial. This is not a counsel of despair but of humility. We cannot map our own path because the path is God's to direct. Waltke: the right response is not fatalism but trust combined with wisdom.

verseByVerse.quote: It is a snare to say rashly, “It is holy,” and to reflect only after making vows. A wise king winnows the wicked and drives the wheel over them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'It is a snare to say rashly, “It is holy”'—the hasty vow dedicated to God creates an obligation that cannot be easily escaped; rash dedication is its own trap. 'To reflect only after making vows'—the order should be reversed: reflect first, commit after. 'A wise king winnows the wicked and drives the wheel over them'—the threshing wheel as image of thorough and relentless justice: the wise king does not merely identify wickedness but works to eliminate it systematically. The threshing wheel separates wheat from chaff definitively; good governance must do the same.

verseByVerse.quote: The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all his innermost parts. Steadfast love and faithfulness preserve the king, and by steadfast love his throne is upheld. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all his innermost parts'—the human spirit is the instrument by which God conducts his interior examination of each person; conscience is God's lamp in the soul. 'Searching all his innermost parts'—the innermost rooms of a house were the most private; the lamp reaches even there. Keller: no self-deception can finally survive this light; the human conscience, however suppressed, is God's agent within us. 'Steadfast love and faithfulness preserve the king'—hesed and emet are the king's security system; no military force protects a throne as reliably as covenant faithfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: The glory of young men is their strength, but the splendor of old men is their gray hair. Blows that wound cleanse away evil; strokes make clean the innermost parts. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The glory of young men is their strength'—each life stage has its proper glory; youth's glory is physical vitality and energy. 'The splendor of old men is their gray hair'—the aged person's glory is not physical capacity but the weight of experience and the wisdom accumulated through years of fear of God. These are not competing but complementary. 'Blows that wound cleanse away evil; strokes make clean the innermost parts'—the cathartic function of severe discipline: painful correction reaches the innermost character and removes what comfortable circumstances leave in place. God's severe mercies are the deepest form of kindness (Heb. 12:10-11).

20.theology: Universal sinfulness and the need for divine cleansing. Proverbs 20:9 — "who can say, 'I have made my heart clean; I have been pure from my sin'?" — is the wisdom literature's contribution to the biblical theology of universal human sinfulness. The rhetorical question's implied answer (no one) is the foundation for the entire New Testament soteriology: if no one can clean their own heart, then the gospel's offer of cleansing through Christ is not a luxury for the morally sensitive but a necessity for every human being. Keller reads Proverbs 20:9 as the point at which the wisdom tradition's self-knowledge leads inevitably to the need for grace: the wise person, who has genuinely attended to the reality of their own heart, discovers what Jeremiah 17:9 states explicitly ("the heart is deceitful above all things and desperately sick — who can understand it?") — and this discovery is the beginning of the openness to the gospel.
20.examples:
Then: "The righteous who walks in his integrity — blessed are his children after him!" (v. 7) is the multigenerational vision of wisdom: the blessing of integrity is not merely personal but propagates to the next generation. The children of the person of integrity grow up in an environment shaped by that integrity — they observe it, absorb it, are formed by it. This is not a guarantee of their own righteousness (each person must make their own choices) but a recognition that the environment of integrity is itself a gift to the next generation, one of the most important things a parent can provide.

Now: "The purpose in a man's heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out" (v. 5) is the wisdom text for all pastoral and counselling ministry. The presenting question is rarely the real question; the stated reason for the decision is rarely the deepest reason; the surface behaviour is rarely the whole story. The person of understanding — who has learned to listen patiently, to ask the question beneath the question, to create the trust that allows the deep water to surface — is one of the most valuable people any community can have. This is pastoral wisdom as Proverbs understands it: not the rapid dispensing of advice but the patient, empathetic drawing out of what is genuinely there.

21.title: The King's Heart
21.text: <sup>1</sup>The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will. <sup>2</sup>Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the heart. <sup>3</sup>To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice. <sup>5</sup>The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance, but everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty. <sup>13</sup>Whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself call out and not be answered. <sup>21</sup>Whoever pursues righteousness and kindness will find life, righteousness, and honor. <sup>23</sup>Whoever keeps his mouth and his tongue keeps himself out of trouble. <sup>30</sup>No wisdom, no understanding, no counsel can avail against the LORD. <sup>31</sup>The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD.
21.overview:
Chapter 21 opens with the most striking statement of divine sovereignty in the book: "the king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will" (v. 1). If the most powerful human being — the king, whose word is law — is in the LORD's hands as easily as a stream of water, then no human power or human plan can ultimately resist the purposes of God. The chapter closes with the companion proverb: "the horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD" (v. 31). Between the king's heart and the battle horse, human agency and divine sovereignty bracket the entire chapter.

The chapter also contains one of Proverbs' most important social ethics proverbs: "whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself call out and not be answered" (v. 13). The connection between our response to others' need and God's response to our need is stated here with stark symmetry: those who do not hear the cry of the poor will not be heard when they cry. This is the justice principle of reciprocity that runs through the entire wisdom tradition and that Jesus will make explicit: "with the measure you use it will be measured to you" (Matt 7:2).

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 21 — God's Sovereignty Over the King, and the Character of the Wise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 21 opens with one of the most powerful sovereignty statements in Proverbs ('The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD') and moves through justice, sacrifice without righteousness, the contentious wife, and the ultimate futility of planning against God. The chapter closes with the war-horse—powerful, prepared, impressive—and the declaration that victory belongs to the LORD alone.
verseByVerse.theology: Justice and righteousness (v.3) is more acceptable to God than sacrifice—a prophetic note inside the wisdom literature (cf. 1 Sam. 15:22; Amos 5:21-24). Religious performance without ethical conformity is rejected. The God of Proverbs is the God of the prophets: he cannot be honored with ritual while his image-bearers are oppressed.
verseByVerse.examples: The verse about giving to the poor (v.13) and the verse about the righteous giving and not sparing (v.26) together create a picture of generosity as a defining characteristic of the righteous. The contrast with the wicked who crave all day long is the contrast between desire governed by love and desire governed by appetite.

verseByVerse.quote: The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will. Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the heart. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD'—the king is the most powerful human being in the ancient world, yet even his will is directed by God with the ease of redirecting irrigation water. Divine sovereignty does not exclude human decision-making but encompasses it entirely. 'Every way of a man is right in his own eyes'—the pervasive theme of self-justification; every person has an internal narrative in which he is the reasonable one. 'The LORD weighs the heart'—the divine counterweight to human self-deception: God's assessment is not swayed by our internal narrative. Sproul: sanctification includes the progressive dismantling of our comfortable self-justifications.

verseByVerse.quote: To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice. Haughty eyes and a proud heart, the lamp of the wicked, are sin. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice'—not that sacrifice is wrong but that it cannot compensate for the absence of justice. The sacrificial system was meant to flow from and return to a life of righteousness; when it becomes a substitute, God rejects it. 'Haughty eyes and a proud heart, the lamp of the wicked, are sin'—the lamp of the wicked (what guides and illuminates their way) is pride. What they navigate by is itself sinful; pride is not a navigational error but a corrupt instrument. Waltke: pride does not merely lead to sin—it is sin, at the root level.

verseByVerse.quote: The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance, but everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty. The getting of treasures by a lying tongue is a fleeting vapor and a snare of death. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance'—diligence paired with planning produces reliable results; neither alone is sufficient. 'Everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty'—speed without thought is the opposite of wisdom; haste that bypasses the planning stage reliably fails. 'The getting of treasures by a lying tongue is a fleeting vapor and a snare of death'—the paradox of fraudulent wealth: it both disappears quickly (vapor) and destroys permanently (snare of death). What is gotten by lying cannot be kept; the attempt to keep it becomes the mechanism of destruction.

verseByVerse.quote: The violence of the wicked will sweep them away, because they refuse to do what is just. The way of the guilty is crooked, but the conduct of the pure is upright. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The violence of the wicked will sweep them away'—the violent person is undone by his own violence; the wave he creates sweeps him away. 'Because they refuse to do what is just'—the refusal of justice is not merely moral failure but the mechanism of self-destruction. 'The way of the guilty is crooked'—the guilty person's path is characteristically indirect, evasive, devious; the crookedness is both moral and practical. 'The conduct of the pure is upright'—uprightness means directness, transparency. The pure person can go straight because he has nothing to hide.

verseByVerse.quote: It is better to live in a corner of the housetop than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife. The soul of the wicked desires evil; his neighbor finds no mercy in his eyes. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'It is better to live in a corner of the housetop than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife'—domestic tranquility is so valuable that even discomfort (a corner of the roof) is preferable to conflict in a full house. This is not a misogynistic comment but a practical observation about the social damage of chronic quarreling. 'The soul of the wicked desires evil'—the wicked person's appetite is constitutively evil; he does not merely do evil but wants it. 'His neighbor finds no mercy in his eyes'—the wicked person's relentless evil-desire excludes mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: When a scoffer is punished, the simple becomes wise; when a wise man is instructed, he gains knowledge. The Righteous One observes the house of the wicked; he throws the wicked down to ruin. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'When a scoffer is punished, the simple becomes wise'—the pedagogical function of public accountability: even those who cannot learn from instruction can sometimes learn from seeing consequences. 'When a wise man is instructed, he gains knowledge'—the wise person learns even without the spectacle of punishment; a word is sufficient. 'The Righteous One observes the house of the wicked'—most commentators take this as a divine title. 'He throws the wicked down to ruin'—God's observation is not passive; it leads to active judgment. The watching God is also the acting God.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself call out and not be answered. A gift in secret averts anger, and a concealed bribe, strong wrath. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself call out and not be answered'—the principle of proportional consequence: the one who refused to hear the cry of need will find his own cry unheard. Sproul: this is one of the most searching promises in Scripture. Our response to human need and God's response to our need are directly correlated. 'A gift in secret averts anger'—private gifts can defuse conflict in ways that public demands cannot. Proverbs notes the social reality of the gift's power without explicitly endorsing every application.

verseByVerse.quote: When justice is done, it is a joy to the righteous but terror to evildoers. One who wanders from the way of understanding will rest in the assembly of the dead. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'When justice is done, it is a joy to the righteous but terror to evildoers'—the same event produces opposite responses depending on which side you are on. Justice is the righteous person's celebration and the wicked person's dread. 'One who wanders from the way of understanding will rest in the assembly of the dead'—the wandering from wisdom has a destination: the gathering of those whose folly destroyed them. Kidner: the way of understanding is the path of life; to wander from it is to wander toward death, even if the process is gradual and the wanderer does not notice.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever loves pleasure will be a poor man; he who loves wine and oil will not be rich. The wicked is a ransom for the righteous, and the traitor for the upright. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever loves pleasure will be a poor man'—the love of pleasure as an organizing principle of life reliably produces poverty; pleasure is a good servant and a terrible master. 'He who loves wine and oil'—the luxuries of the ancient world; those who prioritize consumption over production end in want. 'The wicked is a ransom for the righteous'—the wicked person's punishment sometimes takes the place of the righteous one's. This is a dim anticipation of substitutionary atonement: Christ became our ransom (Mark 10:45) in the fullest sense.

verseByVerse.quote: It is better to live in a desert land than with a quarrelsome and fretful woman. Precious treasure and oil are in a wise man's dwelling, but a foolish man devours it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'It is better to live in a desert land than with a quarrelsome and fretful woman'—the desert is preferable to chronic domestic conflict. The desert is harsh and lonely; chronic quarreling is worse. 'Precious treasure and oil are in a wise man's dwelling'—the wise person accumulates and preserves; his household has surplus because wisdom manages resources well. 'A foolish man devours it'—the fool has whatever he accumulates and immediately consumes it; he cannot build because he cannot resist spending. Kidner: the fundamental economic divide in Proverbs is not between the rich and poor but between the wise and foolish.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever pursues righteousness and kindness will find life, righteousness, and honor. A wise man scales the city of the mighty and brings down the stronghold in which they trust. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever pursues righteousness and kindness will find life, righteousness, and honor'—the active pursuit of righteousness and hesed produces life, more righteousness, and honor. The positive cycle: pursuing good produces more good. 'A wise man scales the city of the mighty and brings down the stronghold in which they trust'—wisdom achieves what military force cannot; the mind guided by wisdom can overcome defenses that brute strength would never breach. Keller: the power of wisdom is disproportionate to its apparent resources. A single wise person can outmaneuver overwhelming opposition.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever keeps his mouth and his tongue keeps himself out of trouble. “Scoffer” is the name of the arrogant, haughty man who acts with arrogant pride. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever keeps his mouth and his tongue keeps himself out of trouble'—the discipline of speech is self-protective; the guarded mouth is the guarded life. The tongue is the most dangerous instrument the person controls. The scoffer is now given a precise character profile: arrogance plus contempt plus pride in action. He is not merely unteachable but actively dismissive of others' wisdom. Waltke: the scoffer is the polar opposite of the teachable person. He has placed himself beyond the reach of wisdom and is therefore the most dangerous kind of fool.

verseByVerse.quote: The desire of the sluggard kills him, for his hands refuse to labor. All day long he craves and craves, but the righteous gives and does not hold back. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The desire of the sluggard kills him, for his hands refuse to labor'—desire without action is lethal; the sluggard wants outcomes he is unwilling to work for, and the frustrated desire eventually destroys him. 'All day long he craves and craves'—the insatiability of appetite without discipline. 'The righteous gives and does not hold back'—the antithesis of craving is generous giving; the righteous person's hands move toward others in giving rather than toward himself in grasping. Sproul: generosity is the fruit of a soul that has found its satisfaction in God rather than in accumulation.

verseByVerse.quote: The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination; how much more when he brings it with evil intent. A false witness will perish, but the word of a man who hears will endure. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination'—even worse than sacrifice from a wicked person is sacrifice deliberately offered as a religious cover for evil intent. God is not deceived by religious performance, however elaborate. 'A false witness will perish'—the lying witness does not escape; death is his destination. 'The word of a man who hears will endure'—the person who receives and internalizes true testimony speaks words that last. The contrast is between fleeting lies and enduring truth.

verseByVerse.quote: A wicked man puts on a bold face, but the upright gives thought to his ways. No wisdom, no understanding, no counsel can avail against the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A wicked man puts on a bold face'—brazenness as a strategy; the wicked person's confidence is performed rather than genuine. 'The upright gives thought to his ways'—the upright person's confidence is earned by careful reflection. 'No wisdom, no understanding, no counsel can avail against the LORD'—one of the most absolute sovereignty statements in Proverbs: human wisdom, intelligence, and strategy, however formidable, cannot stand against the purpose of God. Calvin: no creature-plan can ultimately override the plan of the one in whom all things consist.

verseByVerse.quote: The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD'—the chapter's closing verse is its most compressed statement of the relationship between human preparation and divine outcome. Both are real: preparation is commended, not dismissed. But the outcome belongs to God. Waltke: the believer is neither fatalistic (why prepare, if God decides?) nor self-reliant (my preparation will determine the outcome). He prepares with full effort and holds the outcome with open hands. This is the practical shape of trusting God with the results of our best work.

21.theology: Divine sovereignty over history and the limits of human power. Proverbs 21:1 and 21:30–31 together form the book's most comprehensive statement of divine sovereignty over history. The king's heart, the counsellor's wisdom, the warrior's horse — all are in the LORD's hands. This is not a counsel of fatalism but of faith: the person who knows that the LORD governs the king's heart and secures the victory is freed from the anxiety of ultimate responsibility. They plan, they prepare, they fight — but they hold the outcome loosely, because they know who holds the outcome. This is the Calvinist tradition's "God controls and we are responsible" applied to the full range of human endeavour: political, intellectual, and military. Human agency is real and matters; but it operates within a governance that ensures the LORD's purposes will stand (19:21).
21.examples:
Then: "To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice" (v. 3) was a prophetic challenge to a culture that had learned to separate religious observance from social ethics. The person who offered elaborate sacrifices at the temple while oppressing workers, cheating in business, and ignoring the poor had not understood either sacrifice or justice. The sacrifice is the expression of a life; when the life contradicts the sacrifice, the sacrifice is worse than useless — it is an insult to the God whose character it claims to honour.

Now: "The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD" (v. 31) is the wisdom text for every leader, strategist, and planner who has done everything right and still found the outcome out of their hands. Prepare thoroughly — this is wisdom's consistent counsel. But hold the preparation with an open hand, knowing that the victory is the LORD's to give or withhold according to purposes that exceed your strategy. The leader who has internalised this is both more diligent (because preparation is real responsibility) and more peaceful (because the outcome is not ultimately their burden to carry).

22.title: A Good Name
22.text: <sup>1</sup>A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches, and favor is better than silver or gold. <sup>2</sup>The rich and the poor meet together; the LORD is the maker of them all. <sup>3</sup>The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it. <sup>4</sup>The reward of humility and fear of the LORD is riches and honor and life. <sup>6</sup>Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it. <sup>7</sup>The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is the slave of the lender. <sup>9</sup>Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor. <sup>17</sup>Incline your ear and hear the words of the wise, and apply your heart to my knowledge, <sup>22</sup>Do not rob the poor, because he is poor, or crush the afflicted at the gate, <sup>23</sup>for the LORD will plead their cause and rob of life those who rob them. <sup>29</sup>Do you see a man skillful in his work? He will stand before kings; he will not stand before obscure men.
22.overview:
Chapter 22 opens the collection's most famous verse — "a good name is to be chosen rather than great riches" (v.1) — and then pivots to "the thirty sayings of the wise" (vv.17–24:22), a section with remarkable parallels to the Egyptian wisdom text Instruction of Amenemope. That such wisdom appeared across cultures does not diminish Scripture; it shows that general revelation seeds wisdom broadly, while special revelation perfects and redeems it.

The chapter holds together two great themes: reputation rightly ordered (vv.1–9) and instruction rightly received (vv.17–29). A good name is not a brand to manage but a life poured out in integrity before God. The rich and poor alike bear the LORD's image (v.2) — a leveling that should dismantle both pride and contempt.

Timothy Keller notes that "fear of the LORD" (v.4) is the engine beneath all genuine wisdom. Humility before God produces the kind of person whose name becomes, almost accidentally, a good one. The one who grasps for reputation loses it; the one who fears God gains it freely.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 22 — A Good Name, Train Up a Child, and the Thirty Sayings of the Wise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 22 is transitional: vv.1-16 continue the Solomonic antithetical proverbs, then v.17 introduces 'The Words of the Wise' (22:17-24:22), which bears resemblance to the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope. This section is more extended and instructional in form, addressed directly to the son. The thirty sayings (v.20) are a distinct literary unit within this section.
verseByVerse.theology: The opening verse—a good name chosen over riches—is one of Proverbs' most foundational value statements. Reputation built on integrity is more valuable than wealth. The training of children (v.6) is a call to individualized formation: 'the way he should go' may carry the sense of 'the way suited to him.' The promise is covenantal: faithful formation has reliable results over the long arc of a life.
verseByVerse.examples: The thirty sayings begin with the most urgent social ethics (v.22: do not rob the poor; v.24: avoid the angry man) before moving toward financial wisdom and the skill of the craftsman (v.29). The pedagogy is practical and urgent: these are not theoretical principles but survival wisdom for a young man entering public life.

verseByVerse.quote: A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches, and favor is better than silver or gold. The rich and the poor meet together; the LORD is the maker of them all. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches'—the good name is the reputation of a life of integrity; it is chosen, not inherited or bought. 'Favor is better than silver or gold'—favor (hen, grace) is the goodwill of God and neighbor; both are more valuable than any economic asset. 'The rich and the poor meet together; the LORD is the maker of them all'—the leveling reality of creation: whatever social distinctions exist, both are equally creatures of the same Creator. Waltke: this is the theological foundation of social ethics; to treat the poor with contempt is to dishonor their Maker.

verseByVerse.quote: The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it. The reward of humility and fear of the LORD is riches and honor and life. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The prudent sees danger and hides himself'—wisdom as foresight: the prudent person reads the situation ahead of time and acts before the crisis arrives. 'The simple go on and suffer for it'—the simple person lacks this foresight and walks straight into what the prudent person avoided. 'The reward of humility and fear of the LORD is riches and honor and life'—the threefold reward: material (riches), relational (honor), and vital (life). All three flow from the single root of humble, God-fearing character. Sproul: these are covenantal promises describing the direction and ultimate destination of the wise life.

verseByVerse.quote: Thorns and snares are in the way of the crooked; whoever guards his soul will keep far from them. Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Thorns and snares are in the way of the crooked'—the crooked path is not merely morally wrong but practically dangerous; it is full of obstacles that the straight path avoids. 'Train up a child in the way he should go'—the Hebrew may mean 'according to his way,' suggesting formation fitted to the individual child's character and personality. 'Even when he is old he will not depart from it'—the long-term covenantal promise: faithful, personalized formation produces durable results. Kidner: the grain of the wise life, established early, has a tendency to reassert itself even through seasons of departure.

verseByVerse.quote: The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is the slave of the lender. Whoever sows injustice will reap calamity, and the rod of his fury will fail. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is the slave of the lender'—a clear-eyed description of financial power dynamics; debt is a form of servitude. Proverbs does not endorse this arrangement but observes it as a reality that wisdom navigates carefully. 'Whoever sows injustice will reap calamity'—the agricultural metaphor for inevitable consequence: you cannot plant injustice and harvest justice. 'The rod of his fury will fail'—the violent person's instrument of power will be broken; his strength will not sustain itself indefinitely.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor. Drive out a scoffer, and strife will go out, and quarreling and abuse will cease. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed'—the 'bountiful eye' is the generous eye, the eye that sees others' need as an opportunity rather than a burden. 'He shares his bread with the poor'—sharing food is the concrete expression of the generous eye; generosity is not abstract. 'Drive out a scoffer, and strife will go out'—the scoffer is the source of relational toxicity; when the scoffer is removed, the conflict he was generating stops. Kidner: some relationships, when maintained, perpetuate conflict; when ended graciously but firmly, peace returns.

verseByVerse.quote: He who loves purity of heart, and whose speech is gracious, will have the king as his friend. The eyes of the LORD keep watch over knowledge, but he overthrows the words of the traitor. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'He who loves purity of heart, and whose speech is gracious, will have the king as his friend'—the person of inner purity and gracious speech attracts even the highest levels of society; character creates access. 'The eyes of the LORD keep watch over knowledge'—wisdom and truth-telling are under divine protection; God is invested in the preservation of knowledge. 'He overthrows the words of the traitor'—the treacherous person's words are actively opposed by God. Truth-speaking has a protector and deception has an opponent.

verseByVerse.quote: The sluggard says, “There is a lion outside! I shall be killed in the streets!” The mouth of forbidden women is a deep pit; he with whom the LORD is angry will fall into it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The comedy of the sluggard's excuse-making reaches its peak: a lion is his imagined reason not to go to work. The excuse is technically possible but obviously a pretext. 'The mouth of forbidden women is a deep pit'—a deep pit is invisible from outside and inescapable from within; the forbidden woman's words function exactly like this. 'He with whom the LORD is angry will fall into it'—the one who falls into this pit is not merely foolish but under divine judgment; the moral failure is also a spiritual one. Waltke: adultery is both wisdom's defeat and God's abandonment.

verseByVerse.quote: Folly is bound up in the heart of a child, but the rod of discipline drives it far from him. Whoever oppresses the poor to increase his own wealth, or gives to the rich, will only come to poverty. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Folly is bound up in the heart of a child'—folly is not merely a behavior pattern but is organically present in the child's heart; it is tied there by nature. This is one of Proverbs' most honest statements about human nature. 'The rod of discipline drives it far from him'—discipline is the external force that moves what is bound in the heart. 'Whoever oppresses the poor to increase his own wealth, or gives to the rich, will only come to poverty'—the two perverse economic transactions: taking from those who have nothing and giving to those who have everything. Both produce the opposite of their intended result.

verseByVerse.quote: Incline your ear and hear the words of the wise, and apply your heart to my knowledge, for it will be pleasant if you keep them within you, if all of them are ready on your lips. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Incline your ear and hear the words of the wise'—the new section begins with a direct address; the pedagogical relationship returns with explicit urgency. 'Apply your heart to my knowledge'—not merely intellectual but volitional; the heart must be deliberately directed toward wisdom. 'It will be pleasant if you keep them within you'—internalized wisdom produces pleasantness; the goal is not external compliance but transformed inner life. 'Ready on your lips'—wisdom that has been internalized becomes available for speech when it is needed. Formation shapes response.

verseByVerse.quote: That your trust may be in the LORD, I have made them known to you today, even to you. Have I not written for you thirty sayings of counsel and knowledge, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'That your trust may be in the LORD'—the explicit purpose of wisdom instruction: not self-sufficiency or social success but trust in God. The goal of all the formation in Proverbs is a person who trusts God rather than himself. 'I have made them known to you today, even to you'—the personal address; the father speaks directly to the son as an individual. 'Have I not written for you thirty sayings'—a literary reference to the thirty structured units that follow (22:22-24:22). The number signals a conscious, orderly, complete body of wisdom.

verseByVerse.quote: to make you know what is right and true, that you may give a true answer to those who sent you? Do not rob the poor, because he is poor, or crush the afflicted at the gate, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'That you may give a true answer to those who sent you'—practical training for public life; the wisdom-formed person will be entrusted with missions that require accurate reporting. 'Do not rob the poor, because he is poor'—the most contemptible exploitation: targeting someone specifically because their poverty makes them defenseless.
