'At the gate'—the place of legal judgment; the gate is where the poor are most vulnerable to the corrupt manipulation of legal processes. Waltke: the first prohibition of the thirty sayings is about the abuse of power against the defenseless.

verseByVerse.quote: for the LORD will plead their cause and rob of life those who rob them. Make no friendship with a man given to anger, nor go with a wrathful man, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The LORD will plead their cause'—God is the advocate of the poor who have no other advocate; the divine court reverses the corrupted earthly courts. 'Make no friendship with a man given to anger'—the character-contamination warning: the angry person's pattern is contagious. Close association with chronic anger shapes the associate toward anger. 'Nor go with a wrathful man'—both friendship and accompaniment carry the risk of formation by the other's worst qualities.

verseByVerse.quote: lest you learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare. Be not one of those who give pledges, who put up security for debts. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Lest you learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare'—learning is the danger; we absorb the patterns of those we spend time with, even when we do not intend to. The snare is the pattern of anger becoming habitual. 'Be not one of those who give pledges'—the financial co-signing warning; guaranteeing another's debt is a form of financial recklessness that wisdom consistently counsels against. The wisdom of saying no to financial entanglement protects the generosity that can actually help people.

verseByVerse.quote: If you have nothing with which to pay, why should your bed be taken from under you? Do not move the ancient landmark that your fathers have set. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Why should your bed be taken from under you?'—the rhetorical question makes the consequence vivid: the co-signer who cannot pay loses even his most basic possession. Wisdom protects the vulnerable from this outcome by counseling avoidance upfront. 'Do not move the ancient landmark that your fathers have set'—landmarks marked property boundaries; moving them was theft that was particularly insidious because it was gradual and difficult to detect. Waltke: the injunction protects the inheritance of families across generations.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you see a man skillful in his work? He will stand before kings; he will not stand before obscure men. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Do you see a man skillful in his work? He will stand before kings'—professional excellence creates access to the highest levels of society. The path to royal service is not networking or flattery but demonstrated competence. 'He will not stand before obscure men'—the skillful person's abilities carry him upward; his gifts create opportunities that others must maneuver for. Kidner: genuine competence is noticed and rewarded—not always immediately, but reliably over time.

22.theology:
The LORD as Maker of Rich and Poor. Verse 2 is theologically dense. To say that the LORD made both rich and poor is not to endorse economic inequality as divinely ordained but to strip class of ultimate significance. Both are equally creatures, equally sinners, equally in need of grace. Christian theology presses further: both are equally candidates for redemption, equally called to table fellowship. The cross is the great leveling — "there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free" (Gal. 3:28).

Humility and the Fear of the LORD (v.4). Proverbs keeps returning to this pair. Humility is not self-deprecation; it is accurate sight — seeing oneself as creature before Creator. The fear of the LORD is the relational disposition that keeps that sight clear. Together they produce a life of remarkable freedom: freed from status anxiety, freed from the grasping that destroys the soul. "Riches and honor and life" are given, not seized.
22.examples:
Then: Israelite parents would teach children in the rhythms of daily life — working, eating, traveling (Deut. 6:7). The craftsman's workshop was also a school of character. The "gate" was where elders like Boaz administered justice publicly (Ruth 4:1). Chapter 22's advice was entirely practical for a society where reputation, work quality, and economic justice were intertwined in visible community life.

Now: In an age of curated digital personas, "a good name" (v.1) has never been more misunderstood. The proverb cuts against impression management — the good name Proverbs values cannot be manufactured online. Verse 6 speaks to parents worried their children will abandon the faith: wisdom-shaped formation is deeper than we know, even when the season of apparent departure is long. And verses 22–23 call the church to advocate concretely for economic justice — not as political performance, but as the natural overflow of fearing the God who defends the poor.

23.title: Do Not Wear Yourself Out to Get Rich
23.text: <sup>1</sup>When you sit down to eat with a ruler, observe carefully what is before you, <sup>4</sup>Do not toil to acquire wealth; be discerning enough to desist. <sup>5</sup>When your eyes light on it, it is gone, for suddenly it sprouts wings, flying like an eagle toward heaven. <sup>6</sup>Do not eat the bread of a man who is stingy; do not desire his delicacies, <sup>10</sup>Do not move an ancient landmark or enter the fields of the fatherless, <sup>11</sup>for their Redeemer is strong; he will plead their cause against you. <sup>17</sup>Let not your heart envy sinners, but continue in the fear of the LORD all the day. <sup>18</sup>Surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off. <sup>19</sup>Hear, my son, and be wise, and direct your heart in the way. <sup>22</sup>Listen to your father who gave you life, and do not despise your mother when she is old. <sup>23</sup>Buy truth, and do not sell it; buy wisdom, instruction, and understanding. <sup>29</sup>Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has strife? Who has complaining? Who has wounds without cause? Who has redness of eyes? <sup>30</sup>Those who tarry long over wine, those who go to try mixed wine. <sup>33</sup>Your eyes will see strange things, and your heart utter perverse things.
23.overview:
Chapter 23 is a series of urgent parental instructions addressing three great idols: wealth, food and pleasure, and intoxication. The framing device — a son being warned before a meal with a ruler (vv.1–3) and warned again before wine (vv.29–35) — is deliberate. What we eat and drink, and with whom, shapes character more than we imagine.

The center of the chapter is a pair of commands that belong together: "Let not your heart envy sinners, but continue in the fear of the LORD all the day. Surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off" (vv.17–18). The antidote to the fool's prosperity is not resignation but eschatological confidence — a hope rooted in the character of God, not the circumstances of the moment.

Keller reads verse 23 — "Buy truth, and do not sell it" — as the heart of the chapter. Truth is not a commodity; it is a person (John 14:6). The wisdom tradition points toward One whose price was infinite and whose gift is freely given.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 23 — Table Manners, Ambition, Parental Formation, and the Last Woe
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 23 contains some of Proverbs' most memorable passages: the dinner table with a ruler (vv.1-3), the wealth that sprouts wings (v.5), the appeal to the heart ('give me your heart,' v.26), the parents' joy in the wise child (vv.24-25), and the devastating portrait of the drunkard (vv.29-35). The chapter is more discursive and extended than the short antithetical couplets of chapters 10-22.
verseByVerse.theology: The extended parent-child address of vv.15-25 is one of the emotional high points of the book: 'My son, if your heart is wise, my heart too will be glad' (v.15). The father's joy in the child's wisdom is the goal of all the instruction. The mother's teaching appears explicitly in v.22 alongside the father's; the formation of wisdom is a shared parental project.
verseByVerse.examples: The portrait of the drunkard (vv.29-35) is one of the most vivid character studies in the Bible: the woe questions, the progression of symptoms (redness of eyes, strange sights, perverse speech), and the self-defeating conclusion: 'I will seek it yet again.' This is addiction described with psychological precision two millennia before modern science.

verseByVerse.quote: When you sit down to eat with a ruler, observe carefully what is before you, and put a knife to your throat if you are given to appetite. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'When you sit down to eat with a ruler, observe carefully what is before you'—situational awareness at the table of power; wisdom means reading the context before acting. 'Put a knife to your throat if you are given to appetite'—extreme language for a clear purpose: the appetite that is unchecked in ordinary life becomes catastrophic in a high-stakes context. Waltke: the dinner table with a ruler is not primarily about food but about managing desire in situations where the consequences of losing control are severe. Self-mastery is the prerequisite for social access.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not desire his delicacies, for they are deceptive food. Do not toil to acquire wealth; be discerning enough to desist. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Do not desire his delicacies, for they are deceptive food'—the ruler's hospitality may be a lure; what appears generous may come with strings that cannot be seen until later. 'Do not toil to acquire wealth; be discerning enough to desist'—the command to stop working for wealth as a primary goal requires genuine wisdom to obey; the money-pursuing impulse is strong. Keller: this is one of Proverbs' clearest counter-cultural commands; it directly contradicts the dominant cultural narrative that acquisition is the point of labor.

verseByVerse.quote: When your eyes light on it, it is gone, for suddenly it makes itself wings, flying like an eagle toward heaven. Do not eat the bread of a man who is stingy; do not desire his delicacies, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'It makes itself wings, flying like an eagle toward heaven'—one of Proverbs' most memorable images of wealth: it is here, then it is gone, with the suddenness and finality of an eagle's flight. The person who has organized his life around wealth is organizing his life around the most volatile commodity there is. 'Do not eat the bread of a man who is stingy'—the stingy man's hospitality is a trap; his food is offered with an eye on the cost. The contrast with the generous man (22:9) is pointed.

verseByVerse.quote: for he is like one who is inwardly calculating. “Eat and drink!” he says to you, but his heart is not with you. You will vomit up the morsels you have eaten, and waste your pleasant words. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'He is like one who is inwardly calculating'—the stingy man's mouth says eat and drink while his mind is running a ledger. His hospitality is a performance masking resentment at the cost. 'His heart is not with you'—the gap between speech and heart. 'You will vomit up the morsels you have eaten'—the emotional and spiritual sickness that comes from accepting hospitality that was never freely given. 'Waste your pleasant words'—the conversation was spent on someone who was never genuinely present. Kidner: the stingy man's invitation is a form of emotional fraud.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not speak in the hearing of a fool, for he will despise the good sense of your words. Do not move an ancient landmark or enter the fields of the fatherless, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Do not speak in the hearing of a fool, for he will despise the good sense of your words'—the wisdom of selective speech; some audiences cannot receive wisdom and will only treat it with contempt. The speaker wastes his words and may invite retaliation. 'Do not move an ancient landmark or enter the fields of the fatherless'—the prohibition on boundary-moving extended specifically to the fatherless, who are the most vulnerable to such exploitation. The fatherless have no patriarch to defend their property; God therefore takes up their defense.

verseByVerse.quote: for their Redeemer is strong; he will plead their cause against you. Apply your heart to instruction and your ear to words of knowledge. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Their Redeemer is strong; he will plead their cause against you'—the go'el, the kinsman-redeemer who defends the family interest: God himself is the Redeemer of the fatherless. 'Strong'—the emphasis on divine power; the one who exploits the fatherless is taking on an opponent of infinite strength. 'Apply your heart to instruction and your ear to words of knowledge'—the positive command that follows the warning: having been instructed in what not to do, apply yourself to wisdom. Heart and ear together: will and reception must both be engaged.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not withhold discipline from a child; if you strike him with a rod, he will not die. If you strike him with the rod, you will save his soul from Sheol. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Do not withhold discipline from a child; if you strike him with a rod, he will not die'—the reassurance is needed: parental anxiety about the pain of discipline often leads to its omission. Proverbs insists the child will not be damaged by appropriate correction. 'If you strike him with the rod, you will save his soul from Sheol'—the stakes are ultimate: discipline now or death later. The rod is not cruelty but salvation; the parent who disciplines is choosing the child's life over his momentary comfort. Waltke: the parent who withholds discipline is making a life-or-death mistake in favor of short-term peace.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, if your heart is wise, my heart too will be glad. My inmost being will exult when your lips speak what is right. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'My son, if your heart is wise, my heart too will be glad'—one of Proverbs' most emotionally transparent moments: the father's joy depends on the child's wisdom. 'My inmost being will exult'—the Hebrew refers to the kidneys, considered in ancient thought to be the seat of deepest feeling. The father's delight is not superficial but visceral. 'When your lips speak what is right'—wisdom made audible; the visible confirmation of the invisible formation. Keller: this verse captures the pastoral heart of all Christian formation—the mentor's deepest joy is the flourishing of the one he has formed.

verseByVerse.quote: Let not your heart envy sinners, but continue in the fear of the LORD all the day. Surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Let not your heart envy sinners'—the envy of the wicked is a recurring temptation addressed throughout wisdom literature (cf. Ps. 73; Prov. 24:1,19). The sinners appear to prosper; the righteous appear to suffer. 'Continue in the fear of the LORD all the day'—the antidote to envy is sustained attention to God rather than sustained comparison with others. 'Surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off'—the eschatological anchor: what appears to be the sinner's advantage is temporary; the righteous person's hope has a future that the sinner's apparent prosperity does not.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, my son, and be wise, and direct your heart in the way. Be not among drunkards or among gluttonous eaters of meat, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Hear, my son, and be wise, and direct your heart in the way'—the renewed address: hearing and wisdom and directed will working together. 'Be not among drunkards or among gluttonous eaters of meat'—the warning is about association as well as individual behavior; being among those given to excess is itself a formative danger. The community you inhabit shapes the person you become. Kidner: Proverbs does not merely prohibit the behaviors but the communities that normalize them.

verseByVerse.quote: for the drunkard and the glutton will come to poverty, and slumber will clothe them with rags. Listen to your father who gave you life, and do not despise your mother when she is old. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The drunkard and the glutton will come to poverty, and slumber will clothe them with rags'—the practical consequence: excess produces poverty because it consumes resources and motivation simultaneously. 'Slumber will clothe them with rags'—the sleep of the indulgent is the garment of destitution. 'Listen to your father who gave you life, and do not despise your mother when she is old'—both parents are explicitly honored. The mother's teaching is not secondary; her authority in the home is equal, and her vulnerability in old age demands special protection from contempt.

verseByVerse.quote: Buy truth, and do not sell it; buy wisdom, instruction, and understanding. The father of the righteous will greatly rejoice; he who fathers a wise son will be glad in him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Buy truth, and do not sell it'—truth is to be acquired at any cost and never bartered away for any advantage. 'Buy wisdom, instruction, and understanding'—wisdom comes as a cluster: you cannot buy wisdom without acquiring instruction and understanding with it. 'The father of the righteous will greatly rejoice'—the parental joy theme returns; the righteous child is the father's crown. Waltke: the parent's investment in the child's formation is repaid by the joy of seeing wisdom take root.

verseByVerse.quote: Let your father and mother be glad; let her who bore you rejoice. My son, give me your heart, and let your eyes observe my ways. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Let your father and mother be glad; let her who bore you rejoice'—the imperative form: wisdom is not merely personally beneficial but filially obligatory. The wise child honors his parents by his wisdom. 'My son, give me your heart'—the most intimate command in Proverbs: not your obedience, not your behavior, but your heart. The father wants the inner person, not just external compliance. 'Let your eyes observe my ways'—the apprenticeship model: watch what I do, not just hear what I say. Formation happens by imitation as much as instruction.

verseByVerse.quote: For a prostitute is a deep pit; an adulteress is a narrow well. She lies in wait like a robber and increases the traitors among mankind. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'For a prostitute is a deep pit; an adulteress is a narrow well'—the recurring imagery of depth and entrapment; sexual immorality is a pit from which escape is extremely difficult. 'A narrow well'—a well too narrow to climb out of once you have fallen in. 'She lies in wait like a robber'—the predatory image; she is not a passive temptress but an active hunter. 'Increases the traitors among mankind'—adultery produces a community of broken faith; each act of betrayal multiplies the culture of faithlessness. Sexual immorality is never only private; it degrades the moral fabric of the community.

verseByVerse.quote: Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has strife? Who has complaining? Who has wounds without cause? Who has redness of eyes? Those who tarry long over wine; those who go to mix strong drink. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has strife?'—the rhetorical questions pile up: every form of human misery is attributed to the drunkard's life. The list is comprehensive: psychological (woe, sorrow), social (strife, complaining), physical (wounds, redness of eyes). 'Those who tarry long over wine'—the extended session is the indicator; Proverbs does not condemn wine per se but the person who lingers over it until it controls him. Calvin: the drunkard does not merely use wine; he is used by it. Every form of addiction inverts the proper order of human agency and appetite.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not look at wine when it is red, when it sparkles in the cup and goes down smoothly. In the end it bites like a serpent and stings like an adder. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Do not look at wine when it is red, when it sparkles in the cup'—the warning against the aesthetic pleasure of wine; its appearance is part of the temptation. 'Goes down smoothly'—the deceptive ease of entry. 'In the end it bites like a serpent and stings like an adder'—what begins smooth ends venomous. The person who makes decisions based only on how wine looks and feels going down is ignoring the serpent waiting at the end of the session. Proverbs tracks consequences through time.

verseByVerse.quote: Your eyes will see strange things, and your heart utter perverse things. You will be like one who lies down in the midst of the sea, like one who lies on the top of a mast. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Your eyes will see strange things, and your heart utter perverse things'—the cognitive and moral distortions of intoxication: perception is disordered, and the disordered heart speaks what it would otherwise restrain. 'Like one who lies down in the midst of the sea'—extreme danger experienced as comfort; the drunkard is in mortal danger and does not know it, as relaxed as if in a safe bed while on a rocking mast in open water. Keller: this is a picture of every intoxicant's fundamental deception: it makes danger feel like safety and destruction feel like rest.

verseByVerse.quote: They struck me, you will say, but I was not hurt; they beat me, but I did not feel it. When shall I awake? I must have another drink. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'They struck me, but I was not hurt; they beat me, but I did not feel it'—the anesthesia of addiction: pain without sensation, damage without awareness. 'When shall I awake? I must have another drink'—the devastating self-indictment with which the portrait closes. The drunkard's first thought on waking is to drink again. This is Proverbs' definition of addiction: the compulsive return to what is destroying you. Kidner: the final line is one of the saddest in the book. The drunkard has become his own destroyer, and he cannot stop.

23.theology:
The God Who Redeems. The title goel (v.11) is loaded with covenantal meaning. Ruth's story turns on it; Isaiah uses it for God's redemption of Israel from exile (Isa. 41:14; 43:14); the New Testament sees Christ as the ultimate Redeemer who pays the price no family member could afford. That God is the Redeemer of the fatherless means no one is truly without a defender — which is why the church must embody that advocacy in concrete, particular acts of care.

Eschatological Hope as Wisdom. Verses 17–18 show that wisdom is inseparable from eschatology. To fear the LORD is to orient yourself toward a future guaranteed by the character of God, not by present circumstances. This is not optimism (a temperamental preference for good outcomes) but hope (a theologically grounded confidence in the One who controls the end). The resurrection of Jesus is the anchor of that hope — "your hope will not be cut off" because death itself was cut off at the cross.
23.examples:
Then: A meal with a ruler in the ancient world was a political event — gifts and flattery were expected. The son is warned to see past the knife at his throat and not lose himself to ambitious social climbing (vv.1–3). Landmark boundaries were sacrosanct in Israelite law (Deut. 19:14); moving them was theft dressed as nothing. The wine section (vv.29–35) addressed a culture where wine was the primary social lubricant — wisdom does not prohibit it but demands mastery over it.

Now: The wealth section (vv.4–5) speaks directly to the professional-class anxiety that drives overwork and portfolio obsession. The eschatological correction (vv.17–18) is the only real cure for envy of the successful fool: a longer view. And the wine section remains searingly contemporary — addiction affects every demographic, and Proverbs' anatomical description of it is more clinical than moralistic. The gospel adds to wisdom's diagnosis: the heart craves what only God can give, and the disordered craving for any substance is finally a spiritual hunger misdirected.

24.title: Do Not Envy the Wicked
24.text: <sup>1</sup>Be not envious of evil men, nor desire to be with them, <sup>2</sup>for their hearts devise violence, and their lips talk of trouble. <sup>3</sup>By wisdom a house is built, and by understanding it is established; <sup>4</sup>by knowledge the rooms are filled with all precious and pleasant riches. <sup>10</sup>If you faint in the day of adversity, your strength is small. <sup>11</sup>Rescue those who are being taken away to death; hold back those who are stumbling to the slaughter. <sup>13</sup>My son, eat honey, for it is good, and the drippings of the honeycomb are sweet to your taste. <sup>14</sup>Know that wisdom is such to your soul; if you find it, there will be a future, and your hope will not be cut off. <sup>16</sup>for the righteous falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked stumble in calamity. <sup>17</sup>Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart be glad when he stumbles, <sup>19</sup>Fret not yourself because of evildoers, and be not envious of the wicked, <sup>20</sup>for the evil man has no future; the lamp of the wicked will be put out. <sup>29</sup>Do not say, "I will do to him as he has done to me; I will pay the man back for what he has done."
24.overview:
Chapter 24 returns to the theme of envy with fresh urgency (vv.1, 19–20) and surrounds it with wisdom's great affirmations: the wisdom-built house (vv.3–4), the resilience of the righteous (v.16), the warning against schadenfreude (v.17), and the sweetness of wisdom itself (vv.13–14). The chapter also contains one of Proverbs' most striking ethical demands: rescue those being led to slaughter (vv.11–12), with the sobering reminder that pleading ignorance before the God who weighs hearts will not stand.

The key structural move is the contrast between two futures. The wicked may prosper now, but "the evil man has no future; the lamp of the wicked will be put out" (v.20). Wisdom sees what is coming. The righteous, by contrast, may fall repeatedly — but they rise (v.16). Resurrection hope is embedded in Proverbs' anthropology long before Easter morning.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 24 — Do Not Envy the Wicked, Rescue the Perishing, and the Sluggard's Field
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 24 closes the thirty sayings (vv.1-22), adds a brief section of further sayings of the wise (vv.23-29), then closes with the extended portrait of the sluggard's field (vv.30-34). The chapter is rich in practical ethics: do not envy evildoers, rescue those being led to death, do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and the devastating image of the vineyard overgrown with weeds.
verseByVerse.theology: The rescue-those-being-led-to-death passage (vv.11-12) is one of the most searching ethical demands in Proverbs. The person who says 'I did not know' is explicitly warned that God who weighs the heart knows the truth. Willful ignorance is not innocence. The prophetic tradition (Isa. 58; Amos 5) and the New Testament (James 4:17) make the same point: knowing what is right and failing to do it is sin.
verseByVerse.examples: The sluggard's field (vv.30-34) is Proverbs' most extended narrative vignette: the wise man walks by the field of the sluggard, sees the ruin, and draws a moral lesson. Poverty does not come suddenly but through the gradual accumulation of small decisions to sleep a little longer. The lesson is learned not from a text but from observation—wisdom is drawn from the seen world.

verseByVerse.quote: Be not envious of evil men, nor desire to be with them, for their hearts devise violence, and their lips talk of trouble. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Be not envious of evil men'—envy of the wicked is a recurring temptation precisely because they often appear to flourish. 'Nor desire to be with them'—proximity to evil is formative; the desire for the company of evildoers is itself dangerous. 'Their hearts devise violence, and their lips talk of trouble'—the diagnostic: what is in the heart of the wicked is violence, and their speech is characteristically destructive. Kidner: the person who envies evildoers is envying the externals without seeing the interior. If you could see what they are actually planning, the envy would evaporate.

verseByVerse.quote: By wisdom a house is built, and by understanding it is established; by knowledge the rooms are filled with all precious and pleasant riches. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'By wisdom a house is built'—the house-building metaphor captures wisdom's comprehensive creative function: it constructs, establishes, and fills. The three stages are sequential: wisdom lays the foundation, understanding gives stability, knowledge fills the interior with good things. Waltke: the 'house' is both literal and figurative—the physical home, the family, the household economy, and the inner life of the person are all built or destroyed by the presence or absence of wisdom. This is why wisdom is worth more than any of the riches it enables.

verseByVerse.quote: A wise man is full of strength, and a man of knowledge enhances his might, for by wise guidance you can wage your war, and in abundance of counselors there is victory. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A wise man is full of strength'—wisdom is a form of power, not an alternative to it; the wise person is strong in a more durable and comprehensive way than the merely physically powerful. 'A man of knowledge enhances his might'—knowledge multiplies the effectiveness of whatever other capacities the person has. 'In abundance of counselors there is victory'—the military application of the multitude-of-counselors principle (cf. 11:14; 15:22; 20:18). No military engagement should be undertaken without the wisdom of multiple advisers.

verseByVerse.quote: Wisdom is too high for a fool; in the gate he does not open his mouth. Whoever plans to do evil will be called a schemer. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Wisdom is too high for a fool; in the gate he does not open his mouth'—the gate is where public discourse and judgment happen; the fool has nothing to contribute to these processes. Wisdom is not merely difficult for him but categorically beyond his reach because he has refused the foundation (fear of God) on which wisdom is built. 'Whoever plans to do evil will be called a schemer'—the public identification of the evil-planner; his character will be known and named. The social recognition of the schemer is itself a form of accountability.

verseByVerse.quote: The devising of folly is sin, and the scoffer is an abomination to mankind. If you faint in the day of adversity, your strength is small. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The devising of folly is sin'—not only the action but the planning of folly is itself sinful; intention is morally significant. 'The scoffer is an abomination to mankind'—not merely to God (though also to God, cf. 3:34) but to the human community; the scoffer makes social life toxic for everyone around him. 'If you faint in the day of adversity, your strength is small'—the test of strength is not comfort but crisis. Character is revealed under pressure; the person who collapses under adversity has been revealed to have less inner resource than was apparent in easier times.

verseByVerse.quote: Rescue those who are being taken away to death; hold back those who are stumbling to the slaughter. If you say, “Behold, we did not know this,” does not he who weighs the heart perceive it? Does not he who keeps watch over your soul know it, and will he not repay man according to his work? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Rescue those who are being taken away to death'—one of the most urgent ethical commands in Proverbs; the passive bystander who could intervene and does not is morally implicated. The excuse of willful ignorance is addressed directly: you did know, or you chose not to know. 'Does not he who weighs the heart perceive it?'—God's omniscience reaches the intention behind the excuse. He knows whether the ignorance was genuine or manufactured. Sproul: this verse eliminates the moral comfort of claiming ignorance when we have been capable of knowledge and chose otherwise. We are accountable for what we could have known.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, eat honey, for it is good, and the drippings of the honeycomb are sweet to your taste. Know that wisdom is such to your soul; if you find it, there will be a future, and your hope will not be cut off. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Eat honey, for it is good'—the analogy to wisdom: just as honey is good and its goodness is immediately available to taste, wisdom is good and its goodness can be experienced. 'Know that wisdom is such to your soul'—wisdom is to the soul what honey is to the taste: nourishing, pleasurable, life-sustaining. 'If you find it, there will be a future, and your hope will not be cut off'—wisdom is the guarantee of future and hope; not that everything will go well immediately, but that the wise person's life has a direction that will not end in futility.

verseByVerse.quote: Lie not in wait as a wicked man against the dwelling of the righteous; do no violence to his home; for the righteous falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked stumble in times of calamity. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Lie not in wait as a wicked man against the dwelling of the righteous'—the warning against predatory strategy; ambushing the righteous person is folly because of the righteous person's resilience. 'The righteous falls seven times and rises again'—seven as completeness: no matter how many times the righteous person is knocked down, he gets up. Resilience is his defining characteristic. 'The wicked stumble in times of calamity'—the single fall of the wicked is definitive because they have no root to sustain them. Keller: the righteous person's repeated rising is the fruit of the God who lifts him up (Ps. 3:5; 37:24).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart be glad when he stumbles, lest the LORD see it and be displeased, and turn away his anger from him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Do not rejoice when your enemy falls'—the prohibition on schadenfreude, even toward enemies. The enemy's suffering is not an occasion for satisfaction. 'Lest the LORD see it and be displeased, and turn away his anger from him'—the remarkable consequence: God's displeasure at the gloating heart leads him to redirect his discipline away from the enemy and toward the gloater. The gloater becomes the recipient of the judgment he was celebrating. Waltke: the transformation of the enemy's suffering from our occasion for joy to our occasion for prayer is the mark of genuine Christlike love.

verseByVerse.quote: Fret not yourself because of evildoers, and be not envious of the wicked, for the evil man has no future; the lamp of the wicked will be put out. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Fret not yourself because of evildoers, and be not envious of the wicked'—the double prohibition echoes Ps. 37:1 and addresses a perennial spiritual temptation. 'For the evil man has no future'—the future is the key word; all apparent advantage of the wicked is present-tense and temporary. 'The lamp of the wicked will be put out'—the lamp-metaphor for the vital force of a life; when it is extinguished, it is extinguished. Sproul: the God who sees the beginning from the end is not impressed by the wicked's temporary prosperity. Neither should we be.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, fear the LORD and the king, and do not join with those who do otherwise, for disaster will arise suddenly from them, and who knows the ruin that will come from them both? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Fear the LORD and the king'—a pairing that places earthly and divine authority in the same sentence, without collapsing them; both are to be feared, though for different reasons. 'Do not join with those who do otherwise'—the dissenter from both divine and royal authority invites disaster. 'Disaster will arise suddenly from them'—both God and the king can act swiftly and decisively; the person who has provoked both has exposed himself to compounded consequences. 'Who knows the ruin that will come from them both?'—the rhetorical understatement of combined divine and royal displeasure.

verseByVerse.quote: These also are sayings of the wise: Partiality in judging is not good. Whoever says to the wicked, “You are in the right,” will be cursed by peoples, abhorred by nations; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Partiality in judging is not good'—a brief new section; the first saying of the further collection repeats the prohibition on partiality in justice. The adjudication system is foundational to community; pervert it, and the community corrodes. 'Whoever says to the wicked, You are in the right'—the worst form of judicial corruption: not merely passive bias but active false endorsement of wickedness. 'Will be cursed by peoples, abhorred by nations'—the scale of condemnation is international. False justice is a crime against humanity.

verseByVerse.quote: but those who rebuke the wicked will have delight, and a good blessing will come upon them. Whoever gives an honest answer kisses the lips. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Those who rebuke the wicked will have delight, and a good blessing will come upon them'—the positive case for honest confrontation: courage in speaking truth to wickedness is rewarded with delight and blessing. 'Whoever gives an honest answer kisses the lips'—one of Proverbs' most intimate metaphors for truthful speech: the honest answer is like a kiss—an expression of genuine love and deep affection. Kidner: this rehabilitates confrontation; telling the truth, even difficult truth, is an act of love more intimate than flattery.

verseByVerse.quote: Prepare your work outside; get everything ready for yourself in the field, and after that build your house. Be not a witness against your neighbor without cause, and do not deceive with your lips. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Prepare your work outside; get everything ready for yourself in the field, and after that build your house'—the wisdom of sequencing: establish your economic foundation (the field) before building your domestic infrastructure (the house). The person who builds his house before securing his livelihood builds on an insecure foundation. 'Be not a witness against your neighbor without cause'—the prohibition on unnecessary testimony against the neighbor; even true testimony should not be given without just cause. 'Do not deceive with your lips'—the positive requirement: your speech should be honest.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not say, “I will do to him as he has done to me; I will pay the man back for what he has done.” I passed by the field of a sluggard, by the vineyard of a man lacking sense, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The impulse to equivalent retaliation—paying back in kind—is the natural human response to being wronged. Proverbs prohibits this (cf. 20:22; 25:21-22; Rom. 12:17-19). 'I passed by the field of a sluggard'—the observation section begins: wisdom is drawn not only from texts but from the visible world. The wise man's walk past the neglected field becomes a lesson. This is the empirical strand in wisdom: see, observe, reflect, conclude.

verseByVerse.quote: and behold, it was all overgrown with thorns; the ground was covered with nettles, and its stone wall was broken down. Then I saw and considered it; I looked and received instruction. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'All overgrown with thorns; the ground covered with nettles, and its stone wall broken down'—a precise catalogue of neglect: thorns, nettles, collapsed walls. Each detail accumulates into a picture of comprehensive ruin produced by the absence of work. 'Then I saw and considered it; I looked and received instruction'—the three stages of wisdom-from-observation: see, consider, receive instruction. The wise person does not just look but reflects until the observation yields its lesson. Kidner: the sluggard's field is a more powerful teacher than any abstract principle, precisely because it is visible and particular and real.

verseByVerse.quote: A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest, and poverty will come upon you like a robber, and want like an armed man. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest'—repeated nearly verbatim from 6:10-11; the threefold 'little' is the key. Not one enormous failure but the accumulation of small concessions to rest. Each individual act is defensible; the pattern is ruinous. 'Poverty will come upon you like a robber, and want like an armed man'—the sudden and violent arrival of destitution. The crisis is not the beginning but the visible end of a long accumulation of small surrenders to sleep.

24.theology:
Resurrection Anthropology. Verse 16 embeds a proto-resurrection hope in Proverbs' account of the righteous life. The righteous are not those who are immune to falling but those who are constitutionally oriented toward rising — because the God they fear is the God who raises the dead. Paul develops this in 2 Cor. 4:9: "struck down, but not destroyed." The wicked have no such resource; their stumble in calamity is final because they have no one to raise them.

The Ethics of Rescue. Verses 11–12 establish that wisdom is not passive. Knowing and not acting is its own form of guilt. This anticipates the prophetic tradition (Isa. 1:17; Micah 6:8) and the New Testament (James 1:27). The God who weighs hearts is not fooled by performative ignorance. The church that knows about injustice and does nothing has not yet grasped the wisdom of God.
24.examples:
Then: The "rescue" command (vv.11–12) likely referred to specific situations: wrongful capital punishment at the gate, debt slavery, or unjust judicial proceedings. Witnesses could intervene, elders could speak. "Pleading ignorance" was already a known excuse. The honey metaphor (v.13) connected wisdom to the agricultural bounty of Canaan — wisdom is as Israelite as the honey of the promised land.

Now: Verse 16 is a lifeline for any Christian in a season of repeated failure — addiction recovery, pastoral burnout, protracted grief, marital crisis. The righteous person is not the one who falls least but the one who keeps getting up. Verses 11–12 speak to every generation that faces systemic injustice: the question is always whether those who know will act. And verse 17 confronts social-media culture's delight in public shaming and the downfall of enemies — wisdom calls for a different emotional posture toward those who fail, even those who harmed us.

25.title: A Word Fitly Spoken
25.text: <sup>1</sup>These also are proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied. <sup>2</sup>It is the glory of God to conceal things, but the glory of kings is to search things out. <sup>6</sup>Do not put yourself forward in the king's presence or stand in the place of the great, <sup>11</sup>A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in a setting of silver. <sup>13</sup>Like the cold of snow in harvest time is a faithful messenger to those who send him; he refreshes the soul of his masters. <sup>15</sup>With patience a ruler may be persuaded, and a soft tongue will break a bone. <sup>16</sup>If you have found honey, eat only enough for you, lest you have your fill of it and vomit it. <sup>20</sup>Whoever sings songs to a heavy heart is like one who takes off a garment on a cold day, and like vinegar on soda. <sup>21</sup>If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink, <sup>22</sup>for you will heap burning coals on his head, and the LORD will reward you. <sup>25</sup>Like cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country.
25.overview:
Chapter 25 opens the Hezekiah collection (chapters 25–29), proverbs copied and arranged by the scribes of King Hezekiah around 700 B.C. The chapter is particularly rich in extended similes — a literary hallmark. Where many proverbs state a truth flatly, chapter 25 paints it: apples of gold, cold snow in harvest, a soft tongue breaking bone.

The organizing theme is speech — what it is, what it can do, and how precious it is when used well. A word fitly spoken (v.11) is not merely pleasant; it is a work of art that reflects the beauty of wisdom itself. Speech is also powerful: a soft tongue breaks bone (v.15), meaning patient persuasion accomplishes what force cannot.

The ethical climax is verses 21–22: give bread to your enemy. Paul quotes this in Romans 12:20, embedding it in his great vision of non-retaliation and love. What Proverbs presents as wisdom, Paul presents as the shape of cruciform love — the pattern of a community that does not overcome evil with evil but with good.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 25 — Glory, Restraint, Enemies, and the Right Word at the Right Time
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 25 opens a new collection: 'These also are proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied.' This section (25-29) has a slightly different character: more extended metaphors, more poetic development of a single theme, more explicit use of comparison. Chapter 25 includes royal sayings, social wisdom (don't overstay your welcome, don't brag), and the famous 'coals of fire' proverb about treating enemies with kindness.
verseByVerse.theology: The glory of God is to conceal things; the glory of kings is to search things out (v.2)—one of the most provocative epistemological statements in Proverbs. Mystery is not a failure of knowledge but a divine choice. The king who investigates is imitating the divine character in his search for truth. Investigation is royal; humility before mystery is divine.
verseByVerse.examples: The word fitly spoken (v.11) and the coals of fire on an enemy's head (vv.21-22) are among the most quoted verses in Proverbs. Both concern the social power of the right action at the right moment. Paul quotes the coals-of-fire proverb in Romans 12:20 as the summary of Christian social ethics.

verseByVerse.quote: These also are proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied. It is the glory of God to conceal things, but the glory of kings is to search things out. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'These also are proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied'—a historical note about the transmission of wisdom; Hezekiah's court was a center of literary activity (cf. 2 Chron. 29-31). Wisdom is preserved by those who value it. 'It is the glory of God to conceal things'—mystery is not a deficiency but a divine attribute; God's hiddenness is part of his glory. 'The glory of kings is to search things out'—the king's calling is investigation: to pursue knowledge, to judge rightly. Waltke: the tension between divine mystery and human investigation is the proper environment of wisdom—we search what God has concealed, knowing we will never exhaust it.

verseByVerse.quote: As the heavens for height, and the earth for depth, so the heart of kings is unsearchable. Take away the dross from the silver, and the smith has material for a vessel; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The heart of kings is unsearchable'—the king's inner life is as complex and hidden as the cosmos; this is a warning against presuming to know royal intentions. 'Take away the dross from the silver, and the smith has material for a vessel'—the metallurgical metaphor for refinement: what appears to be raw silver is not yet useful until the impurities are removed. The process of removing what is wrong is what makes what remains valuable and functional. Sproul: sanctification is exactly this—the Spirit's long work of removing dross to reveal the image of God.

verseByVerse.quote: take away the wicked from the presence of the king, and his throne will be established in righteousness. Do not put yourself forward in the king's presence or stand in the place of the great, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Take away the wicked from the presence of the king, and his throne will be established in righteousness'—continuing the metallurgical metaphor: removing wicked advisers from the king's court purifies the center of power. The king's throne is established not by military force alone but by the righteous counsel surrounding it. 'Do not put yourself forward in the king's presence'—the social wisdom of restraint; self-promotion in the presence of power is both tactically unwise and personally undignified. Kidner: Proverbs consistently values the person who is capable of more than he claims rather than one who claims more than he can deliver.

verseByVerse.quote: for it is better to be told, “Come up here,” than to be put lower in the presence of a noble. What your eyes have seen do not hastily bring into court, for what will you do in the end, when your neighbor puts you to shame? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'It is better to be told, Come up here'—Jesus quotes this principle directly (Luke 14:10); the wisdom of occupying a lower place and being invited upward beats claiming a higher place and being forced down. 'Do not hastily bring into court'—the wisdom of not rushing to litigation; what you witnessed may not sustain legal scrutiny once your neighbor presents his side. 'When your neighbor puts you to shame'—the public humiliation of the overconfident litigant who has brought a case prematurely. The person who sues too quickly may win the argument and lose the relationship, the reputation, and the case.

verseByVerse.quote: Argue your case with your neighbor himself, and do not reveal another's secret, lest he who hears you bring shame upon you, and your ill repute have no end. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Argue your case with your neighbor himself'—direct confrontation of the person who wronged you rather than litigation or third-party gossip. Jesus echoes this (Matt. 18:15). 'Do not reveal another's secret'—in the heat of a dispute, the temptation to expose private information about the opponent is strong; Proverbs forbids it. 'Lest he who hears you bring shame upon you'—the exposure of another's secret in court may backfire: the third party may judge you for the betrayal. 'Your ill repute have no end'—a reputation for betraying confidences is extremely difficult to recover.

verseByVerse.quote: A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in a setting of silver. Like a gold ring or an ornament of gold is a wise reprover to a listening ear. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in a setting of silver'—perhaps the most celebrated verse in Proverbs on the power of language. 'Fitly spoken'—on wheels, rolling smoothly to its destination at exactly the right moment. The image of gold apples in a silver frame: the right word at the right time is an aesthetic and moral work of art. 'Like a gold ring or an ornament of gold is a wise reprover to a listening ear'—the combination of the wise reprover and the listening ear produces something precious. Neither alone is sufficient; the gold ring needs the hand that wears it and appreciates it.

verseByVerse.quote: Like the cold of snow in the time of harvest is a faithful messenger to those who send him; he refreshes the soul of his masters. Like clouds and wind without rain is a man who boasts of a gift he does not give. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Like the cold of snow in the time of harvest is a faithful messenger'—in the heat of harvest, cold refreshment is exactly what is needed; the faithful messenger brings the relief of reliable information at the moment of greatest need. 'He refreshes the soul of his masters'—the faithful servant's fidelity is not merely practical but life-giving. 'Like clouds and wind without rain is a man who boasts of a gift he does not give'—the promising clouds that produce nothing. The person who promises generosity and delivers nothing has created expectation and then crushed it—worse than if he had promised nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: With patience a ruler may be persuaded, and a soft tongue will break a bone. If you have found honey, eat only enough for you, lest you have your fill of it and vomit it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'With patience a ruler may be persuaded, and a soft tongue will break a bone'—the paradox of persuasive power: patience and gentleness are more effective than force or urgency with those in authority. 'A soft tongue will break a bone'—the seemingly fragile instrument overcomes what seems impenetrable. 'If you have found honey, eat only enough for you, lest you have your fill of it and vomit it'—the wisdom of moderation even with good things; too much of a genuine good becomes illness. Proverbs applies this to social visits (v.17) as well: even the welcome guest becomes unwelcome if he stays too long.

verseByVerse.quote: Let your foot be seldom in your neighbor's house, lest he have his fill of you and hate you. A man who bears false witness against his neighbor is like a war club, or a sword, or a sharp arrow. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Let your foot be seldom in your neighbor's house, lest he have his fill of you and hate you'—the social wisdom of restraint: even good relationships can be exhausted by over-presence. The welcome guest becomes the unwelcome one not by doing anything wrong but by staying too long too often. 'A man who bears false witness against his neighbor is like a war club, or a sword, or a sharp arrow'—three weapons of progressive range: the club at close quarters, the sword at arm's length, the arrow at a distance. False testimony destroys at any range.

verseByVerse.quote: Trusting in a treacherous man in time of trouble is like a bad tooth or a foot that slips. Whoever sings songs to a heavy heart is like one who takes off a garment on a cold day, and like vinegar on soda. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Trusting in a treacherous man in time of trouble is like a bad tooth or a foot that slips'—the painful irony of misplaced trust: what you lean on for support fails precisely at the moment of greatest need. 'Whoever sings songs to a heavy heart is like one who takes off a garment on a cold day'—social wisdom about emotional attunement: cheerfulness offered to grief is not comfort but cruelty, like stripping warmth from someone who is already cold. 'Like vinegar on soda'—a chemical reaction: the wrong thing at the wrong moment produces an explosive, unpleasant result.

verseByVerse.quote: If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink, for you will heap burning coals on his head, and the LORD will reward you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat'—one of the most radical social commands in Proverbs. The enemy's need is not an opportunity for withholding but for giving. 'You will heap burning coals on his head'—the most debated image in Proverbs. Ancient Egyptian penitential ritual may be the background: carrying coals on the head was a sign of remorse. Kindness to enemies produces shame in them—the kind of shame that leads to repentance. 'The LORD will reward you'—ultimate motivation: not the enemy's response but the divine response. Paul quotes this in Romans 12:20 as the summary of Christian social ethics.

verseByVerse.quote: The north wind brings forth rain, and a backbiting tongue, angry looks. It is better to live in a corner of the housetop than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The north wind brings forth rain, and a backbiting tongue, angry looks'—just as the north wind reliably produces rain, the backbiting tongue reliably produces the anger it conceals. There is an inevitability to the consequences of slander. 'It is better to live in a corner of the housetop than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife'—the third occurrence of this domestic proverb (cf. 21:9,19); the repetition suggests it was a particularly memorable and widely applicable piece of wisdom. The message is the same: relational peace outweighs material comfort.

verseByVerse.quote: Like cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country. Like a muddied spring or a polluted fountain is a righteous man who gives way before the wicked. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Like cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country'—water to the dehydrated is one of Proverbs' most powerful analogies for the impact of news from distant loved ones. 'Like a muddied spring or a polluted fountain is a righteous man who gives way before the wicked'—the righteous person who compromises under pressure is like a spring that has been stirred up and made useless. His righteousness was a source of life; when he yields, that source is polluted. Sproul: the righteous person who compromises does not merely fail personally—he renders himself useless as a source of the life his community needed from him.

verseByVerse.quote: It is not good to eat much honey, nor is it glorious to seek one's own glory. A man without self-control is like a city broken into and left without walls. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'It is not good to eat much honey, nor is it glorious to seek one's own glory'—the parallel extends the honey-moderation lesson to the social domain: just as too much honey is not good physically, too much self-promotion is not good socially. 'A man without self-control is like a city broken into and left without walls'—one of Proverbs' most memorable images of vulnerability. Without walls, the city is indefensible; without self-control, the person is open to every temptation and enemy. Keller: the most unprotected person in the world is not the person with few resources but the person with no self-mastery.

25.theology:
The Theology of Speech. Proverbs 25 presents speech as one of the central moral acts of human existence. The fitly spoken word (v.11), the faithful messenger (v.13), the soft tongue (v.15), the inappropriate song (v.20) — each is a form of power, either rightly or wrongly exercised. The New Testament elevates this: the Word became flesh (John 1:14), and the Spirit is given to fill our speech with wisdom. Speech is not merely communication; it is the primary medium of love and harm.

Cruciform Ethics. Verses 21–22 anticipate the Sermon on the Mount and Romans 12. Proverbs is not merely a book of prudential advice; it contains an ethics of enemy-love rooted in God's own character. The LORD rewards the one who feeds the enemy (v.22b), confirming that this is not merely clever strategy but a reflection of divine generosity — a God who causes his sun to rise on evil and good alike (Matt. 5:45).
25.examples:
Then: The Hezekiah scribal collection reflects a royal court that valued the art of persuasion and the discipline of speech. Ambassadors, advisors, and court officials lived or died by their words. The apples-of-gold image (v.11) suggests the aesthetic dimensions of wisdom that Israelite court culture cultivated. Verse 25's "good news from a far country" may have evoked the joy of a merchant's return or a military dispatch — news that changed everything.

Now: The pastoral word of verse 20 indicts the relentless positivity that refuses to make room for grief. Grief communities, cancer wards, and counseling rooms require the wisdom to be quiet when songs are wrong and to speak when silence has run its course. Verses 21–22 have a direct application in the age of social media retaliation and culture-war contempt: feeding the enemy is not weakness but the most subversive act available to the Christian. It reclaims the narrative from the logic of revenge.

26.title: Like a Dog Returns to Its Vomit
26.text: <sup>1</sup>Like snow in summer or rain in harvest, so honor is not fitting for a fool. <sup>2</sup>Like a sparrow in its flitting, like a swallow in its flying, a curse that is causeless does not alight. <sup>4</sup>Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest you be like him yourself. <sup>5</sup>Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes. <sup>11</sup>Like a dog that returns to its vomit is a fool who repeats his folly. <sup>12</sup>Do you see a man who is wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him. <sup>13</sup>The sluggard says, "There is a lion in the road! There is a lion in the streets!" <sup>17</sup>Whoever meddles in a quarrel not his own is like one who takes a passing dog by the ears. <sup>20</sup>For lack of wood the fire goes out, and where there is no whisperer, quarreling ceases. <sup>26</sup>though his hatred be covered with deception, his wickedness will be exposed in the assembly. <sup>28</sup>A lying tongue hates its victims, and a flattering mouth works ruin.
26.overview:
Chapter 26 is Proverbs' extended anatomy of foolishness, containing the book's most sustained portrait of three types: the fool (vv.1–12), the sluggard (vv.13–16), and the quarrelsome gossip (vv.17–28). It is the longest concentrated treatment of folly in the Bible, and it is written with a sharp, almost satirical wit.

The famous contradiction of verses 4–5 — "Answer not a fool... Answer a fool" — is deliberate. It is not an error but wisdom's acknowledgment that no single rule fits every case. Sometimes engaging a fool drags you down to his level; sometimes silence leaves him unchallenged in his self-delusion. The wise person reads the situation and responds accordingly. This is wisdom's practical epistemology: principles must be applied with judgment, not mechanical rule-following.

The chapter closes with the liar and flatterer (vv.23–28) — people whose words are weapons disguised as gifts. The hidden hatred will eventually be exposed (v.26). Proverbs consistently returns to this: truth is the ultimate victor because God, who is truth, governs history.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 26 — The Fool's Portrait Gallery and the Whisperer's Destruction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 26 is the most sustained satire in Proverbs: the first twelve verses are an extended portrait of the fool, using some of the most vivid comparisons in the book (snow in summer, a fluttering sparrow, a dog returning to its vomit). Then comes the sluggard (vv.13-16) and finally the quarrelsome, slanderous, deceptive person (vv.17-28). The chapter is a literary tour de force of negative wisdom—wisdom taught by negative example.
verseByVerse.theology: The apparent contradiction of vv.4-5 ('Do not answer a fool... Answer a fool...') is intentional: wisdom is not a formula but a judgment. Sometimes engaging a fool dignifies him; sometimes leaving him unanswered lets him appear wise. The wise person must read the situation and choose which danger is greater. No rule replaces discernment.
verseByVerse.examples: The dog returning to its vomit (v.11) is one of Scripture's most shocking images—Peter quotes it in 2 Peter 2:22 about those who return to false teaching after escaping it. The fool who repeats his folly is not just foolish but compulsively, self-destructively foolish. The image is meant to produce revulsion: do you really want to be that?

verseByVerse.quote: Like snow in summer or rain in harvest, so honor is not fitting for a fool. Like a fluttering sparrow or a darting swallow, a curse without cause does not alight. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Like snow in summer or rain in harvest, so honor is not fitting for a fool'—the incongruity is the point: snow in summer and rain at harvest are not merely unusual but actively harmful. So honor given to a fool damages the social fabric that honor is meant to reinforce. 'A curse without cause does not alight'—one of Proverbs' most pastorally comforting statements: groundless curses are ineffective. The person who fears being cursed by enemies can rest; a curse without moral warrant is like a bird that cannot land. Waltke: the cosmos itself is structured so that unjust speech cannot ultimately reach its target.

verseByVerse.quote: A whip for the horse, a bridle for the donkey, and a rod for the back of fools. Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest you be like him yourself. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A whip for the horse, a bridle for the donkey, and a rod for the back of fools'—each creature requires the appropriate correction suited to its nature; the fool requires external correction because he cannot self-correct. 'Answer not a fool according to his folly'—the first answer to the two-proverb paradox: sometimes engagement is wrong because stooping to the fool's level makes you foolish. Kidner: the wisdom of walking away from certain arguments is not cowardice but discernment. Not every challenge deserves a response.

verseByVerse.quote: Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes. Whoever sends a message by the hand of a fool cuts off his own feet and drinks violence. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes'—the second answer: sometimes silence lets the fool's error stand unchallenged and he becomes more entrenched. The wise person reads the situation and chooses. Sproul: discernment is the ability to know which wisdom applies when; both proverbs are true, and knowing when to apply each is itself the wisdom. 'Whoever sends a message by the hand of a fool cuts off his own feet'—entrusting important communication to an unreliable person is self-harm; the fool will distort, lose, or botch the message.

verseByVerse.quote: Like a lame man's legs, which hang useless, is a proverb in the mouth of fools. Like one who binds the stone in the sling is one who gives honor to a fool. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Like a lame man's legs, which hang useless, is a proverb in the mouth of fools'—wisdom in the mouth of someone who cannot live it is like limbs that cannot function: the form is there but not the capacity. The fool can quote Proverbs without being shaped by them. 'Like one who binds the stone in the sling is one who gives honor to a fool'—the stone bound in the sling cannot be flung; it defeats the purpose of the weapon. Honoring a fool similarly defeats the purpose of honor: it cannot do its work of reinforcing and rewarding virtue when given to someone without it.

verseByVerse.quote: Like a thorn that goes up into the hand of a drunkard is a proverb in the mouth of fools. Like an archer who wounds everyone is one who hires a passing fool or drunkard. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Like a thorn that goes up into the hand of a drunkard is a proverb in the mouth of fools'—the thorn in the drunkard's hand is dangerous not to others so much as to himself, because he cannot feel the damage. The fool's proverb wounds without the fool being aware of the wounding he is doing. 'Like an archer who wounds everyone is one who hires a passing fool or drunkard'—the random incompetence of the hired fool hits everyone indiscriminately; the person who staffs key positions with unreliable people exposes his whole community to the damage of that unreliability.

verseByVerse.quote: Like a dog that returns to his vomit is a fool who repeats his folly. Do you see a man who is wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Like a dog that returns to his vomit is a fool who repeats his folly'—one of the most viscerally shocking comparisons in Proverbs, used by Peter (2 Pet. 2:22) to describe apostates who return to corruption. The disgust is intentional: do you want to be this? The repeated return to folly is not just weakness but compulsion—the fool cannot stop. 'There is more hope for a fool than for him'—the person who is wise in his own eyes has a worse prognosis than the acknowledged fool, because self-awareness is at least the beginning of the possibility of change.

verseByVerse.quote: The sluggard says, “There is a lion in the road! There is a lion in the streets!” As a door turns on its hinges, so does a sluggard on his bed. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The sluggard's excuse-making continues: now the lion is not just outside (22:13) but specifically in the road and the streets—he has refined his alibi. The escalation is comic. 'As a door turns on its hinges, so does a sluggard on his bed'—the door is attached to its hinges; the sluggard is attached to his bed. Both make motion—the door swings, the sluggard rolls—but neither goes anywhere. The movement is circular and produces nothing. Kidner: the sluggard is not idle in any simple sense; he is very busy doing nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: The sluggard buries his hand in the dish; it wears him out to bring it back to his mouth. The sluggard is wiser in his own eyes than seven men who can answer sensibly. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The sluggard buries his hand in the dish; it wears him out to bring it back to his mouth'—the ultimate in comic laziness: he has gotten as far as the food and cannot complete the motion. The effort of eating exhausts him. 'The sluggard is wiser in his own eyes than seven men who can answer sensibly'—seven represents completeness; the sluggard thinks himself wiser than a full council of wise men. Self-deception has produced utter incompetence combined with absolute confidence. Waltke: the sluggard's defining characteristic is not his laziness but his self-justification of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever meddles in a quarrel not his own is like one who takes a passing dog by the ears. Like a madman who throws firebrands, arrows, and death (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever meddles in a quarrel not his own is like one who takes a passing dog by the ears'—you cannot let go, and you cannot hold on safely. The meddler has inserted himself into a situation he cannot control and cannot exit without harm. 'Like a madman who throws firebrands, arrows, and death'—the image of the madman who throws weapons: dangerous, erratic, unpredictable. Both the meddler and the madman cause damage not from malice but from incompetent and unauthorized involvement in affairs that require more skill than they possess.

verseByVerse.quote: is the man who deceives his neighbor and says, “I am only joking!” For lack of wood the fire goes out, and where there is no whisperer, quarreling ceases. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I am only joking!'—the most cowardly retreat from a deliberately harmful act: deception dressed as humor. Proverbs refuses to accept this excuse; the harm done is real regardless of the claimed intent. 'For lack of wood the fire goes out, and where there is no whisperer, quarreling ceases'—one of Proverbs' most practically useful proverbs for community management: conflict does not sustain itself without fuel. The whisperer is the fuel. Remove the gossiper and the fire goes out. This is the logic of church discipline (cf. Titus 3:10): removing the divisive person is an act of community health, not punishment.

verseByVerse.quote: As charcoal to hot embers and wood to fire, so is a quarrelsome man for kindling strife. The words of a whisperer are like delicious morsels; they go down into the inner parts of the body. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'As charcoal to hot embers and wood to fire, so is a quarrelsome man for kindling strife'—the quarrelsome person is a pyromaniac of social relations; he brings fuel to every situation. 'The words of a whisperer are like delicious morsels'—repeated from 18:8 verbatim; the double occurrence underscores how deep the appeal of gossip runs. It feels satisfying to hear and repeat; the 'delicious' quality is the danger. 'They go down into the inner parts of the body'—once received, they cannot be unheard. The damage is interior, below the surface, permanent.

verseByVerse.quote: Like the glaze covering an earthen vessel are fervent lips with an evil heart. Whoever hates disguises himself with his lips and harbors deceit in his heart; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Like the glaze covering an earthen vessel are fervent lips with an evil heart'—the glaze makes cheap clay look like precious metal; fervent speech makes an evil heart look like a good one. The deception is in the coating, not the substance. 'Whoever hates disguises himself with his lips and harbors deceit in his heart'—the two-level structure of the hypocrite: surface speech (lips) and inner life (heart) are moving in opposite directions. Waltke: this is the most dangerous form of social evil—not the open enemy but the smiling betrayer.

verseByVerse.quote: when he speaks graciously, believe him not, for there are seven abominations in his heart; though his hatred be covered with deception, his wickedness will be exposed in the assembly. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'When he speaks graciously, believe him not'—the warning against being taken in by the very charm that makes the hypocrite dangerous. Gracious speech from a known deceiver should increase, not decrease, vigilance. 'Seven abominations in his heart'—seven as fullness: his inner life is completely given over to what God finds revolting. 'His wickedness will be exposed in the assembly'—the temporal comfort: exposure is coming. Hidden evil does not stay hidden permanently. The assembly is both the civic gathering (law court) and the eschatological gathering before God.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, and a stone will come back on him who starts it rolling. A lying tongue hates its victims, and a flattering mouth works ruin. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, and a stone will come back on him who starts it rolling'—the boomerang principle of malicious scheming: the trap set for others catches the schemer; the rolling stone of destruction returns to crush its initiator. 'A lying tongue hates its victims'—lying is not merely instrumental but expressive of contempt for the person being deceived. 'A flattering mouth works ruin'—the closing summary: flattery appears harmless or even pleasant but is a form of destruction. Kidner: chapter 26 ends where it began—with the folly that is incongruous, self-defeating, and ultimately destructive.

26.theology:
The Anatomy of Folly. Chapter 26 shows that folly is not a single trait but a complex of related failures: the misallocation of honor (vv.1–3), the inability to learn (v.11), the closed-loop self-confidence (v.12), the laziness that rationalizes itself (vv.13–16), and the tongue used as weapon (vv.17–28). These are not unrelated vices but expressions of the one root: life lived as if God does not exist, with the self as the final reference point. Keller's insight is that the fool is the secularist — not necessarily the atheist, but the one who functionally excludes God from practical decisions.

Self-Deception and Grace. The man wise in his own eyes (v.12) is the hardest case because he is impervious to correction. The gospel's answer is not better argument but encounter with the living God — the experience that brought Isaiah to his knees ("Woe is me!") and Paul to the Damascus road. Conversion is the radical undoing of self-deception, and it is entirely a work of grace.
26.examples:
Then: Court politics made the sluggard (vv.13–16) a recognizable type — the official who invented elaborate reasons for inaction. The whisperer (v.20) operated in every ancient institution, and Proverbs knew that political conflict was usually sustained by informers and gossips, not by genuine grievances alone. The honor-for-fools warning (v.1) addressed a patronage culture where rulers could elevate incompetent favorites with destructive results.

Now: The social media age has made the man wise in his own eyes (v.12) ubiquitous — the confident amateur whose Dunning-Kruger blindness is now amplified to thousands. Verse 20 is a direct diagnosis of online conflict: Twitter feuds, church splits, and family estrangements are almost always sustained by whisperers adding wood. The vv.4–5 tension about answering the fool is the daily dilemma of anyone with a public platform: engaging every foolish take validates it; ignoring every challenge abandons truth. Wisdom, not a rule, is required.

27.title: Do Not Boast About Tomorrow
27.text: <sup>1</sup>Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring. <sup>2</sup>Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips. <sup>5</sup>Better is open rebuke than hidden love. <sup>6</sup>Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of a flatterer. <sup>9</sup>Oil and perfume make the heart glad, and the sweetness of a friend comes from his earnest counsel. <sup>12</sup>The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it. <sup>17</sup>Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another. <sup>19</sup>As in water face reflects face, so the heart of man reflects the man. <sup>20</sup>Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied, and never satisfied are the eyes of man. <sup>21</sup>The crucible is for silver, and the furnace is for gold, and a man is tested by his praise. <sup>23</sup>Know well the condition of your flocks, and give attention to your herds, <sup>27</sup>There will be enough goats' milk for your food, for the food of your household and maintenance for your girls.
27.overview:
Chapter 27 is one of Proverbs' warmest chapters, centering on the gifts of genuine friendship (vv.5–10, 17) while bookending with humility about the future (v.1) and the discipline of faithful work (vv.23–27). The famous verse — "Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another" (v.17) — is embedded in a larger account of what makes friendship transformative rather than merely pleasant.

The chapter distinguishes sharply between the flatterer and the faithful friend. Flattery gives kisses; friendship gives wounds. The wound of a friend is painful but constructive — it is love that refuses to leave you in your blind spots. The flatterer's kisses are pleasant but corrosive, feeding the self-deception that Proverbs constantly diagnoses as the root of folly.

The closing pastoral image (vv.23–27) is often overlooked: the wise man tends his flocks attentively, knowing that wealth is temporary and natural abundance cycles. This is wisdom applied to economics — attention, stewardship, patience. It is a far cry from the "riches sprout wings" speculation of the fool.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 27 — Friendship, Flattery, Faithful Wounds, and the Uncertain Future
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 27 is one of the most relationally rich chapters in Proverbs: the faithful wounds of a friend (v.6), the sweetness of earnest counsel (v.9), iron sharpening iron (v.17), and the heart satisfied by being known (v.19). The chapter also addresses boasting about the future (v.1), the contentious wife (v.15), and closes with a meditation on the diligent shepherd who knows his flocks.
verseByVerse.theology: The friend who wounds faithfully (v.6) versus the enemy who kisses abundantly is one of the most searching relational distinctions in the book. True friendship is willing to cause pain for the sake of the friend's good; false friendship maximizes pleasant feelings at the expense of honest engagement. The church needs more people who can give and receive faithful wounds.
verseByVerse.examples: Iron sharpening iron (v.17) has become one of Proverbs' most quoted metaphors for community: people form each other, the pressure of genuine relationship produces the friction that sharpens. But the metaphor is not only positive—friction implies contact, resistance, sometimes sparks. True community is not comfortable; it is formative.
